The first portion ('For attractive lips... helping hand at the end of each of your arms') is Sam Levenson's poem 'Time Tested Beauty Tips,' written for his newborn grandchild and published in his 1973 book. Hepburn reportedly read it aloud to her sons at Christmas near the end of her life, which is how her name became attached; her son Sean Hepburn Ferrer has publicly credited Levenson. The later sentences here ('The beauty of a woman is not in the clothes she wears...') are a separate accretion from anonymous chain-letter circulation and are not Levenson's either. This text is a composite, and the Hepburn credit is wrong. | Suggested reattribution: Sam Levenson (first portion); remainder anonymous

author: Ayya Khema
text: Mindfulness is not just a word or a discourse by the Buddha, but a meaningful state of mind. It means we have to be here now, in this very moment, and we have to know what is happening internally and externally. It means being alert to our motives and learning to change unwholesome thoughts and emotions into wholesome ones. Mindfulness is a mental activity that in due course eliminates all suffering.
keywords: mindfulness; present; internal; external; within; motives; learning; change; thoughts; emotions; transform; wholesome; suffering; freedom; buddha; mind; presence
notes: Ayya Khema (1923-1997), the German-born Theravada nun who wrote 'Being Nobody, Going Nowhere,' is a plausible author: the vocabulary (wholesome/unwholesome, mindfulness as a state rather than a discourse) matches her teaching idiom closely. But I cannot place this passage in a specific book or dhamma talk, and much of her published material is transcribed talks, which makes exact sourcing hard. Attribution is credible but unverified.

author: Babe Ruth
text: The way a team plays as a whole determines its success. You may have the greatest bunch of individual stars in the world, but if they don't play together, the club won't be worth a dime.
notes: Consistently attributed to Babe Ruth across sports-quote collections, but I know of no primary source: no interview, autobiography passage, or contemporary newspaper citation I can name. Ruth is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphorisms about teamwork and perseverance. Plausible but unsourced.

author: Banksy
text: Art should comfort the disturbed and disturb the comfortable.
notes: The formula long predates Banksy. Its ancestor is Finley Peter Dunne's 1902 Mr. Dooley line about the newspaper that 'comforts th' afflicted, and afflicts th' comfortable,' which was subsequently applied to journalism generally and then adapted to art. The art-specific phrasing is most often credited to the artist and educator Cesar A. Cruz. Banksy is a magnet for unsourced art aphorisms and I know of no place in 'Wall and Piece' or in his documented statements where he claims this line. Reattribution offered with the caveat that the Cruz credit is itself weakly sourced. | Suggested reattribution: Cesar A. Cruz (art phrasing); formula ultimately from Finley Peter Dunne, 1902

author: Barbara Rose
text: Even the most daring and accomplished people have undergone tremendous difficulty. In fact, the more successful they became, the more they attributed their success to the lessons learned during their most difficult times. Adversity is our teacher. When we view adversity as a guide towards greater inner growth, we will then learn to accept the wisdom our soul came into this life to learn.
keywords: difficulties; challenges; growth; life; wisdom; soul
notes: Barbara Rose is a contemporary self-help/spirituality author ('Individual Power,' 'If God Was Like Man'). The passage matches her register, and the attribution is consistent across the inspirational-quote ecosystem, but I cannot locate it in a specific title from training knowledge. Note also the name collision with Barbara Rose the art historian, which makes aggregator attributions less reliable than they look.

author: Barbara Rose
text: No matter what difficulty you are facing, it is coming from Divine Light to bring you to a higher place within. Write down every conceivable reason that this situation can contribute towards your growth. Write down every way this experience can possibly set the stage for serving to uplift others. When you are complete, and have come to the other side of this experience, you will then know 'why' it happened.
notes: Same situation as the other Barbara Rose entry in this batch: register and attribution are consistent with her published self-help writing, and the exercise-style prompts suggest a book or newsletter with a workbook element, but I cannot name the source. No independent evidence beyond quote-site repetition.

author: Barbara Sher
text: All the people we call ‘geniuses’ are men and women who somehow escaped having to put that curious, wondering child in themselves to sleep.
keywords: genius; people; curiosity; child; sleep; escape; wonder; artist
notes: Barbara Sher is very likely the real author; this is one of her signature ideas and the phrasing matches her voice. My recollection points to 'Wishcraft: How to Get What You Really Want' (1979, with Annie Gottlieb) as the probable source, but I cannot confirm that with enough certainty to record it as a citation, so I am leaving the print-source field null rather than guessing. Attribution credible, source unconfirmed.

author: Barry Brailsford
text: When we see ourselves as greater than others, when we place humankind above other creatures, above and beyond the realms of the birds and the fishes, outside the world of stone and the colors, we give away our power. Only when we see we are part of everything, joined to creation, bound to all the realms and integrated into the web of life, do we begin to call on our full potential.
keywords: see; perception; unity; oneness; animals; birds; fish; power; creation; womb; life; potential; connection; web; self
notes: Barry Brailsford is a New Zealand author and storyteller associated with Waitaha and Maori traditions ('Song of Waitaha,' 'Wisdom of the Four Winds'). The content is consistent with his body of work, but I cannot place the passage in a specific book. Worth flagging separately that Brailsford's Waitaha material is itself contested by some Maori scholars regarding its provenance as traditional knowledge, which is a sourcing concern beyond the quote attribution.

author: Barry LePartner
text: Good judgment comes from experience, and experience comes from bad judgment.
notes: Two problems. First, the author name is misspelled: the person usually credited is Barry LePatner, a New York construction attorney. Second, and more important, the aphorism substantially predates him. Versions of 'good judgment comes from experience, and experience comes from bad judgment' circulated in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and have been variously attributed to Will Rogers, Mark Twain, Rita Mae Brown, Jim Horning, and an anonymous cowboy or Persian proverb. It is a floating saying with no established originator; the LePatner credit appears to be a modern quote-book convention. I cannot name the true source, so no reattribution is offered.

author: Ben Irwin
text: Most of us spend our lives as if we have another one in the bank.
notes: I cannot identify this Ben Irwin or place this line in any published work. The name is common enough (a contemporary author writing on faith, among others) that the attribution cannot be pinned to a specific person with confidence. The line reads like an anonymous aphorism that acquired a name in circulation. Honest answer: unknown.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: The Constitution only gives people the right to pursue happiness. You have to catch it yourself.
notes: No source in Franklin's writings, letters, or almanacs. The internal evidence argues against him outright: the right to pursue happiness appears in the Declaration of Independence, not the Constitution, and Franklin, a signer of both, would be an unlikely person to confuse them. The line reads as a 20th-century American aphorism retrofitted onto Franklin, who is one of the heaviest misattribution magnets in the corpus alongside Twain and Lincoln. I cannot identify an actual originator, hence apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

author: Bennett W. Goodspeed
text: The difference between a comedy and a tragedy is that in a comedy the characters figure out reality in time to do something about it.
notes: Bennett W. Goodspeed was an investment writer best known for 'The Tao Jones Averages: A Guide to Whole-Brained Investing' (1983), a book built around exactly this kind of right-brain/left-brain aphorism, and my recollection associates the line with him. I cannot confirm the book or page with enough certainty to record a citation, so the print-source field stays null. Attribution plausible, source unconfirmed.

author: Bernie Siegel
text: I don’t think God cares where we were graduated or what we did for a living. God wants to know who we are. Discovering this is the work of the soul – it is our true life’s work.
keywords: work; god; career; being; self; discover; soul; life
notes: Bernie Siegel, the surgeon and author of 'Love, Medicine and Miracles' (1986) and 'Peace, Love and Healing,' is a plausible author and the sentiment is squarely within his body of work. I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and Siegel's material is heavily excerpted in devotional anthologies without citation, which is how unsourced attributions to him propagate. Credible but unverified.

author: Bertrand Russell
text: The biggest cause of trouble in the world today is that the stupid people are so sure about things and the intelligent folks are so full of doubts.
keywords: stupidity; doubt; intelligence; world; trouble; difficulty
notes: The idea is genuinely Russell's but this exact wording is not sourced. The documented original is from his 1933 essay 'The Triumph of Stupidity': 'The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt.' Several loose paraphrases circulate, including the popular 'the whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts,' which Wikiquote carries as unsourced. The text here ('the biggest cause of trouble... stupid people... intelligent folks') is another such variant, with an American register that does not sound like Russell. Recommend replacing with the sourced 1933 wording if this quote is wanted in the corpus.

author: Betty Eadie
text: If our ego is to know spirit, we must make the first move. Spirit does not come down and knock on our door. It sits waiting for us to acknowledge it. We must want to change and take the initiative and persevere. The love of spirit will embrace us. But we must take the first steps. In what areas of your life are you ready for change? What step can you take to open the door to new possibilities? It starts with you. Faith is not complacent; faith is action. You don’t have faith and wait. When you have faith, you move."
keywords: faith; movement; ego; spirit; knock; door; sit; wait; acknowledgment; change; initiative; perseverance; love; embrace; step; life; possibilities; self; action
notes: Betty Eadie is the author of 'Embraced by the Light' (1992) and 'The Awakening Heart.' The passage's shift into second-person reflective prompts mid-paragraph suggests a devotional or workbook context rather than her narrative memoir, and it may be a compiler's stitching of separate lines. I cannot place it in a specific title. Also note the stray closing double-quote at the end of the text, which should be cleaned before publication.

author: Betty Reese
text: If you think you’re too small to be effective, you’ve never been in bed with a mosquito.
notes: The Betty Reese credit is the conventional one in quote books from roughly the 1980s onward, where she is usually identified only as an American public relations executive — an unusually thin biographical trail for an attribution. The mosquito image belongs to a larger family of sayings, including the widely circulated 'if you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito,' which is variously credited to the Dalai Lama and to an African proverb, none of them with a solid primary source. Attribution exists but is weak.

author: Bill Cosby
text: I don't know the key to success, but the key to failure is to try to please everyone.
notes: Consistently and long attributed to Bill Cosby, who is generally reported to have said it in interviews; the attribution is stable and I am not aware of any competing claimant or earlier appearance, which is why this sits above the pure-unverified tier. But I cannot name the interview, book, or date, so it falls short of the 0.80 promotion bar. Separate from provenance, the corpus owner may want to consider whether Cosby attributions belong in an inspirational collection at all.

author: Bill Gates
text: As we look ahead into the next century, leaders will be those who empower others.
notes: Ubiquitous in leadership training material and consistently credited to Gates, usually with a vague pointer to a late-1990s speech, but I cannot name the occasion or a printed text. The 'next century' framing places the origin plausibly in the 1990s, which is consistent with the attribution without confirming it. Widely repeated is not the same as sourced.

author: Billie Holiday
text: You can be up to your boobies in white satin, with gardenias in your hair and no sugar cane for miles, but you can still be working on a plantation.
earliest_print_source: Lady Sings the Blues, Billie Holiday with William Dufty, 1956 (as commonly cited; I cannot confirm the page)
notes: My recollection places this line in Holiday's autobiography 'Lady Sings the Blues,' and the imagery — white satin, gardenias, the plantation — is characteristic of that book's account of touring as a Black singer with white bands. Two caveats keep it below the promotion bar: I cannot confirm the page or chapter, and the book was ghostwritten by William Dufty, with scholars (notably Farah Jasmine Griffin and John Szwed) documenting that substantial parts of it are unreliable or not in Holiday's own words. The sentiment is authentically hers; the exact authorship of the sentence is shared with Dufty.

author: Black Elk
text: Everything sacred moves in a Circle.
notes: The circle teaching is authentically Black Elk's, but this terse six-word phrasing does not match the known texts. The famous passage in 'Black Elk Speaks' (John G. Neihardt, 1932) runs 'Everything the Power of the World does is done in a circle,' continuing through the round sky, the round sun and moon, and the whirling wind; 'The Sacred Pipe' (Joseph Epes Brown, 1953) develops the same idea. 'Everything sacred moves in a Circle' appears to be a condensation that circulates without a source. Additional caveat: both books are non-Lakota interlocutors' renderings of Black Elk's words, so even the canonical wordings are mediated. Recommend replacing with the sourced Neihardt line if this idea is wanted.

author: Brian Greene
text: The boldness of asking deep questions may require unforeseen flexibility if we are to accept the answers.
notes: Consistent with Brian Greene's voice and subject matter, and I recall it circulating from 'The Elegant Universe' (1999), in the discussion of how relativity forces us to give up intuitions about space and time. I cannot place the chapter or page with enough certainty to cite it, so the print source is left null rather than guessed. No competing attribution exists, which supports the author even without a located source.

author: Brian Tracy
text: The way you respond to disappointment is usually an accurate predictor of how likely you are to achieve great success. If you respond to disappointment by learning the very most from it, and then by putting it behind you, and then pressing forward, you are very likely to accomplish great things in the course of your life.
keywords: disappointment; success; perseverance; learning; accomplish; great; life; prediction; work
notes: Brian Tracy is a real motivational author whose seminars and books (e.g. 'Maximum Achievement', 'Goals!') repeat this theme, and the attribution is consistent across quote aggregators. But the passage reads like transcribed seminar speech and I cannot place it in a specific book, article, or recorded talk. Plausible but unsourced; no competing attribution.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Your success in life will be in direct proportion to what you do after you do what you’re expected to do.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Brian Tracy across quote collections and his own promotional material, with no rival claimant I know of. However the maxim belongs to a large family of older success-literature sayings about 'going the extra mile' (Napoleon Hill and Elbert Hubbard both worked this ground), so an earlier ancestor is possible. No specific book or talk locatable.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Always give without remembering and receive without forgetting.
notes: The line is much older than Brian Tracy. The known original is Elizabeth Bibesco (1897-1945, daughter of H. H. Asquith): 'Blessed are those who can give without remembering and take without forgetting.' It appears in her posthumous collection 'Haven' (1951) and is standardly attributed to her. Tracy and other motivational speakers quote it, which is how his name became attached. I am confident about Bibesco as the source of the saying but am not citing a page, so the print field is null. | Suggested reattribution: Elizabeth Bibesco

author: Bruce Lee
text: Life is about change, but growth is optional.
notes: I cannot place this in any authenticated Bruce Lee material ('Tao of Jeet Kune Do', 'Striking Thoughts', 'Artist of Life', or the interview record). It reads as a reworded version of the well-known aphorism 'Change is inevitable; growth is optional,' which is generally attributed to John C. Maxwell. Because the wording here differs materially and I cannot confirm the derivation chain, I am not asserting a reattribution. Bruce Lee is a moderate misattribution magnet: his notebooks copied maxims from mid-century self-help writers, and quote sites then credit him for them.

author: Bruce Lee
text: Don't get set into one form, adapt it and build your own, and let it grow, be like water.
keywords: build; growth; transformation; self; water; form
notes: Genuinely Bruce Lee in substance. The 'be like water' teaching is documented on film in two 1971 sources: the Pierre Berton Show interview (December 1971) and the Longstreet episode 'The Way of the Intercepting Fist,' which carries the famous 'Be water, my friend.' The exact sentence quoted here appears to be a compressed/merged rendering of that spoken material rather than a verbatim line from a single source, so I am withholding a specific citation. Author attribution is safe; wording is approximate.

author: Bruce Lee
text: What is defeat? Nothing but education; nothing but the first step to something better.
notes: This is Wendell Phillips, the American abolitionist orator: 'What is defeat? Nothing but education, nothing but the first step to something better.' It is a well-established Phillips line from his mid-19th-century speeches and appears in standard quotation dictionaries under his name. Bruce Lee transcribed passages from other writers into his personal notebooks, and posthumous compilations plus quote sites have credited several such borrowings to him. Confident in Phillips as the originator. | Suggested reattribution: Wendell Phillips

author: Bruce Lee
text: Keep your mind on the things you want and off those you don't.
notes: Circulates under Bruce Lee's name but I cannot place it in his authenticated writings, and the phrasing is pure mid-century American positive-thinking literature (Napoleon Hill / Norman Vincent Peale register). Lee read and copied from those authors, so this may be another borrowed maxim recorded in his notebooks. I do not have a specific prior source, so no reattribution is asserted.

author: Bruce Lee
text: Mistakes are always forgivable, if one has the courage to admit them.
notes: Among the better-supported Bruce Lee lines. I recall it from his own written notes as collected in the John Little-edited volumes, most likely 'Striking Thoughts: Bruce Lee's Wisdom for Daily Living' (2000). I am confident enough in Lee's authorship to call it attributed, but not confident enough about the exact volume and page to enter a print citation, so that field is null.

author: Bruce Lee
text: The successful person is the average person with laser-like focus.
notes: The widely circulated form is 'The successful warrior is the average man, with laser-like focus'; this entry is a de-gendered variant of that. I cannot locate either form in Bruce Lee's authenticated writings or interviews, and 'laser-like focus' is a late-20th-century business-motivation idiom rather than Lee's vocabulary. Probably a modern coinage that acquired his name. No alternative originator known.

author: Bruno Gröning
text: Is there a principle, which can form the basis for one's whole life? Yes. Love for your fellow human beings.
notes: Bruno Gröning (1906-1959) was a German faith healer, and this sentiment matches the teaching material published by the Bruno Gröning Circle of Friends, which is essentially the only body that transmits his sayings. That transmission is devotional and post-hoc rather than documentary, and I know of no contemporaneous published text or recording I could point to for this line. The attribution is plausible within that tradition but unverifiable from what I know.

author: Buckminster Fuller
text: A designer is an emerging synthesis of artist, inventor, mechanic, objective economist, and evolutionary strategist.
notes: Authentic Fuller vocabulary and syntax; in his own usage the subject is 'the comprehensive designer,' described as an emerging synthesis of artist, inventor, mechanic, objective economist and evolutionary strategist. My recall places it in 'Ideas and Integrities: A Spontaneous Autobiographical Disclosure' (1963), where the comprehensive designer is his central figure, but I am not certain enough to enter that as the citation. Author attribution is solid; the quoted version has been trimmed from 'comprehensive designer' to 'designer.'

author: Buddhist saying
text: Thought manifests as the word. Word manifests as the deed. Deeds form into habit. Habit hardens character.
notes: Not canonical Buddhism. This is a member of the 'watch your thoughts, they become words' family of sayings, which has been variously credited to the Buddha, Lao Tzu, Gandhi, and Margaret Thatcher, and whose traceable modern ancestors are the 'sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny' formula (attributed in the 19th century to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles) and a 1977 newspaper version credited to Frank Outlaw. None of these is Buddhist. I cannot identify which specific link in that chain produced this wording, so no reattribution is asserted.

author: Buddhist saying
text: If we could see the miracle of a single flower clearly, our whole life would change.
notes: Not canonical. My recall places this in Jack Kornfield's 'Buddha's Little Instruction Book' (1994), a collection of Kornfield's own modern distillations written in the Buddha's voice, which is the documented origin of a whole cluster of pseudo-Buddha quotes now in circulation. The generic label 'Buddhist saying' is not false in spirit, but the line is a contemporary Western teacher's composition rather than a traditional saying. Reattribution offered with moderate rather than high confidence. | Suggested reattribution: Jack Kornfield

author: Buddhist saying, paraphrasing the Kalama Sutta
text: Believe nothing because a wise man said it. Believe nothing because it is generally held true. Believe nothing because it is written. Believe nothing because it is said to be divine. Believe nothing because someone else believes it. But believe only what you yourself judge to be true.
notes: The input's own label is the honest one: this is a paraphrase, not a translation. The Kalama Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.65) is genuine canon and does urge the Kalamas not to accept teachings merely on the grounds of report, tradition, hearsay, scripture, logic, or a teacher's authority. But this English wording is a loose 19th/20th-century Western rendering of unknown authorship, and its final clause ('believe only what you yourself judge to be true') distorts the sutta, which asks the listener to test claims against whether they lead to harm or benefit and to weigh the judgment of the wise, not to make private judgment the sole criterion. Canonical basis real; this specific text unsourced and tendentious.

author: Buddhist saying
text: Only those who go where few have gone can see what few have seen.
notes: I can find no canonical or traditional Buddhist basis for this in what I know, and the aphorism's shape - an epigram about exploration and rarity - belongs to modern inspirational writing rather than to Pali or Mahayana sources. Origin unknown; the 'Buddhist saying' label appears to be decorative.

author: Buddhist saying
text: Thousands of candles can be lit from a single candle, and the life of the candle will not be shortened. Happiness never decreases by being shared.
keywords: happiness; fire; flame; candle; sharing; generosity
notes: There is a genuine Buddhist antecedent for the candle image: the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters uses the simile of a torch from which many torches are lit without the original's light being diminished, applied to rejoicing in another's giving. So the first sentence has real textual ancestry. The second sentence, 'Happiness never decreases by being shared,' is a modern English addition, and the combined form circulating under the Buddha's name is not a translation of any single canonical passage. Genuine root, modern composite wording.

author: Buddhist saying
text: Concentration is the foundation of wisdom.
notes: Doctrinally unobjectionable - samadhi as the proximate cause of panna is standard Theravada teaching, and Dhammapada 282 says meditation gives rise to wisdom - but I cannot match this seven-word sentence to any canonical verse or standard translation. It reads as a modern summary of the threefold training rather than a quotation. Sentiment traditional, wording unsourced.

author: Buddhist saying
text: When you see the unborn, uncreated, unconditioned, you are liberated from everything born, created, and conditioned.
keywords: birth; creation; conditioned; emptiness; see; perception; buddhist; freedom
notes: This is a recognisable paraphrase of Udana 8.3 (the Nibbana Sutta): 'There is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned. If there were not, there would be no escape from the born, become, made, conditioned.' The canonical source is secure, so the Buddhist attribution is sound, but the sentence as quoted matches no standard translation I know - it converts the sutta's existence claim into a claim about seeing and being liberated. Cited as a paraphrase, not a translation; no print citation entered because I cannot identify which populariser produced this wording.

author: Buddhist saying
text: Generosity brings happiness at every stage of its expression. We experience joy in forming the intention to be generous. We experience joy in the actual act of giving something. And we experience joy in remembering the fact that we have given.
keywords: generosity; joy; intention; giving; buddhist; action; remember
notes: The threefold structure is canonical - Anguttara Nikaya teaches that the giver's mind is gladdened before giving, during giving, and on recollecting the gift afterwards. But this English passage is modern expository prose, not a translation, and its register suggests a contemporary Western vipassana teacher (Sharon Salzberg's 'Lovingkindness' and Joseph Goldstein's writing both cover this ground). I cannot confirm which, so I am naming no author. Doctrine authentic, wording modern and unattributed.

author: Byron Katie
text: You are the one you have been waiting for.
notes: The phrase long predates Byron Katie in its plural form: June Jordan's 'Poem for South African Women' (1978) gives 'we are the ones we have been waiting for,' later popularised via the Hopi elders' prophecy and Alice Walker's 2006 book title. The singular form used here is also the title of Richard Schwartz's Internal Family Systems book 'You Are the One You've Been Waiting For' (2008). Byron Katie may well say it in her workshops - it fits The Work - but I cannot confirm she originated it or place it in her books, and the earlier uses make an exclusive attribution to her unsafe. No reattribution asserted because I cannot establish who coined the singular form.

author: Byron Katie
text: Until the mind loves itself, there is no love.
notes: Consistent with Byron Katie's idiom and with themes in 'Loving What Is' (2002) and 'A Thousand Names for Joy' (2007), but I cannot place this exact sentence in any of her books, transcripts, or interviews I know. Her published lines on this theme run closer to 'I am the only one who can love me' and 'When the mind is loved, there is nothing left to seek.' Treat the wording as unsourced paraphrase until someone checks a primary text.

author: Byron Katie
text: Hell is what you are believing that takes you away from heaven, now.
notes: Byron Katie does speak of heaven and hell as functions of believed thoughts ('When I believe my thoughts, I suffer; when I don't, I don't'), so the sentiment is squarely hers. But I cannot locate this precise formulation in a specific book or recorded event. Most likely a transcribed remark from an event or an approximate rendering. No primary citation available from my knowledge.

author: Byron Katie
text: There's only one of us here.
notes: This is one of Byron Katie's genuine signature phrases — she uses it repeatedly in The Work events and in her writing to point at the absence of separation between self and other. Attribution to her is consistent and I have no competing claimant. Held below the promotion bar only because I cannot name a specific book and page; 'A Thousand Names for Joy' (2007) is the likeliest home but I am not confirming it.

author: Byron Katie
text: The world is what I believe to be true.
notes: Katie's documented formulations run 'The world is nothing but my perception of it' and 'I am the world I perceive.' This variant reads like a compressed retelling of that idea rather than a sentence I can match to a source. Attribution to Katie is plausible; the wording is unverified.

author: Byron Katie
text: The truth has no concern for what we think it should be.
notes: Generic enough that it could come from many contemplative teachers. I cannot place it in Byron Katie's published work, and nothing in the phrasing is distinctively hers. No traceable source in my knowledge; honest answer is 'I don't know.'

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Prayer doesn’t change God. It changes me.
notes: Two problems. First, the popular phrasing traces to the Lewis CHARACTER in William Nicholson's 'Shadowlands' (stage play 1989, film 1993), where Anthony Hopkins as Lewis says roughly 'I pray because I can't help myself... It doesn't change God, it changes me.' That is Nicholson's dialogue, not Lewis's prose. Second, the underlying aphorism is much older and is solidly Kierkegaard's: 'Prayer does not change God, but it changes him who prays.' Lewis wrote at length on petitionary prayer in 'Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer' (1964) but I know of no passage there matching this sentence. Confidence value reflects the weak attribution to Lewis; I hold the misattribution verdict itself with reasonable certainty. | Suggested reattribution: William Nicholson (Shadowlands screenplay, 1993) for this phrasing; Søren Kierkegaard for the underlying aphorism

author: C. West Churchman
text: It's always wise to raise questions about the most obvious and simple assumptions.
notes: C. West Churchman, the systems scientist, made questioning of foundational assumptions the core of his method, and this line circulates in systems-thinking and operations-research literature attributed to him. 'The Systems Approach' (1968) and 'Challenge to Reason' (1968) are the plausible homes, but I cannot confirm which book or page, so I am not asserting a print source. Attribution is plausible and uncontested; the citation is missing.

author: Camus
text: Your success and happiness are forgiven you only if you generously consent to share them with others.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Albert Camus, and a French original circulates ('On ne vous pardonne votre bonheur et vos succès que si vous consentez généreusement à les partager'), which is a good sign of genuine provenance rather than an English-only invention. I cannot confirm the work — candidates include the Carnets and the essays of 'L'Été' — so no print source is asserted. Note also that the corpus record's author field is the bare surname 'Camus' and the context field reads 'Philosopher, Architect,' which looks like a data error worth fixing regardless of the provenance verdict.

author: Camus
text: There is only misfortune in not being loved; there is misery in not loving.
notes: Consistently attributed to Camus with a circulating French original ('Il n'y a que le malheur à n'être pas aimé: il y a la misère à ne point aimer'), and the malheur/misère distinction is characteristically his. I believe it comes from the Carnets or an early essay, but I cannot confirm the work, so no print source is claimed. Same data note as q_0407: author is recorded as bare 'Camus' with a 'Philosopher, Architect' context string.

author: Carl Jung
text: Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will continue to direct your life and you will call it fate.
notes: This is the internet's favourite Jung line and it is a paraphrase, not his sentence. The documented original is from 'Aion' (1951), CW 9ii, para. 126: 'When an inner situation is not made conscious, it appears outside as fate.' The 'until you make the unconscious conscious... and you will call it fate' rendering has no located primary text and is generally listed among Jung's unsourced or paraphrased attributions. The idea is genuinely his; the wording is not. Consider replacing with the Aion sentence, which is citable.

author: Carl Jung
text: If we want to understand the psyche we have to include the whole world.
notes: The sentiment is consistent with Jung's late thinking on the psyche's continuity with the world (the unus mundus and synchronicity material), so attribution is plausible. But I cannot place this sentence in the Collected Works, the letters, or the seminars, and I am not going to guess a volume. Unverified wording.

author: Carl Sagan
text: Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.
notes: One of the most-repeated Sagan lines and one of the least sourced. It does not appear in Cosmos, The Demon-Haunted World, Pale Blue Dot, or Broca's Brain as far as I know, and it is generally listed among Sagan's unsourced or disputed attributions rather than in the sourced sections. Sagan may well have said something like it in an interview, but no primary citation exists in my knowledge. Do not promote. Note also that this quote is duplicated in this batch as q_0418.

author: Carl Sagan
text: Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.
notes: Exact duplicate of q_0416 (same text, same author; only the category field differs — q_0416 has a null category). Same verdict: widely circulated, no located primary source in any Sagan book or documented broadcast, generally treated as unsourced. Recommend deduplicating these two records regardless of the provenance decision.

author: Carl Sagan
text: One glance at a book and you hear the voice of another person, perhaps someone dead for 1,000 years. To read is to voyage through time.
notes: Sagan definitely wrote and said a passage of this kind — the well-documented version is from Cosmos, 'The Persistence of Memory' (episode 11 and the corresponding book chapter): 'What an astonishing thing a book is... One glance at it and you're inside the mind of another person, maybe somebody dead for thousands of years.' The compressed phrasing here, ending 'To read is to voyage through time,' is close to but not identical with that text, and it may instead come from his later writing on literacy in 'The Demon-Haunted World.' Author attribution is safe; the exact wording and source are not pinned, so I am not asserting a print citation. Someone should check the Cosmos chapter and align the wording before promotion.

author: Carl Sagan
text: Frederick Douglas taught that literacy is the path from slavery to freedom. There are many kinds of slavery and many kinds of freedom, but reading is still the path.
keywords: slavery; freedom; books; learning; reading; path
notes: The Frederick Douglass and literacy material is genuinely Sagan's territory — 'The Demon-Haunted World' (1995) devotes a chapter to Douglass teaching himself to read and to literacy as liberation, which is the near-certain home of this passage. I cannot confirm the exact sentence or page, so no print source is asserted. Separately, the corpus text misspells the name: it should be Frederick Douglass with two s's. Fix that before any promotion.

author: Carl Sagan
text: We make our world significant by the courage of our questions and the depth of our answers
keywords: questions; answers; depth; courage; world; meaning
notes: Consistently attributed to Sagan, usually to Cosmos (1980), and consistent with his voice. My hesitation: it is suspiciously close to the better-documented line 'We can judge our progress by the courage of our questions and the depth of our answers...' (see q_0432), and one may be a circulated compression of the other. I cannot place this exact sentence at a specific page or chapter from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing at Cosmos.

author: Carl Sagan
text: We are star-stuff contemplating the stars.
keywords: star; contemplation; self; awareness; oneness; universe
notes: The idea is genuinely Sagan's, but this exact wording appears to be a popular condensation. The documented Cosmos (1980, ch. 13) phrasings I know are 'starstuff pondering the stars' and 'We are star stuff which has taken its destiny into its own hands'; Cosmos also has 'We are star stuff harvesting starlight.' 'Star-stuff contemplating the stars' reads like a paraphrase that hardened into a quotation. Not a misattribution to another author — a wording problem. Recommend replacing with a documented variant if the corpus wants an exact quotation.

author: Carl Sagan
text: Every aspect of Nature reveals a deep mystery and touches our sense of wonder and awe. Those afraid of the universe as it really is, those who pretend to nonexistent knowledge and envision a Cosmos centered on human beings will prefer the fleeting comforts of superstition. They avoid rather than confront the world. But those with the courage to explore the weave and structure of the Cosmos, even where it differs profoundly from their wishes and prejudices, will penetrate its deepest mysteries.
keywords: nature; mystery; deep; touch; wonder; awe; fear; universe; human; superstition; world
earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980 (chapter unconfirmed)
notes: Confident this is authentic Sagan prose — the cadence, the framing of superstition as avoidance, and 'the weave and structure of the Cosmos' are all his. Less confident about the locus: it is generally cited to Cosmos (1980), but I cannot rule out Broca's Brain (1979), which covers similar ground. Recording the book with an explicit caveat rather than inventing a chapter.

author: Carl Sagan
text: You're an interesting species. An interesting mix. You're capable of such beautiful dreams, and such horrible nightmares. You feel so lost, so cut off, so alone, only you're not. See, in all our searching, the only thing we've found that makes the emptiness bearable, is each other.
keywords: human; species; beautiful; dream; nightmares; lost; alone; isolated; search; emptiness; companionship
notes: This is film dialogue, not Sagan's writing. It is spoken by the extraterrestrial (appearing as Ellie's father) in the 1997 Warner Bros. film Contact, whose screenplay was written by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg. Sagan and Ann Druyan wrote the original story on which the film was based, and Sagan died in December 1996 before its release, but I do not believe this speech appears in Sagan's 1985 novel. Attributing it to Sagan as an author is not supportable; it belongs to the screenwriters. | Suggested reattribution: Contact (1997 film), screenplay by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg

author: Carl Sagan
text: You have to know the past to understand the present.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Sagan, commonly to Cosmos (1980) and to the television series. It is short and aphoristic, which is exactly the shape of quotation that drifts, and I cannot place it at a specific page from memory. Nothing suggests another author — this is uncertainty about sourcing, not about attribution. Below the promotion bar on locus alone.

author: Carl Sagan
text: We inhabit a universe where atoms are made in the centers of stars; where each second a thousand suns are born; where life is sparked by sunlight and lightning in the airs and waters of youthful planets; where the raw material for biological evolution is sometimes made by the explosion of a star halfway across the Milky Way; where a thing as beautiful as a galaxy is formed a hundred billion times - a Cosmos of quasars and quarks, snowflakes and fireflies, where there may be black holes and other universe and extraterrestrial civilizations whose radio messages are at this moment reaching the Earth. How pallid by comparison are the pretensions of superstition and pseudoscience; how important it is for us to pursue and understand science, that characteristically human endeavor.
keywords: universe; science; stars; atoms; sun; birth; spark; sunlight; water; planets; evolution; explosion; beauty; galaxy; earth; superstition; understand; human
earliest_print_source: Broca's Brain: Reflections on the Romance of Science, Carl Sagan, 1979 (chapter unconfirmed)
notes: Unmistakably Sagan's prose — the catalogue structure ('quasars and quarks, snowflakes and fireflies') and the closing turn on 'the pretensions of superstition and pseudoscience' are his. My recollection places it in Broca's Brain, most likely the pseudoscience essay 'Night Walkers and Mystery Mongers,' but I hold that loosely; it could belong to Cosmos or The Demon-Haunted World, which cover the same terrain. Author confident, locus uncertain.

author: Carl Sagan
text: It is the tension between creativity and skepticism that has produced the stunning and unexpected findings of science.
notes: The creativity/skepticism tension is one of Sagan's signature arguments — most fully developed in 'The Burden of Skepticism' (Skeptical Inquirer, 1987) and in the introduction to Broca's Brain (1979), where he writes of an 'exquisite balance' between the two. This particular sentence is consistently attributed to him and fits, but I cannot confidently assign it to either source, so I am leaving the print citation null rather than picking one.

author: Carl Sagan
text: The universe is a pretty big place. If it's just us, seems like an awful waste of space.
notes: To my knowledge this is dialogue from the 1997 film Contact — spoken by Ted Arroway to young Ellie and echoed by her later — and not text Sagan wrote. I recall it being listed among misattributions on Sagan's Wikiquote page for exactly this reason. Sagan wrote the novel and co-wrote the story, so the association is understandable, but the screenplay is by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg. I am not certain the line is absent from the 1985 novel, which is why this is 'likely' rather than settled; a text search of the novel would resolve it. | Suggested reattribution: Contact (1997 film), screenplay by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg

author: Carl Sagan
text: The visions we offer our children shape the future.
earliest_print_source: Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, Carl Sagan, 1994 (chapter unconfirmed)
notes: This is the opening of a longer Sagan passage that continues 'It matters what those visions are. Often they become self-fulfilling prophecies. Dreams are maps.' My recollection places it in Pale Blue Dot, but I cannot confirm the chapter and cannot rule out one of his Parade essays from the same period. Author attribution is solid; the citation is offered with an explicit caveat. Note also that the single-sentence excerpt is weaker than the full passage.

author: Carl Sandburg
text: Time is the coin of your life. It is the only coin you have, and only you can determine how it will be spent. Be careful lest you let other people spend it for you.
notes: Consistently attributed to Carl Sandburg across quotation collections and never, to my knowledge, to anyone else, which is mild evidence for authenticity. I cannot place it in a specific poem, essay, or interview, and I have no recollection of a primary citation. Attribution is stable but unverified at the source level.

author: Carlo Carretto
text: You say you have no faith? Love - and faith will come. You say you are sad? Love - and joy will come. You say you are alone? Love - and you will break out of your solitude. You say you are in hell? Love - and you will find yourself in heaven.
keywords: love; sadness; faith; joy; alone; isolated; solitude; hell; heaven; discover; transform; change
notes: Carlo Carretto (1910-1988), Little Brother of Jesus, is the consistent attribution and the passage matches his devotional style and his repeated 'Love, and...' constructions. Most likely from Letters from the Desert (Lettere dal deserto, 1964) or The God Who Comes, but I cannot confirm which book or verify the English translation wording, so no print source is asserted.

author: Carlos Castaneda
text: The basic difference between an ordinary man and a warrior is that a warrior takes everything as a challenge while an ordinary man takes everything either as a blessing or a curse.
notes: Reads as a don Juan teaching from the Castaneda corpus and the vocabulary ('warrior', 'ordinary man', 'challenge') is characteristic of Tales of Power (1974) and the aphorism compilation The Wheel of Time (1998). I cannot pin the volume or page. Separate caveat for the corpus: Castaneda's don Juan material is widely held by scholars to be fiction, so 'Castaneda wrote it' is a different claim from 'a Yaqui teacher said it'.

author: Carlos Fuentes
text: Cruelty is a lack of imagination.
notes: The Fuentes attribution circulates in quotation aggregators but I cannot locate it in any of his novels, essays, or interviews from memory. The underlying idea ('cruelty is a failure of imagination') is a commonplace that has been voiced by several writers, which makes single-author attribution weak. Honest answer: unplaced.

author: Catherine Ponder
text: When you hold resentment toward another, you are bound to that person or condition by an emotional link that is stronger than steel. Forgiveness is the only way to dissolve that link and get free.
notes: Catherine Ponder, New Thought minister, is the uniform attribution and the phrasing ('bound to that person by an emotional link stronger than steel') matches her prosperity-and-forgiveness teaching. Probably from The Dynamic Laws of Prosperity (1962) or a companion Dynamic Laws title, but I cannot confirm the book or edition, so no citation is asserted.

author: Catherine the Great
text: The more a man knows, the more he forgives.
notes: Attributed to Catherine the Great in English quotation dictionaries, but I know of no primary Russian or French source in her correspondence or memoirs. The sentiment closely tracks the older French maxim 'tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner' (associated with Mme de Stael, Corinne, 1807), and the line is also floated under Confucius, which is a classic sign of a free-floating aphorism. Attribution is plausible but unsupported.

author: Cavett Robert
text: If we study the lives of great men and women carefully and unemotionally we find that, invariably, greatness was developed, tested and revealed through the darker periods of their lives. One of the largest tributaries of the river of greatness is always the stream of adversity.
notes: Cavett Robert (1907-1997), founder of the National Speakers Association, is the consistent attribution and the passage is idiomatic of mid-century American motivational speaking, so authorship is plausible. His material circulated largely through recorded talks rather than books, and I cannot cite a published source or a datable first appearance.

author: Charles Darwin
text: It is not the strongest of the species that survive, nor the most intelligent, but the one most responsive to change.
earliest_print_source: 'Lessons from Europe for American Business', Leon C. Megginson, Southwestern Social Science Quarterly, vol. 44, 1963
notes: Not Darwin. This is one of the best-documented misattributions in the corpus: it originates as Leon C. Megginson's 1963 paraphrase of ideas in On the Origin of Species ('...it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment...'). Later compression into a terse epigram, plus quotation marks, converted the paraphrase into a fake Darwin quote. Wikiquote lists it under Darwin's misattributed section. Darwin himself never wrote it; 'survival of the fittest' was Herbert Spencer's phrase, adopted by Darwin only in later editions. | Suggested reattribution: Leon C. Megginson (1963), paraphrasing Darwin

author: Charles Darwin
text: A man who dares to waste one hour of time has not discovered the value of life.
keywords: waste; man; time; discover; life; value
notes: Unlike q_0458 this one is generally treated as genuine Darwin and is usually said to come from his correspondence, plausibly by way of The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (ed. Francis Darwin, 1887). I cannot identify the specific letter, recipient, or date from memory, so I will not assert a citation. Given that Darwin is a misattribution magnet, moderate rather than high confidence is the honest reading.

author: Charles du Bos
text: The important thing is this: to be able at a moment's notice to sacrifice what we are for what we could become.
notes: Uniformly attributed to the French critic Charles du Bos (1882-1939), most likely from his Approximations essays or his Journal, and the aphoristic register fits him. I cannot confirm the French original or a volume, and the English wording varies ('at a moment's notice' / 'at any moment'), which suggests translation drift. No citation asserted.

author: Charles Eames
text: The details are not the details. They make the design.
notes: Well established as Charles Eames and quoted throughout design literature and Eames Office material; it is one of the lines the Eames Office itself repeats. Circulates in two variants ('They make the design' and '...they make the product'), which indicates it comes from spoken remarks or interviews rather than a fixed printed text. Strong attribution, no single primary source I can cite.

author: Charles John Quarto
text: If you open your heart, love opens your mind.
notes: Charles John Quarto is a real songwriter and poet, but I have no independent knowledge of this line in his published work. It appears to circulate only through quotation aggregators. No traceable source; 'I don't know' is the accurate verdict.

author: Charles R. Swindoll
text: This may shock you, but I believe the single most significant decision I can make on a day-to-day basis is my choice of attitude. It is more important than my past, my education, my bankroll, my successes or failures, fame or pain, what other people think of me or say about me, my circumstances, or my position. Attitude is that "single string" that keeps me going or cripples my progress. It alone fuels my fire or assaults my hope. When my attitudes are right, there's no barrier too high, no valley too deep, no dream too extreme, no challenge too great for me.
keywords: attitude; success; failure; pain; progress; dream; challenge; fire
notes: Genuine Swindoll in substance: this is from his much-anthologized 'Attitude' material, the same body of writing as the far more famous 'The longer I live, the more I realize the impact of attitude on life' passage. My recollection places it in Strengthening Your Grip (1982), in the chapter on attitudes, but I am not confident enough in the book or year to assert it as a citation. Note that Swindoll's attitude texts are heavily paraphrased online, so the exact wording here may not be his published wording.

author: Charles Schwab
text: The person who does not work for the love of work but only for money is not likely to make money nor to find much fun in life.
keywords: work; love; money; success; fun; enjoyment; person
notes: Attributed to 'Charles Schwab' without disambiguation. Period and diction point to Charles M. Schwab (1862-1939) of Bethlehem Steel, not Charles R. Schwab the modern broker; if genuine it most likely comes from his popular business writing of the 1910s-20s, possibly Succeeding With What You Have (1917). I cannot confirm the source, and the ambiguity of the bare name is itself a provenance defect worth fixing in the corpus. | Suggested reattribution: Charles M. Schwab (Bethlehem Steel, 1862-1939) - disambiguation, not reattribution

author: Chief Tecumseh, Shawnee Nation
text: So live your life that the fear of death can never enter your heart. Trouble no one about their religion; respect others in their view, and demand that they respect yours. Love your life, perfect your life, beautify all things in your life. Seek to make your life long and its purpose in the service of your people. Prepare a noble death song for the day when you go over the great divide. Always give a word or a sign of salute when meeting or passing a friend, even a stranger, when in a lonely place. Show respect to all people and grovel to none. When you arise in the morning give thanks for the food and for the joy of living. If you see no reason for giving thanks, the fault lies only in yourself. Abuse no one and nothing, for abuse turns the wise ones to fools and robs the spirit of its vision. When it comes your time to die, be not like those whose hearts are filled with the fear of death, so that when their time comes they weep and pray for a little more time to live their lives over again in a different way. Sing your death song and die like a hero going home.
keywords: life; death; fear; heart; religion; respect; love; perfect; beauty; service; song; friend; gratitude; food; joy; wisdom; fool; vision; spirit; sing; hero; native american
notes: Almost certainly not Tecumseh. Tecumseh died in 1813 and his authenticated speeches survive only through interpreters and hostile or secondhand transcription; this polished English passage is not among them and has no contemporaneous record. Its wide circulation is modern - it spread through 20th-century 'Native American wisdom' anthologies and then explosively through the 2012 film Act of Valor, which used it as a closing text. The style (aphoristic, individualist, self-help cadence) reads as 20th-century composition. I cannot identify the actual author, so apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed. Recommend not promoting it under a named historical figure.

author: Chinese proverb
text: Be not afraid of changing slowly; be afraid only of standing still.
notes: This is a genuine Chinese proverb rather than a floating Western invention: it renders the common saying bu pa man, jiu pa zhan (不怕慢，就怕站), 'do not fear going slow, fear only standing still'. The corpus text says 'changing slowly' where the standard English rendering is 'growing slowly' - a variant, not a different proverb. Confidence reflects that the genre label 'Chinese proverb' is accurate; a proverb by nature has no single author or first printing.

author: Chinese proverb
text: If you are patient in one moment of anger, you will escape a hundred days of sorrow.
notes: Corresponds to the widely used Chinese saying ren yi shi zhi qi, mian bai ri zhi you (忍一时之气，免百日之忧), 'endure a moment's anger, avoid a hundred days of sorrow'. The label 'Chinese proverb' is therefore accurate as a genre attribution. As with all proverbs there is no author and no first-print source to verify.

author: Chinese proverb
text: The miracle is not to fly in the air, or to walk on the water; but to walk on the earth.
notes: The 'Chinese proverb' label is doubtful. The thought is Chan/Zen rather than proverbial - closest classical antecedent is Layman Pang's 'my miraculous power and spiritual activity: drawing water and carrying firewood'. The specific modern English phrasing most resembles Thich Nhat Hanh's line 'The miracle is not to walk on water; the miracle is to walk on the green earth', which is Vietnamese Zen, not a Chinese proverb. I am not confident enough to name a true source, so no reattribution is suggested, but the current label should be treated as unreliable.

author: Chinese proverb
text: Tell me, I'll forget. Show me, I may remember. But involve me and I'll understand.
notes: A much-laundered saying: variously credited to Confucius, Xunzi, Benjamin Franklin, Native American sources, and 'Chinese proverb', which is the signature of an aphorism with no real home. There is a genuine classical antecedent in the Xunzi (ch. 8): hearing is not as good as seeing, seeing is not as good as knowing, knowing is not as good as putting into practice - but the modern tell/show/involve triad appears to be a 20th-century Western educational formulation rather than a translation. Label is unreliable; true origin unidentified.

author: Chinese proverb
text: A bit of fragrance always clings to the hand that gives roses.
notes: Circulates as both a Chinese proverb and as a line by Hada Bejar, and neither attribution has support I can verify. I know of no Chinese original for it, which weakens the proverb label. Untraceable from training knowledge.

author: Christina Baldwin
text: Spirituality is the sacred center out of which all life comes, including Mondays and Tuesdays and rainy Saturday afternoons in all their mundane and glorious detail. ... The spiritual journey is the soul's life commingling with ordinary life.
keywords: spirituality; sacred; center; life; mundane; soul; ordinary
notes: Christina Baldwin is the consistent attribution and the passage matches her journal-writing and spiritual-practice books, most likely Life's Companion: Journal Writing as a Spiritual Quest (1990). I cannot confirm the book or page. Note also that the corpus text is elided with an ellipsis, so it splices two non-adjacent sentences - worth flagging independent of authorship.

author: Christopher LaBrec
text: Everybody builds a dream in their lifetime. You’re either going to build your dream, or somebody else's. So build your own!
notes: I have no knowledge of Christopher LaBrec as a published author or public figure, and no recollection of this line outside quotation aggregators. It has the shape of a motivational-poster attribution of unknown origin. Honest verdict: unverifiable.

author: Clarence Francis
text: You can buy a person's time; you can buy their physical presence at a given place. You can even buy a measured number of their skilled muscular motions per hour, but you cannot buy enthusiasm... you can not buy loyalty. You cannot buy the devotion of hearts, minds, or souls. You must earn these.
keywords: money; work; purchase; enthusiasm; loyalty; devotion; heart; mind; soul; earn
notes: Clarence Francis, chairman of General Foods (1935-1954), is the standard and stable attribution in management literature, typically credited to a speech or company address in the 1940s-50s. I cannot name the speech or date. The corpus text is gender-neutralized ('a person's time... their physical presence'); the circulating original reads 'a man's time... his physical presence', which should be noted if the quote is promoted.

author: Clarissa Pinkola Estes
text: Anything you do from the soulful self will help lighten the burdens of the world. Anything. You have no idea what the smallest word, the tiniest generosity can cause to be set in motion. Be outrageous in forgiving. Be dramatic in reconciling. Mistakes? Back up and make them as right as you can, then move on. Be off the charts in kindness. In whatever you are called to, strive to be devoted to it in all aspects large and small. Fall short? Try again. Mastery is made in increments, not in leaps. Be brave, be fierce, be visionary. Mend the parts of the world that are within your reach. To strive to live this way is the most dramatic gift you can ever give to the world.
keywords: soul; self; action; burden; world; small; word; speech; generosity; motion; forgiveness; mistakes; right; kindness; devotion; large; mastery; brave; vision; heal; life; gift; service; purpose; support; help
notes: Genuine Clarissa Pinkola Estes. This passage is from her widely circulated essay known as 'We Were Made for These Times' / 'Letter to a Young Activist During Troubled Times', which spread online in the early 2000s and was later collected in her published work. I am confident about the essay but not about its first print appearance or exact date, so no citation is asserted. Caveat: the online versions of this essay vary in wording and are sometimes reordered, so the exact text here may be a circulated variant.

author: Cochise
text: You must speak straight so that your words may go as sunlight to our hearts.
keywords: sunlight; speech; heart; words; native american
notes: A staple of Native American oratory anthologies, consistently attributed to Cochise and plausibly drawn from accounts of his 1871-72 negotiations with U.S. officers (the Howard/Jeffords parleys). I cannot confirm an original transcript or the anthology that first printed it. All surviving Cochise speech is mediated through interpreters and later journalistic reconstruction, so even a genuine source would be a secondhand rendering. Honest answer: plausible, unconfirmed.

author: Confucius
text: By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest.
notes: Does not appear in the Analects or any Confucian classic that I know of. This is a modern English-language aphorism that spread through 20th-century quotation books and later quote sites; the tidy 'noblest / easiest / bitterest' rhetorical triad is characteristic of Western epigram construction, not of the Analects' terse recorded exchanges. I do not know who actually composed it, so I offer no reattribution. Confucius is a magnet for invented maxims of exactly this shape.

author: Course in Miracles
text: Will you allow yourself to be hostage to the ego or host to God?
earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 (Text)
notes: The antithesis 'host to God or hostage to the ego' is genuine ACIM language and recurs in the Text; I am confident of the source work but not of the exact chapter/section, so I have not cited one. The line as given here is phrased as a question and reads as a rewording of the canonical declarative sentence rather than a verbatim quotation, which is why this is 'attributed' rather than 'verified'. Anyone promoting this should check the wording against the FIP Text.

author: Cyrus Curtis
text: There are two kinds of people who never amount to much: those who cannot do what they are told, and those who can do nothing else.
notes: Consistently attributed to Cyrus H. K. Curtis, the Curtis Publishing / Saturday Evening Post publisher, in mid-20th-century business-epigram collections of the B. C. Forbes type. I cannot place a primary source — no speech, letter, or interview I can name — and business aphorisms of this vintage migrate freely between Curtis, Carnegie, and other publisher-industrialist figures. Plausible but unconfirmed.

author: D. T. Suzuki
text: To see directly into one’s original nature, this is Zen... This Nature is the Mind, and the Mind is Buddha, and the Buddha is the Way, and the Way is Zen.
keywords: zen; buddhism; nature; true; mind; buddha; way; insight; self
notes: The content and idiom are consistent with D. T. Suzuki's expository writing on Zen (An Introduction to Zen Buddhism, Essays in Zen Buddhism, and the Barrett-edited Selected Writings), and the closing chain 'Nature is Mind, Mind is Buddha, Buddha is the Way, the Way is Zen' echoes the Chan formulations he liked to render in English. But I cannot place the volume or page, and the ellipsis suggests the line has been stitched from a longer passage. Note also that quote sites routinely confuse D. T. Suzuki with Shunryu Suzuki, so the attribution deserves a source check.

author: D. T. Suzuki
text: If you understand real practice, then archery or other activities can be Zen. If you don't understand how to practice archery in its true sense, then even though you practice very hard, what you acquire is just technique. It won't help you through and through. Perhaps you can hit the mark without trying, but without a bow and arrow you cannot do anything. If you understand the point of practice, then even without a bow and arrow the archery will help you. How you get that kind of power or ability is only through right practice.
earliest_print_source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Shunryu Suzuki, Weatherhill, 1970
notes: This is Shunryu Suzuki, not D. T. Suzuki. The passage is from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind — the plainspoken lecture voice ('it won't help you through and through', 'without a bow and arrow you cannot do anything') is Shunryu Suzuki's transcribed dharma-talk register, not D. T. Suzuki's scholarly prose. My confidence in the reattribution to Shunryu Suzuki is high (~0.85); the 0.2 above reflects confidence in the stated author, D. T. Suzuki, which is low. I am confident of the book but not of the chapter, so none is cited. This is the single most common Suzuki/Suzuki mix-up in quote corpora. | Suggested reattribution: Shunryu Suzuki

author: Daisaku Ikeda
text: People who cease to grow can't inspire others. Leadership begins with challenging oneself.
keywords: growth; leadership; challenge; self; inspiration; people
notes: Consistent with Ikeda's enormous published output of guidance essays, editorials, and daily-encouragement columns circulated through SGI publications, and I have no reason to doubt it. But that same output is the problem: his aphorisms circulate detached from the essay or speech they came from, and I cannot name the source. Plausible, unplaced.

author: Dalai Lama
text: The period of greatest gain in knowledge and experience is the most difficult period in one’s life.
notes: Ubiquitous on quote sites under the Dalai Lama's name, but I can identify no book, talk, or interview behind it. The generic phrasing is typical of lines that accrete to him rather than originate with him. The 14th Dalai Lama is a strong misattribution magnet — the volume of translated, transcribed, and paraphrased teaching makes him easy to attach anything to.

author: Dalai Lama
text: We can let the circumstances of our lives harden us so that we become increasingly resentful and afraid, or we can let them soften us, and make us kinder. We always have the choice.
notes: This is Pema Chodron, not the Dalai Lama. The harden/soften antithesis closing on 'We always have the choice' is one of her signature passages, from her late-1990s/early-2000s books (When Things Fall Apart, 1997, and The Places That Scare You, 2001 are the two candidates I would check first) — I am confident of the author but not of which book, so I cite neither rather than guess. Confidence in the reattribution to Chodron is roughly 0.75; the 0.2 above reflects the stated attribution to the Dalai Lama. | Suggested reattribution: Pema Chodron

author: Dalai Lama
text: This is my simple religion. There is no need for temples; no need for complicated philosophy. Our own brain, our own heart is our temple; the philosophy is kindness.
keywords: religion; kindness; philosophy; brain; heart; temple
notes: One of the better-supported Dalai Lama attributions: it appears in edited collections of his teachings from around 1990 onward and is quoted with unusually stable wording, which usually indicates a real printed origin rather than internet drift. It also matches his repeated public formulation 'my religion is kindness.' I cannot name the specific volume or talk, so I leave the source null rather than guess at one. Strong secondary evidence, no primary source in hand.

author: Dalai Lama
text: The problem isn't materialism as such. Rather it is the underlying assumption that full satisfaction can arise from gratifying the senses alone. Unlike animals whose quest for happiness is restricted to survival and to the immediate gratification of sensory desires, we human beings have the capacity to experience happiness at a deeper level which, when achieved, can overwhelm unhappy experiences.
keywords: happiness; materialism; assumption; gratification; senses; survival; transformation; depth
notes: The length, the qualified argument, and the human/animal contrast are characteristic of the Dalai Lama's book-length ethical writing of the late 1990s (Ethics for the New Millennium, The Art of Happiness with Howard Cutler) rather than of a fabricated aphorism — invented quotes are rarely this long or this hedged. That raises my confidence that it is genuine, but I cannot place the book or article, and passages of this kind are often lightly edited by whoever excerpts them.

author: Dalai Lama
text: The deep root of failure in our lives is to think, ‘Oh how useless and powerless I am.’ It is essential to think strongly and forcefully, ‘I can do it,’ without boasting or fretting.
notes: Widely circulated under the Dalai Lama's name, often via daily-wisdom compilations of the Path to Tranquility type edited by Renuka Singh. The content matches his standard teaching against self-disparagement, which he treats as a distinctively Western affliction. No primary source I can name, and compilation books rarely cite their own origins, so the chain of custody is weak.

author: Dalai Lama
text: The essence of all religions is love, compassion, and tolerance. Kindness is my true religion. The clear proof of a person's love of God is if that person genuinely shows love to fellow human beings.
keywords: essence; love; religion; compassion; kindness; god; authenticity; human; devotion
notes: Reads as a composite: three separate Dalai Lama themes welded into one paragraph. 'Kindness is my true religion' is a real and characteristic formulation of his; the sentences on either side circulate independently elsewhere. Composite quotes are common on aggregator sites and are individually genuine but collectively unsourceable. I would not promote this as a single utterance without finding a source that carries all three sentences together.

author: Dalai Lama
text: Be kind whenever possible. It is always possible.
notes: Extremely famous and almost universally attributed to the Dalai Lama, but to my knowledge it sits in the unsourced/attributed section on Wikiquote rather than the sourced section — no book, speech, or interview has been pinned to it. Fame is not evidence: this is a case where near-universal attribution coexists with zero documented provenance. Honest verdict is low confidence despite how well known the line is.

author: Dalai Lama
text: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
notes: A near-ubiquitous Dalai Lama attribution with very stable wording, and it faithfully renders a real and repeated theme in his teaching on compassion as self-interested as well as altruistic. But I cannot locate a primary source, and like several of his most-shared lines it may be a compressed paraphrase of a longer spoken passage rather than a verbatim quotation.

author: Dalai Lama
text: If you were to spend a few minutes every day thinking about and trying to develop compassion, eventually compassion, the essence of spiritual practice, will become part of your life. When that happens I am convinced that not only will your life be happier but you will also make a direct contribution of peace and happiness in the world as a whole.
keywords: compassion; essence; spiritual; practice; life; happiness; peace; world; whole; contribution
notes: Length and the first-person 'I am convinced' make a genuine spoken or written origin likely — this reads like transcript, not aggregator invention. Consistent with his talks and writings on compassion practice (The Compassionate Life and similar collections would be where I would look). No source I can name, so the attribution stays unverified.

author: Dalai Lama
text: We need not only a trained intelligence, but also a warm heart. Then a sense of community and a sense of responsibility will arise naturally.
notes: 'Warm heart' and 'warm-heartedness' are genuine signature terms of the Dalai Lama's public teaching, which supports the attribution at a thematic level. But the intelligence-plus-heart construction is also a widely shared moral commonplace — compare King's 'intelligence plus character' — and I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his talks or books. Thematically plausible, textually unplaced.

author: Dale Carnegie
text: Success is getting what you want; happiness is wanting what you get.
notes: Contested and probably not Carnegie. This chiasmus circulates under several names — Dale Carnegie, Ingrid Bergman, and others — which is the classic signature of a floating aphorism that predates all of its claimed authors. I do not recall encountering it in How to Win Friends and Influence People or How to Stop Worrying and Start Living. Because I cannot identify a probable true origin, I am recording this as unverified rather than as a misattribution, but the Carnegie credit should be treated as weak.

author: Dale Turner
text: Dreams are renewable. No matter what our age or condition, there are still untapped possibilities within us and new beauty waiting to be born.
keywords: dreams; age; possibilities; beauty; birth; within; self
notes: Attributed to Dale E. Turner, the Seattle-area minister and long-running Seattle Times columnist, and the sentiment and cadence fit his inspirational column work. His columns are the likely origin, but individual columns are rarely cited by the quote collections that reprint him, and I cannot name a date or title. Plausible, unconfirmed.

author: Dan Millman
text: Conscious evolution begins as we take responsibility for clearing our own obstructions.
notes: Consistent with Dan Millman's vocabulary — 'conscious evolution', 'obstructions' — and with his post-Peaceful Warrior instructional books (No Ordinary Moments, The Life You Were Born to Live, The Laws of Spirit). Millman is a living author who circulates his own lines, so the attribution itself is low-risk, but I cannot name the book or page.

author: Dan Millman
text: When we feel stuck, going nowhere - even starting to slip backward - we may actually be backing up to get a running start.
notes: A recognizable Millman line with a distinctive image (backing up to get a running start) that argues against generic invention, and consistent with his 1990s books. Attribution to Millman is low-risk; the specific source is unplaced in my knowledge, so it stays unverified.

author: Dan Millman
text: Energy follows thought. We move toward, but not beyond, what we can imagine. By expanding our deepest beliefs about what is possible, we change our experience of it.
notes: 'Energy follows thought' is a New Thought commonplace that long predates Millman, but the surrounding sentences ('we move toward, but not beyond, what we can imagine') are his phrasing and consistent with his instructional writing. So the passage as a whole is plausibly his composition even though its opening maxim is inherited. No source located.

author: Dan Millman
text: Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't ever really live at all.
earliest_print_source: Way of the Peaceful Warrior, Dan Millman, 1980 (widely cited to this book; page/edition unverified)
notes: I recall this line as spoken by the 'Socrates' character in Millman's Way of the Peaceful Warrior (1980), usually quoted as 'Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't really live at all.' The attribution to Millman is consistent everywhere I have seen it and the voice matches the book. I cannot confirm the exact page or edition from memory, so I am holding this below the primary-source band.

author: Dan Millman
text: The secret of happiness is not found in seeking more, but in developing the capacity to enjoy less.
notes: Circulates widely and consistently under Dan Millman's name, but I cannot place it in any specific book of his. The sentiment is close to his 'peaceful warrior' material, which makes the attribution plausible rather than evidenced. No primary source known to me.

author: Dan Millman
text: Managing your money does not depend upon becoming wealthy or declaring vows of poverty. Rather, it is about creating stability and sufficiency – a balanced flow of monetary energy through your life.
keywords: money; finances; wealth; poverty; creation; flow; energy; life
notes: Reads like Millman's prose and likely comes from Everyday Enlightenment: The Twelve Gateways to Personal Growth (1998), which contains a gateway on managing finances framed around sufficiency rather than wealth or poverty. I cannot confirm the passage, so I am not asserting that book as the source.

author: Dave Ramsey
text: How you handle or mishandle your money tells us who you are and, more important, it tells YOU who you are. Your priorities, passions, goals, and fears are shown clearly in the flow of your money. Your value system, or lack of one causes money to flow around you, past you, or to you. When money is in your possession, what you do with it screams loudly who you are.
notes: This passage is consistently attributed to Dave Ramsey and matches his voice and his standard theme that money behavior reveals character. It most likely comes from The Total Money Makeover or the Financial Peace material, but I cannot pin the book or page, so no print source is asserted. Attribution is strong; the citation is not.

author: David Brinkley
text: A successful person is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks that others throw at him or her.
notes: Standardly attributed to broadcaster David Brinkley (usually as 'A successful man is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks others have thrown at him'), but I know of no speech, broadcast, or book of his where it originates. Variants of the 'foundation from thrown bricks' aphorism circulated in American inspirational writing before Brinkley's prominence, which makes him a plausible popularizer rather than a confirmed author. The text here has also been gender-neutralized from the common form.
