notes: Very consistently attributed to Beecher and characteristic of his pulpit style; most likely from one of the Plymouth Pulpit compilations (Proverbs from Plymouth Pulpit, 1887, or Life Thoughts, 1858). I cannot confirm the volume or page from memory, so no print source is claimed. Probably genuine but held below the promotion bar.

author: Henry Youngman
text: I've already got all the money I'll ever need - if I die by four o'clock this afternoon.
notes: A standard Henny Youngman one-liner, consistently attributed to him across joke anthologies and obituary-era retrospectives; no competing attribution that I know of. I cannot place its first print appearance or a specific routine. Note the author field is misspelled: the comedian is Henny Youngman (1906-1998), not 'Henry'. | Suggested reattribution: Henny Youngman (spelling correction, same person)

author: Heraclitus
text: To transcend personality, you must descend to the source of personality.
notes: I know of no Heraclitus fragment resembling this. The surviving fragments (Diels-Kranz) concern logos, flux, fire, opposites, and the soul's depth - not 'personality', which is a post-classical and largely modern psychological concept. The vocabulary and the transcend/descend construction read as 20th-century spiritual writing. I cannot identify the real author, so I am not offering a reattribution.

author: Herm Albright
text: A positive attitude may not solve all your problems, but it will annoy enough people to make it worth the effort.
notes: Ubiquitously attributed to Herm Albright, usually with the dates 1876-1944 and sometimes with a credit to The Saturday Evening Post or Reader's Digest. I am not aware of anyone having located the line in a text Albright actually wrote, and Albright himself is an obscure figure (a German-American engraver) whose name appears in circulation almost solely as the tag on this one quote - a pattern typical of quote-anthology attributions that were never sourced. Plausible but unverified.

author: Herman Hesse
text: There are numerous ways in which God can make us lonely and lead us back to ourselves.
notes: Reads as authentic Hesse and is consistently attributed to him with no competing author. My recollection places it in the Narcissus and Goldmund / aphorism-collection territory (the English Reflections, ed. Volker Michels, gathers many such lines), but I cannot confirm the work, so I am not naming one. Attribution to Hesse is solid; the source is not. | Suggested reattribution: Hermann Hesse (spelling correction, same person)

author: Herman Hesse
text: One who says no to himself cannot say yes to God.
notes: I cannot place this in any Hesse work I know. The theological framing (self-affirmation as a precondition for affirming God) is compatible with Hesse's post-Demian thought but is also standard 20th-century Protestant-existentialist phrasing, so the resemblance is weak evidence. Short aphorisms of this shape circulate under Hesse's name from the Reflections compilation without individual sourcing. Honest answer: I do not know.

author: Herman Hesse
text: The life of a hedonist is the best preparation for being a mystic.
notes: I cannot place this line in Hesse. The hedonist-to-mystic idea is thematically at home in Steppenwolf and Narcissus and Goldmund, but thematic fit is not evidence of authorship, and the epigrammatic English phrasing does not match any passage I can recall. Possible it derives from a compiler's condensation of a longer Hesse passage rather than a sentence he wrote. Unverified.

author: Herman Hesse
text: Prayer is as holy, as sanctifying as song. Prayer is trust, is confirmation. Whoever prays truly does not ask for anything, he merely recounts his condition and his wants, he sings forth his suffering and his thanks, as little children sing. So the blessed hermits prayed in their oasis among the deer... So trees also pray, and animals. In the pictures of a good painter, every tree and every mountain prays.
keywords: prayer; song; trust; ask; desire; sing; suffering; gratitude; children; hermit; trees; animals; painter; artist; mountain; art
notes: A long translated passage rather than an aphorism, which itself argues for authenticity - fabricated quotes are rarely this extended or this specific ('the blessed hermits... in their oasis among the deer'; 'in the pictures of a good painter, every tree and every mountain prays'). The voice and imagery are strongly Hesse. I believe it is genuine but I cannot identify which work it comes from, so I am leaving the source null rather than guessing between Narcissus and Goldmund, Wandering, and the essays. | Suggested reattribution: Hermann Hesse (spelling correction, same person)

author: Hildegard von Bingen
text: We shall awaken from our dullness and rise vigorously toward justice. If we fall in love with Creation more and more deeply, we will respond to its endangerment with a sacred passion.
keywords: justice; creation; awaken; love; deep; respond; threat; passion; sacred; protect
notes: The language is anachronistic for a 12th-century abbess. 'Creation... its endangerment' frames an ecological crisis that has no 12th-century counterpart, and 'rise vigorously toward justice' reads as modern social-justice idiom. Lines of this kind entered circulation through the Matthew Fox creation-spirituality treatments of Hildegard in the 1980s, which are loose renderings and adaptations rather than translations. I am fairly confident this is not a faithful Hildegard text, but I cannot pin the specific modern author or book, so I am not naming Fox as the source.

author: Hindu Proverb
text: When we take one step toward God, God takes seven steps toward us.
keywords: step; god; self; intention; support; help
notes: Folk-proverbial with no traceable source. Near-identical formulations appear across several traditions - a hadith qudsi ('if he draws near to Me a hand's span, I draw near to him an arm's length; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running'), a Talmudic version, and Sufi and Sikh retellings - which is the signature of a migrating saying rather than a fixed Hindu text. I know of no Sanskrit scriptural locus for the 'one step / seven steps' form.

author: Hindu Proverb
text: If God wished to hide, God would chose man to hide in.
notes: I cannot trace this to any Hindu source. It resembles a widely retold parable in which the gods hide divinity inside the human being as the last place anyone would look - a story usually presented as 'Hindu legend' in Western popular writing but with no scriptural citation I know of. The epigram itself reads as a modern English formulation. Also note the typo in the stored text: 'chose' should be 'choose'.

author: Hippocrates
text: Let food be your medicine, and medicine be your food.
notes: A well-documented misattribution. The line does not appear in the Hippocratic Corpus; the standard reference on this is Diana Cardenas's 2013 paper in e-SPEN Journal, 'Let not thy food be confused with thy medicine: The Hippocratic misquotation', which searched the corpus and found no such statement, and which traces the saying's spread to 20th-century nutrition and natural-health writing. The Hippocratic texts do discuss diet as part of regimen, but that is a general theme, not this sentence. Treat any 'Hippocrates' tag on this as false; the true originator is not identifiable.

author: Hodding Carter, Jr.
text: There are two lasting bequests we can give our children: One is roots. The other is wings.
notes: Attribution to Hodding Carter Jr. (1907-1972) is near-universal, but as far as I know nobody has located the sentence in anything Carter wrote or in a dated speech. Quote Investigator's work on 'roots and wings' found earlier and anonymous variants circulating before the Carter tag became standard, which suggests he popularized rather than coined it. The saying is also sometimes given as a 'Chinese proverb' or attributed to Goethe, both without support. Plausible but unsourced.

author: Horace
text: Well begun is half done.
earliest_print_source: Horace, Epistles I.2, line 40 (c. 20 BCE): 'Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet'
notes: The Horatian line is genuine and is the usual ancestor cited for this English proverb, but it literally says 'he who has begun has half the deed done' - the 'well begun' element is the English proverb's addition. The same idea is older and Greek-proverbial (Hesiod's 'the beginning is half of the whole'; Aristotle quotes the proverb in the Politics and Nicomachean Ethics), so 'Well begun is half done' is better described as a proverb with a Horatian pedigree than as a Horace quotation. Attribution defensible, exact wording not his.

author: Hubert Selby, Jr.
text: Sometimes we have the absolute certainty that there's something inside us that's so hideous and monstrous that if we ever search it out we won't be able to stand looking at it. But it's when we're willing to come face to face with that demon that we face the angel.
notes: Consistently attributed to Hubert Selby Jr. with no competing author, and the cadence and preoccupations match him closely. My recollection is that it comes from a late-career interview or from the documentary material about him rather than from a novel, but I cannot pin a specific interview, publication, or date, so I am leaving the source null.

author: Hubert Selby, Jr.
text: Being an artist doesn't take much, just everything you got. Which means, of course, that as the process is giving you life, it is also bringing you closer to death. But it's no big deal. They are one and the same and cannot be avoided or denied. So when I totally embrace this process, this life/death, and abandon myself to it, I transcend all this meaningless gibberish and hang out with the gods. It seems to me that that is worth the price of admission.
keywords: art; artist; life; giving; death; embrace; transcend; gods; price; worth
notes: Consistently attributed to Selby and stylistically unmistakable - the vernacular register ('it's no big deal', 'worth the price of admission') alongside the life/death framing is his. Its length and specificity argue against fabrication. I recall it as coming from Selby's own prose or an interview about the work, but I cannot identify the piece, so no source is claimed.

author: Huston Smith
text: All other attributes of a realized being must be relativized against this one absolute: an acute sense of the astonishing mystery of everything.
notes: Reads as authentic Huston Smith - 'relativized against this one absolute' is his comparative-religion register, and the primacy of astonishment over other marks of realization is a recurring Smith theme. I have a weak recollection of the phrasing but cannot place the book (Why Religion Matters, The Way Things Are, and Cleansing the Doors of Perception are all plausible and I will not guess among them). Attribution likely correct, source unverified.

author: IDEO
text: Enlightened trial and error succeeds over the planning of the lone genius.
notes: A genuine IDEO maxim, closely associated with David Kelley and with the firm's design-thinking teaching materials; it circulates widely in innovation literature with the attribution to IDEO-as-organization held stable. I believe it appears in the Kelley brothers' published work on IDEO's method but I cannot confirm which book or page, so I am not citing one. Attributing to an organization rather than a person is itself appropriate here.

author: Ifeanyi Onuoha
text: Teamwork is the secret that makes common people achieve uncommon results.
notes: Attributed on quote aggregators to Ifeanyi Enoch Onuoha, a contemporary Nigerian author and speaker, but I know of no book, talk, or dated publication where it appears - aggregator-only attributions of this kind are weak evidence. The line is also a close derivative of the widely circulated Andrew Carnegie teamwork quotation ('the fuel that allows common people to attain uncommon results'), which is itself of doubtful Carnegie provenance. Possible restatement rather than original coinage.

author: Imogen Cunningham
text: Which of my photographs is my favorite? The one I’m going to take tomorrow.
keywords: photograph; image; photographer; artist; tomorrow; favorite
notes: A signature Imogen Cunningham line, given in interviews in her last years and repeated in profiles and documentary material about her; the attribution is stable and I am not aware of it being claimed for any other photographer. I cannot cite the specific interview or its date, so the source stays null, but the attribution itself is strong.

author: Indian Proverb
text: When you were born, you cried and the world rejoiced. Live your life in such a way so that when you die, the world cries and you rejoice.
notes: Untraceable and multiply claimed. The same saying circulates as an 'Indian proverb', a 'Native American proverb' (often tagged to a 'White Elk', a figure of doubtful historicity), a 'Cherokee saying', and in Persian and Islamic devotional forms. That spread across unrelated traditions is characteristic of a modern inspirational composition retrofitted with an exotic attribution. I know of no Sanskrit or other original text for it.

author: Indira Gandhi
text: My grandfather once told me that there were two kinds of people: those who do the work and those who take the credit. He told me to try to be in the first group; there was much less competition.
notes: Consistently attributed to Indira Gandhi and internally coherent - her grandfather was Motilal Nehru, so the framing device fits her biography rather than being generic. It appears in political-quotation collections with the attribution stable. Note this is Indira Gandhi, not Mohandas Gandhi, so the usual Gandhi misattribution magnet does not apply here. I cannot cite the speech or interview of origin.

author: Inscribed on St. Paul's Monastery, Mt. Athos
text: If you die before you die, then you won't die when you die.
notes: The attribution to an inscription at St Paul's Monastery on Mount Athos comes largely from Eckhart Tolle, who cites it that way in The Power of Now (1997). I am not aware of any independent documentation that the inscription exists or of a transcription by anyone who visited. The underlying formula is old and widespread - the Sufi and hadith-derived 'die before you die', and the Christian ascetic tradition of dying to self - so the sentiment is genuinely ancient even if this English epigram and its Athos provenance are not confirmable. Source claim unverified.

author: Irish Proverb
text: Give cheerfully with one hand and you will gather well with two.
notes: I cannot trace this to any proverb collection I know. Generic 'Irish proverb' tags are among the least reliable in quotation corpora - they are frequently applied to modern greeting-card sentiments and to translations of sayings from other traditions. The give-with-one-hand / gather-with-two structure is a common proverbial shape without a fixed home. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know.

author: Irish Proverb
text: God is good, but never dance in a small boat.
notes: Circulates widely in proverb collections and greeting-card compilations as an Irish saying, but I cannot place it in any Irish-language source, folklore collection, or dated print appearance. 'Irish Proverb' is a common catch-all label attached to humorous one-liners of uncertain origin. Honest answer: origin unknown; the folk-attribution is plausible but unevidenced.

author: Isaac Mizrahi
text: Style makes you feels great because it takes your mind off the fact that you're going to die.
notes: Consistently and widely attributed to fashion designer Isaac Mizrahi, and the sentiment and phrasing match his public persona and interview style (his remarks around the 1995 documentary 'Unzipped' and later press). I cannot place the specific interview or publication, so no print source is given. Note the input text reads 'makes you feels great' — an apparent transcription error for 'makes you feel great'.

author: Italian Proverb
text: Often he who does too much does too little.
notes: Appears in English-language proverb dictionaries under the Italian heading, likely rendering something on the order of 'Chi troppo fa, nulla fa' / 'Chi troppo vuole nulla stringe'. I cannot confirm a specific Italian original or an earliest print appearance. Generic proverb attribution, no traceable source.

author: J. L. Borges
text: To die for a religion is easier than to live it absolutely.
notes: I recall this as genuine Borges, from the story 'Deutsches Requiem' (collected in 'El Aleph', 1949; English in 'Labyrinths'), Spanish along the lines of 'Morir por una religión es más simple que vivirla con plenitud.' The attribution to Borges is strong and consistent; because I am recalling rather than verifying the exact volume and translation, I have left earliest_print_source null rather than assert a citation I cannot check.

author: Jack Kornfield
text: The greater the challenge, the greater the heat. The greater the heat, the greater the purification.
notes: I cannot place this in Kornfield's published work. The crucible/purification metaphor is common across contemporary spiritual writing and is not distinctively his idiom (his register tends toward the plainer and more psychological). No evidence of a specific book, talk, or dated source. Attribution unsupported by anything I actually know.

author: Jack Kornfield
text: The true task of spiritual life is not found in faraway places or unusual states of consciousness. It is here in the present. It asks of us a welcoming spirit to greet all that life presents to us with a wise, respectful, and kindly heart. We can bow to both beauty and suffering, to our entanglements and confusion, to our fears and to the injustices of the world. Honoring the truth in this way is the path to freedom.
keywords: spiritual; life; discovery; consciousness; present; welcome; spirit; wisdom; heart; kindness; beauty; suffering; buddhist; confusion; fear; injustice; world; honoring; truth; freedom; path
notes: Strongly consistent with Jack Kornfield's voice and central themes — the ordinary present over exotic states, the 'wise and kindly heart', bowing to both beauty and suffering — and reads like a closing passage from 'A Path with Heart' (1993) or 'After the Ecstasy, the Laundry' (2000). I cannot confirm which book or page, so no citation is given. Author plausible and likely; source unlocated.

author: Jack Kornfield
text: In honoring our own unique destiny, we allow our most personal life to become an expression of the Buddha in a new form.
keywords: destiny; unique; personal; life; self; expression; form; individuality
notes: Idiomatically consistent with Kornfield (the theme of one's particular life as the vehicle of awakening runs through 'A Path with Heart'), but I cannot locate the passage. The 'Buddhism, Theravada' context tag matches his lineage and adds nothing independent. Author plausible; unverified.

author: Jack Kornfield
text: A spiritual life doesn't make you a good person. You are a good person; you are a holy being when you are born. What spiritual life does is remind us that this is who we really are.
keywords: spiritual; life; good; person; holy; birth; remind; self; true
notes: Reads like transcribed spoken teaching — an interview or dharma talk rather than a book — which is a common source for quotes circulating under Kornfield's name and also a common source of loose paraphrase. The 'original goodness' framing is genuinely his, but I cannot tie this wording to a specific talk or publication.

author: Jack Parr
text: My life seems like one long obstacle course, with me as the chief obstacle.
notes: Consistently attributed to the American talk-show host Jack Paar (1918-2004), whose self-deprecating style this matches; it is often associated with his memoir 'I Kid You Not' (1960), though I cannot confirm that placement. Note the author field misspells his surname as 'Parr' — it should be Paar. Attribution to Paar is solid; the print source is not. | Suggested reattribution: Jack Paar (spelling correction; not 'Jack Parr')

author: Jack Welch
text: The world beyond will not belong to 'managers' or those who can make the numbers dance. The world will belong to passionate, driven leaders — people who will not only have enormous amounts of energy but who can energize those whom they lead.
notes: Genuine Jack Welch, and I recall the fuller original as 'The world of the Nineties and beyond will not belong to managers or those who can make the numbers dance...' from his letter to shareholders in a General Electric annual report of the early 1990s (1991 is the year I associate with it). The quoted text here has clipped 'of the Nineties' out of the opening phrase, leaving the ungrammatical 'The world beyond'. Attribution strong; exact document and year recalled but not verified, so no citation asserted.

author: Jackie Gleason
text: Our dreams are firsthand creations, rather than residues of waking life. We have the capacity for infinite creativity; at least while dreaming, we partake of the power of the Spirit, the infinite Godhead that creates the cosmos.
keywords: dreams; creation; life; infinite; creativity; power; god; universe
notes: The attribution is doubtful. Jackie Gleason did have a serious documented interest in parapsychology and the occult and assembled a large library on it, which is probably why the name attracts material like this, but the diction here ('firsthand creations, rather than residues of waking life', 'the infinite Godhead that creates the cosmos') reads as academic dream-studies or transpersonal-psychology prose, not a comedian's remark. I suspect it originates in a book on dreaming and was later mislabeled, but I cannot identify the real author, so I am not proposing one.

author: Jacob Needleman
text: What is the role of money in the search for meaning? Is our relationship to it one of the chief factors that keeps us in our prison, or could it also be a tool for breaking out, for awakening to a life filled with intensity of purpose?
keywords: money; meaning; prison; tool; awakening; life; purpose
notes: The subject and framing match Jacob Needleman's 'Money and the Meaning of Life' (1991) closely enough that I believe it is his — the book is built on exactly this question of whether money imprisons or can be turned toward awakening. I cannot confirm the wording or locate the page, so the citation is left null rather than asserted from a topical match.

author: Jacob Needleman
text: God acts in history: that is, God provides ideas, methods, and experiences intended to bring comprehension to man, an understanding heart, a conscious life.
keywords: god; history; ideas; experiences; understanding; people; heart; life; conscious
notes: Compatible with Needleman's religious-philosophical writing ('Lost Christianity', 1980; 'The American Soul', 2002) and with the Gurdjieffian vocabulary of 'conscious life' and 'understanding heart' that runs through his work, but I cannot place the sentence in any specific book. Author plausible; source unlocated.

author: Jalaja Bonheim
text: Ecstasy blows our minds open to a reality that is wild, beautiful, loving, abundant beyond our wildest dreams.
notes: Jalaja Bonheim is a real author on embodied spirituality whose books include 'Aphrodite's Daughters' (1997) and 'The Hunger for Ecstasy' (2001); this line's subject matter points to the latter. The attribution is plausible and I know of no competing claimant, but I cannot confirm the passage, so this stays unverified.

author: James A. Baldwin
text: Those who say it can't be done are usually interrupted by others doing it.
notes: This is a floating saying with many earlier variants ('Let no one who says it cannot be done interrupt the one doing it'; 'The person who says it cannot be done should not interrupt the person doing it'), circulating from the early twentieth century and credited over the years to a Chinese proverb, Confucius, George Bernard Shaw, and Elbert Hubbard — a pattern that indicates no settled origin. I have no evidence that any James Baldwin, novelist or otherwise, originated it, and the 'James A. Baldwin' form suggests a name that accreted rather than a documented author. Because I cannot identify the true origin, I am not proposing a reattribution.

author: James Allen
text: Our life is what our thoughts make it. A man will find that as he alters his thoughts toward things and other people, things and other people will alter towards him.
notes: This is a splice of two different authors presented as one quotation. The first sentence, 'Our life is what our thoughts make it', is Marcus Aurelius, from the 'Meditations'. The second sentence is genuine James Allen, from 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), where it reads 'A man will find that as he alters his thoughts towards things and other people, things and other people will alter towards him.' Attributing the combined text to Allen alone is wrong; the two halves should be separated or the Marcus Aurelius line dropped. | Suggested reattribution: Composite: sentence 1 Marcus Aurelius (Meditations); sentence 2 James Allen (As a Man Thinketh, 1903)

author: James Allen
text: You are today where your thoughts have brought you; you will be tomorrow where your thoughts take you.
notes: Consistently attributed to James Allen and fully consistent with the argument of 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), but I cannot confirm that this exact aphorism appears there rather than in one of his other volumes ('The Path of Prosperity', 'Above Life's Turmoil') or in a later paraphrase of his ideas. Its neat antithetical shape is typical of summary lines that get condensed out of longer passages, so I am not asserting a citation.

author: James Allen
text: You will become as small as your controlling desire, or as great as your dominant aspiration.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to James Allen, usually to 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), and the desire/aspiration contrast is squarely his. As with the companion line, I cannot confirm the exact volume or wording — the commonly seen form uses a semicolon, 'as small as your controlling desire; as great as your dominant aspiration' — so no print citation is asserted.

author: James Allen, As a Man Thinketh
text: The dreamers are the redeemers of the world.
earliest_print_source: As a Man Thinketh, James Allen, 1903
notes: The author and source in the input are correct, but the wording is a variant. The original line in the 'Visions and Ideals' chapter of 'As a Man Thinketh' reads 'The dreamers are the saviours of the world.' 'Redeemers' is a later substitution. Recommend restoring 'saviours' (or 'saviors') to match the 1903 text; the attribution itself is sound.

author: James Arthur Baldwin
text: To defend one's self against fear is simply to ensure that one will, one day, be conquered by it; fears must be faced.
notes: I believe this is authentic James Baldwin — the cadence, the semicolon construction, and the moral argument are unmistakably his essayistic voice, and it is generally cited to his early-1960s essays, most often 'Nobody Knows My Name' (1961). I cannot confirm the specific essay or page, so no citation is asserted. Note this is the same person as q_0775's 'James Baldwin'; the corpus should normalize the author name across both.

author: James Arthur Ray
text: There is no happiness if the things you believe are different than the things you do.
notes: This closely tracks a well-known line by the British travel writer Freya Stark, usually quoted as 'There can be no happiness if the things we believe in are different from the things we do', associated with her writing collected in 'The Journey's Echo'. The version here is a loose reworded form credited to the self-help author James Arthur Ray. I am confident the underlying thought is Stark's; recommend reattributing and restoring her wording, or dropping the quote. | Suggested reattribution: Freya Stark

author: James Arthur Ray
text: It is noble to charge a fortune for your services if you provide a fortune in value.
keywords: noble; value; money; service; fortune; work
notes: Consistent with James Arthur Ray's prosperity-teaching material ('Harmonic Wealth', 2008) and with the seminar idiom of that genre, but I cannot place it in a specific book or talk. Worth flagging for editorial reasons independent of provenance: Ray was convicted of negligent homicide following the 2009 Sedona sweat-lodge deaths, which the corpus owner may wish to weigh before promoting quotes under his name.

author: James Baldwin
text: We are all miracles but seldom act like miracles.
notes: I cannot place this in James Baldwin's essays, novels, or interviews, and the flat inspirational-poster phrasing is unlike his prose, which is dense, ironic, and syntactically complex. The name 'James Baldwin' attracts unsourced uplift of this kind. I have no candidate true author, so no reattribution is proposed — but the attribution should be treated as unsupported.

author: James G. Bilkey
text: You never will be the person you can be if pressure, tension and discipline are taken out of your life.
notes: Circulates in motivational quote compilations attributed to 'James G. Bilkey,' a figure I cannot place with any biographical certainty — no book, speech, or article of his that I know of. The attribution is consistent across quote sites but that is echo, not evidence. No primary source in my knowledge.

author: James King
text: Our purpose is hidden in our joy, our inspiration, our excitement. As we act on what shows up in our life our purpose shows up.
notes: 'James King' is too common a name to anchor an attribution, and I have no recall of this line in any identifiable work. It reads like generic late-20th-century self-help prose. Honest answer: I don't know who wrote it.

author: James Levin
text: Follow effective action with quiet reflection. From the quiet reflection will come even more effective action.
notes: Contested attribution. This line is far more commonly attributed to Peter F. Drucker in management literature than to 'James Levin,' and I cannot verify either. I have no primary Drucker source for it, so I am not asserting a reattribution — but the 'James Levin' credit is the minority claim and should be treated as weak. Flag for human review.

author: James Oppenheim
text: The foolish man seeks happiness in the distance, the wise grows it under his feet.
notes: James Oppenheim (1882-1932) was a real American poet and novelist (best known for 'Bread and Roses'), and this line is consistently credited to him across quotation collections, which is mildly reassuring. But I cannot place it in any specific poem, novel, or essay of his, and the consistency may just reflect a single anthology entry copied forward.

author: James Thornton
text: ... no matter what our difficulties may be, we recognize that there is a deep untroubled stream flowing below all surface troubles and that we are of one substance with that stream. The soul knows no difficulties.
notes: There is a James Thornton (environmental lawyer and author) who wrote 'A Field Guide to the Soul' (1999), and the vocabulary here — soul, untroubled stream, one substance — would fit that book. That is inference from style, not recall of the passage, so I am not recording it as a source. Attribution unconfirmed.

author: Jay-Z
text: Artists can have greater access to reality; they can see patterns and details and connections that other people, distracted by the blur of life, might miss. Just sharing that truth can be a very powerful thing.
notes: Plausibly Jay-Z — the register matches his memoir 'Decoded' (2010), which contains extended reflection on artists and perception, and he has spoken this way about Basquiat in interviews. But I cannot locate this exact passage in 'Decoded' or in a specific interview from memory, so I will not cite it.

author: Jean Shinoda Bolen
text: To know how to choose a path with heart is to learn how to follow intuitive feeling. Logic can tell you superficially where a path might lead to, but it cannot judge whether your heart will be in it.
notes: Consistently attributed to Jean Shinoda Bolen and most often traced to 'The Tao of Psychology: Synchronicity and the Self' (1979). The 'path with heart' framing is Bolen engaging Castaneda's Don Juan, which fits that book's argument well. I have moderate recall of the association but not of the page or exact edition, so I am leaving the print source null rather than manufacturing a citation.

author: Jean Shinoda Bolen
text: I think that whenever soul is present, it’s because what you’re doing, whom you’re with, where you are, evokes love without your thinking about it. You are totally absorbed in the place or person or event, without ego and without judgment.
notes: The 'I think that...' opener and the conversational cadence suggest a spoken interview rather than a book, which would fit Bolen's many magazine interviews (Common Boundary, New Dimensions, etc.). The content is consonant with her work on soul and Jungian psychology, but I cannot identify the specific interview or book, so the attribution stands unverified.

author: Jean-Michel Basquiat
text: I don’t listen to what art critics say. I don’t know anybody who needs a critic to find out what art is.
notes: Widely and consistently credited to Basquiat and entirely in keeping with his documented hostility to critics. It most likely comes from one of his early-1980s interviews (the Henry Geldzahler conversation in Interview magazine, 1983, is the usual candidate), but I cannot confirm which interview, so no citation is recorded.

author: Jean-Paul Sartre
text: Freedom is what you do with what's been done to you.
notes: A popular English condensation rather than a translated Sartre sentence. The authentic Sartre formulation is 'L'important n'est pas ce qu'on fait de nous, mais ce que nous faisons nous-meme de ce qu'on a fait de nous' — what matters is not what has been made of us but what we make of what has been made of us — from 'Saint Genet' (1952) and echoed in 'Search for a Method' (1957). The idea is genuinely Sartre's; this exact aphoristic wording is not traceable to him. Use with care if quoted as his words.

author: Jeanne Kirkpatrick
text: We have war when at least one of the parties to a conflict wants something more than it wants peace.
notes: The author's name is misspelled in the corpus: the US diplomat and political scientist was Jeane J. Kirkpatrick (not Jeanne). The line is commonly credited to her and matches her realist idiom from the UN ambassadorship years, but I cannot place it in a specific speech, column, or book. Correct the spelling regardless of the provenance verdict. | Suggested reattribution: Jeane J. Kirkpatrick (spelling correction — same author)

author: Jeff Brown
text: When you love someone fully, you are always kissing the divine.
notes: Jeff Brown is a contemporary author ('Soulshaping,' 'Love It Forward,' 'Grounded Spirituality') whose aphorisms circulate heavily on social media, and this is stylistically his. Because his short lines are published as standalone posts and later collected, the original venue is hard to pin down; I cannot confirm a book or date.

author: Jeff Esper
text: The success of the decisions you make depends ultimately on what you make of your decisions.
notes: I have no knowledge of 'Jeff Esper' as an author or speaker, and no recall of this line anywhere. It has the shape of a filler entry in a bulk quote database. I don't know who wrote it.

author: Jeffrey Leaver
text: Love is the final destination of the soul, and the road that leads it home.
notes: 'Jeffrey Leaver' is not an author I can identify, and I have no recall of this line in print. Attractive phrasing, untraceable origin — the honest verdict is that I don't know.

author: Jennie Jerome Churchill
text: Treat your friends as you do your pictures, and place them in their best light.
notes: Standard attribution to Lady Randolph Churchill (Jennie Jerome Churchill, 1854-1921), and it appears in older printed quotation dictionaries rather than only in modern web lists, which is a point in its favor. Her memoir 'The Reminiscences of Lady Randolph Churchill' (1908) is the plausible origin but I cannot confirm the passage. Note: not Winston Churchill — worth guarding against downstream drift, given Churchill's status as a misattribution magnet.

author: Jerry Gillies
text: You will recognize your own path when you come upon it, because you will suddenly have all the energy and imagination you will ever need.
notes: Jerry Gillies is a real author ('Moneylove,' 1978; 'Psychological Immunity'), and the attribution is consistent across quote collections. I cannot locate the line in a specific book of his, and the evidence is entirely secondary.

author: Jim Allen
text: Recognize that life is what you get when you’re born... living is what you do with it.
notes: 'Jim Allen' is unidentifiable as an author here, and I have no recall of this aphorism in any source. Unknown origin.

author: Jim Rohn
text: I have found in life that if you want a miracle you first need to do whatever it is you can do - if that's to plant, then plant; if it is to read, then read; if it is to change, then change; if it is to study, then study; if it is to work, then work; whatever you have to do. And then you will be well on your way of doing the labor that works miracles.
notes: The cadence — the list of parallel conditionals, 'the labor that works miracles' — is characteristically Jim Rohn's seminar delivery, and the attribution is consistent. But Rohn's material lives mostly in recorded seminars and later transcript compilations, so a specific book and date are hard to fix, and I cannot supply one.

author: Jim Rohn
text: If you go to work on your goals, your goals will go to work on you. If you go to work on your plan, your plan will go to work on you. Whatever good things we build end up building us.
notes: A signature Jim Rohn formulation; 'whatever good things we build end up building us' is one of his most-repeated lines and is uncontested in attribution. It is usually cited from his seminar material and the compilation 'The Treasury of Quotes' (1994), but since Rohn's aphorisms were spoken first and printed later, I cannot fix a first appearance and am not recording a citation.

author: Joan Baez
text: The easiest kind of relationship is with ten thousand people, the hardest is with one.
notes: Consistently attributed to Joan Baez and usually traced to her 1968 memoir 'Daybreak,' whose fragmentary, confessional style fits this line well. I have moderate recall of that association but not of the passage itself, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting it.

author: Joan Baez
text: Action is the antidote to despair.
notes: A well-known Baez line, uncontested in attribution and one she has repeated across decades of interviews and activist speeches — it functions almost as a personal motto. No competing claimant that I know of. I cannot name the first documented utterance, so no citation is recorded.

author: Joan Borysenko
text: Learning to be aware of feelings, how they arise and how to use them creatively so they guide us to happiness, is an essential lifetime skill.
notes: Consonant with Joan Borysenko's mind-body work ('Minding the Body, Mending the Mind,' 1987), and I know of no competing attribution, but I cannot place this sentence in a specific book or article of hers. Attribution plausible, evidence thin.

author: Joan Borysenko
text: If we don’t forgive ourselves for our mistakes, and others for the wounds they have inflicted upon us, we end up crippled with guilt. And the soul cannot grow under a blanket of guilt, because guilt is isolating, while growth is a gradual process of reconnection to ourselves, to other people, and to a larger whole.
keywords: forgiveness; mistakes; wounds; guilt; cripple; soul; growth; isolation; whole; connection; self; people; vast
notes: Strongly in Borysenko's voice and squarely in the territory of 'Guilt Is the Teacher, Love Is the Lesson' (1990) and 'Fire in the Soul' (1993). That is a thematic match, not a located passage, so I am not recording either as the source. Attribution plausible but unverified.

author: Joe Sparano
text: Good design is obvious. Great design is transparent.
notes: Ubiquitous in design-quote roundups credited to 'Joe Sparano,' a graphic designer, but I cannot identify a talk, article, book, or interview where he said it, nor much about him beyond the quote itself. This is the classic profile of an attribution that propagated through listicles from a single unsourced entry. Treat with suspicion despite its familiarity.

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: To think is easy. To act is difficult. To act as one thinks is the most difficult.
notes: A German original circulates alongside the English ('Denken ist leicht, handeln schwer, handeln nach Gedanken das Unbequemste auf der Welt'), which is a good sign the line is genuinely Goethe's rather than an English-language invention. My recollection places it in the Wilhelm Meister material / Maximen und Reflexionen, but I cannot confirm the exact work or locus, so I am not naming one. Attribution consistent and long-standing; the specific citation is what is missing.

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: My greatest wealth is the deep stillness in which I strive and grow and win what the world cannot take from me with fire or sword.
keywords: wealth; quiet; stillness; grow; win; world fire; sword; effort
notes: Circulates widely in gratitude and creativity anthologies attributed to Goethe, and a German rendering also circulates, but I cannot place it in any Goethe work, letter, or conversation I know. The imagery ('with fire or sword') is plausible for Goethe but equally plausible as a loose translation or an anthology-era paraphrase. No source named; honest uncertainty.

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: As soon as you trust yourself, you will know how to live.
notes: I recognize the German line 'Sobald du dir vertraust, sobald weisst du zu leben' and associate it with Faust, Part One (1808), spoken by Mephistopheles. I am confident enough in the German original to call the Goethe attribution sound, but not confident enough in the exact scene or line number to print a citation, so earliest_print_source is left null rather than guessed.

author: Johannes A. Gaertner
text: To speak gratitude is courteous and pleasant, to enact gratitude is generous and noble, but to live gratitude is to touch Heaven.
earliest_print_source: Worldly Virtues: A Catalogue of Reflections, Johannes A. Gaertner, 1990
notes: Gaertner (Lafayette College art historian) is the consistent and essentially exclusive attribution for this line, and my recollection ties it to his aphorism collection Worldly Virtues. The book and author are real and the pairing is stable across sources; I am slightly hedged on whether 1990 is the first edition year, hence 0.7 rather than higher. Attribution itself is not in doubt.

author: John Balguy
text: Contentment is a pearl of great price, and whoever procures it at the expense of ten thousand desires makes a wise and a happy purchase.
notes: John Balguy (1686-1748), English divine, is the standard attribution, and the line appears in nineteenth-century compilations such as Tryon Edwards' A Dictionary of Thoughts. But dictionary-of-quotations attributions of that era are frequently unsourced or laundered, and I cannot place this sentence in any of Balguy's own writings (Divine Rectitude, the Foundation of Moral Goodness, etc.). Plausible but unverified.

author: John Berry
text: The bird of paradise alights only on the hand that does not grasp.
notes: Consistently attributed to the American novelist John Berry, and my recollection associates it with his novel Flight of White Crows (1961) - but I am not confident enough in that title-to-quote link to print it as a citation. The attribution to Berry is stable across sources; the source work is the uncertain part.

author: John Bradshaw
text: Our sadness is an energy we discharge in order to heal. …Sadness is painful. We try to avoid it. Actually discharging sadness releases the energy involved in our emotional pain. To hold it in is to freeze the pain within us. The therapeutic slogan is that grieving is the ‘healing feeling.’

notes: The voice, vocabulary ('discharge', 'the healing feeling', 'therapeutic slogan') and subject matter are strongly characteristic of John Bradshaw's recovery writing, most likely Homecoming: Reclaiming and Championing Your Inner Child (1990) or Healing the Shame That Binds You (1988). I cannot determine which book or page, and long prose passages like this are often stitched together from non-adjacent sentences (note the internal ellipsis), so the exact wording may not match any single printed passage.

author: John Cage

author: John E. Southard
text: The only people with whom you should try to get even are those who have helped you.

author: John F. Kennedy
text: The problems of the world cannot possibly be solved by skeptics or cynics whose horizons are limited by the obvious realities. We need people who can dream of things that never were.
keywords: problems; difficulties; solution; skeptic; cynic; horizon; limit; obvious; reality; people; dream; possibilities; imagination
notes: Authentic Kennedy in substance and phrasing; he returned repeatedly to the George Bernard Shaw line 'I dream things that never were and say why not' (Back to Methuselah), most famously in his address to the Irish Parliament, 28 June 1963. WORDING NOTE: Kennedy said 'We need men who can dream of things that never were'; the corpus text has been silently modernized to 'people'. If promoted, either restore the original or mark it as adapted.

author: John F. Kennedy
text: I am certain that after the dust of centuries has passed over our cities, we, too, will be remembered not for victories or defeats in battle or in politics, but for our contribution to the human spirit.
keywords: dust; time; victory; defeat; battle; war; politics; contribution; spirit; human; purpose; work
notes: Authentic Kennedy from his set of remarks on the arts and national culture. My recollection points to either the Amherst College address honoring Robert Frost (26 October 1963) or his remarks for the National Cultural Center (1962); both are real speeches with closely related language, and I cannot tell which contains this sentence. Attribution to JFK is solid; the specific occasion is not, so no source is printed.

author: John Foster Dulles
text: The measure of success is not whether you have a tough problem to deal with, but whether it's the same problem you had last year.
notes: Attributed to Dulles with fair consistency in management and leadership literature, but I cannot tie it to any speech, dispatch, or writing of his. The formulation reads more like postwar business-book aphorism than diplomatic prose, which raises the possibility that a management author coined or reshaped it and the Dulles name attached later. No evidence of a specific alternate author, so no reattribution suggested.

author: John Gray
text: When we experience the pain of another person, we instinctively want to take away that pain. But by taking away the other person’s pain, we also take away his or her opportunity to grow. To be truly compassionate, we must be able to share another person’s suffering and pain - knowing there is nothing we can do to relieve it and that we are not responsible for it, and yet knowing and understanding what that pain feels like.
keywords: pain; person; help; suffering; growth; compassionate; nothing; responsible; understanding; feeling
notes: Cannot place this passage. 'John Gray' is ambiguous: the self-help author of Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus and What You Feel, You Can Heal; the political philosopher (Straw Dogs); and others. The therapeutic register suggests the self-help John Gray, but the specific argument (that removing another's pain removes their growth) is a commonplace of pastoral-care and codependency writing and could belong to several authors. Unverified on both source and which John Gray.

author: John Keats
text: Don't be discouraged by a failure. It can be a positive experience. Failure is, in a sense, the highway to success, inasmuch as every discovery of what is false leads us to seek earnestly after what is true, and every fresh experience points out some form of error which we shall afterwards carefully avoid.
keywords: discouragement; failure; positive; experience; highway; success; discovery; false; path; true; fresh; error; avoid
notes: Two problems. (1) The core sentence, 'Failure is, in a sense, the highway to success...', appears in nineteenth-century quotation dictionaries credited to Keats, but I cannot locate it in his letters or poems, and the reasoning about 'discovery of what is false' is uncharacteristically didactic-empiricist for Keats. (2) The opening two sentences ('Don't be discouraged by a failure. It can be a positive experience.') read as a modern motivational preamble grafted onto the older sentence - flat, contemporary diction unlike the rest. Recommend not promoting; at minimum strip the prepended sentences.

author: John Kennedy
text: When written in Chinese the word 'crisis' is composed of two characters. One represents danger, and the other represents opportunity.
notes: The attribution is broadly sound - Kennedy did use this line in campaign-era speeches (I associate it with his 1959-60 addresses, including a United Negro College Fund speech in Indianapolis, April 1959) - but two things should block promotion. (1) FACTUALLY FALSE: the etymology is wrong. Sinologist Victor Mair has repeatedly debunked it; the second character in weiji is ji, meaning incipient moment or crux, not 'opportunity'. (2) NOT ORIGINAL: the trope predates Kennedy in English-language missionary writing on China (Quote Investigator traces it to the late 1930s), so he popularized rather than coined it. Also note the author field reads 'John Kennedy'; should be 'John F. Kennedy'. Recommend rejection on accuracy grounds even though the speaker is real.

author: John MacEnulty
text: Truth is unique to each moment. You cannot step in the same stream twice. So wipe the slate clean. Wake up in this moment and truly be here. Let go of what you think happened. It is gone. It no longer exists. Tell your stories, but don't get stuck in them. This moment is like no other.
keywords: truth; clean; presence; thought; story; now
notes: I have no reliable knowledge of John MacEnulty as a published author and cannot locate this passage in anything I know. The content is a restatement of the Heraclitean river commonplace ('You cannot step in the same stream twice') wrapped in contemporary mindfulness language, which makes independent verification harder rather than easier. No source, no date, no corroborating attribution. Honest answer is that I do not know.

author: John Maeda
text: Design is a solution to a problem. Art is a question to a problem.
notes: Genuine Maeda - the design/art distinction is one of his recurring formulations, expressed in his talks, interviews, and writing (including his TED remarks on art, technology and design). Contemporary and well documented as his, but I cannot pin the first appearance to a specific book, post, or talk transcript, so no citation is printed. Attribution itself is not in question.

author: John Muir
text: Keep close to Nature's heart, yourself; and break clear away, once in a while, and climb a mountain or spend a week in the woods. Wash your spirit clean.
notes: Genuine Muir, from his correspondence rather than a published book; it is reproduced in the standard Muir biographical literature (Bade's The Life and Letters of John Muir, 1924, and Wolfe's John of the Mountains, 1938). I am confident it is his but cannot confirm which volume carries it or the letter's recipient and date, so no citation is printed. Attribution strong, locus unconfirmed.

author: John Muir
text: If one pulls on a single thread in nature, you'll find it attached to everything else.
notes: The thought is Muir's but this is not his wording. It is a loose modern paraphrase of the authentic sentence in My First Summer in the Sierra (1911): 'When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe' - which the corpus already holds correctly as q_0822. The 'pull a single thread' rewording has no basis in Muir's text and also breaks grammatical agreement ('If one pulls... you'll find'). Recommend dropping this in favor of q_0822 rather than promoting a corrupted variant.

author: John Muir
text: The power of imagination makes us infinite.
earliest_print_source: John of the Mountains: The Unpublished Journals of John Muir, ed. Linnie Marsh Wolfe, 1938
notes: Consistently attributed to Muir in the Sierra Club's John Muir quotation collection, which cites his unpublished journals as gathered in John of the Mountains (1938). I recall that pairing but cannot confirm the page or the journal date from memory, so this rests on strong secondary evidence rather than a primary check. No rival claimant known.

author: Anon.
text: A forest is a cathedral where the priest is nature.
notes: Credited to 'Anon.', and I can place no source at all. The line reads as a modern aphorism working a very old trope — the forest-as-cathedral figure runs from Bryant's 'The groves were God's first temples' (1825) through Muir and countless nature writers — but this specific sentence has no traceable origin I know of. Honest answer: unknown, probably an internet-era composition.

author: John Petit-Senn
text: Not what we have but what we enjoy, constitutes our abundance.
notes: Attributed with unusual consistency to Jean-Antoine (John) Petit-Senn (1792-1870), the Swiss-French aphorist whose 'Bluettes et Boutades' was Englished in the 19th century and mined heavily by Victorian quotation dictionaries. The style matches his epigrams and no competing author is ever named. I cannot place the specific collection or year from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing at a title.

author: John Quincy Adams
text: Patience and perseverance have a magical effect before which difficulties disappear and obstacles vanish.
notes: Ubiquitously attributed to John Quincy Adams in quotation compilations, and the sentiment and register are period-plausible, but I cannot locate it in his diaries, letters, or public papers from memory. Wide repetition in secondary collections is not evidence of origin. No contrary attribution known either, so this is honest uncertainty rather than suspicion of a specific misattribution.

author: John Quincy Adams
text: If your actions inspire others to dream more, learn more, do more and become more, you are a leader.
keywords: action; inspiration; learning; more; leader; leadership
notes: A known misattribution magnet. This is modern leadership-seminar prose — 'dream more, learn more, do more, become more' — and its diction is late-20th-century American management writing, not early-19th-century political English. Quote Investigator examined it and found no support in John Quincy Adams's writings, with the earliest sightings in the 1990s motivational literature. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I am not proposing a replacement author.

author: John Quincy Adams
text: Patience and perseverance have a magical effect before which difficulties disappear and obstacles vanish.
keywords: patience; perseverance; difficulties; obstacles; disappear; magic; action
notes: Exact duplicate of q_0829 (same text, same author, different category tag) — flagging for dedupe. Same verdict: consistently attributed to John Quincy Adams across quotation compilations, but I cannot locate it in his diaries, letters, or public papers from training knowledge, and repetition in secondary collections is not provenance.

author: John Randolph Price
text: The time will come when you will satisfy a need for money by steadfastly depending on the Master Self within - and not on anything in the world of form. Until you do this, you will continue to experience the uncertainties of supply for the rest of your life. Every soul must learn this lesson, and until it does, it will be given opportunity after opportunity in the form of apparent lack and limitation. You may be experiencing such a challenge right at this moment. Realize that this is the opportunity you have been waiting for to demonstrate the truth of your birthright.
keywords: money; finance; self; form; soul; learning; opportunity; limitation; experience; challenge
notes: The vocabulary is distinctively John Randolph Price's — 'the Master Self within', 'the world of form', 'your birthright', 'demonstrate the truth' — all core New Thought terms he used throughout The Superbeings (1981) and The Abundance Book (1987), and the subject (money as a spiritual demonstration) is squarely his. Attribution is plausible on internal evidence, but I cannot say which book or page this passage comes from, so I will not name one.

author: John Schaar
text: The future is not some place we are going, but one we are creating. The paths are not to be found, but made. And the activity of making them changes both the maker and their destination.
earliest_print_source: Legitimacy in the Modern State, John H. Schaar, 1981
notes: Genuinely Schaar, the political theorist at UC Santa Cruz, and usually cited to Legitimacy in the Modern State (1981). The canonical wording is longer and slightly different: 'The future is not a result of choices among alternative paths offered by the present, but a place that is created — created first in the mind and will, created next in activity. The future is not some place we are going to, but one we are creating. The paths are not to be found, but made, and the activity of making them changes both the maker and the destination.' The corpus text is an accurate condensation, but 'their destination' is a drift from 'the destination'.

author: John Wesley
text: Do all the good you can, in all the ways you can, to all the souls you can, in every place you can, at all the times you can, with all the zeal you can, as long as you can.
keywords: action; good; time; enthusiasm; consistency; service
notes: Known as 'Wesley's Rule' and printed on a great deal of Methodist material, but Wesley scholars — including the editors of the Wesley Works project and the denomination's own historians — have searched his sermons, journals, and letters and cannot find it. The consensus is that it does not appear anywhere in his authenticated writings; sightings begin well after his death. The attribution is traditional rather than evidenced. I do not know who composed it, so no reattribution.

author: John Wooden
text: Things turn out the best for the people who make the best of the way things turn out.
notes: Wooden used this line constantly in his talks and books and it is one of his signature maxims, so the attribution is not wrong in spirit. But Wooden was a habitual quoter — he credited many of his sayings to his father Joshua and to older sources — and near-identical folk formulations of 'make the best of the way things turn out' circulated in American newspapers before his coaching fame. Safest reading: Wooden is the popularizer, possibly not the originator. Cannot place a first printing.

author: Jorge Luis Borges
text: The history of literature is not the history of authors and their careers, but the history of 'Spirit as the producer and consumer of literature.'
keywords: literature; creation; consumption; history; authors; writers
earliest_print_source: "The Flower of Coleridge" ("La flor de Coleridge"), in Other Inquisitions, Jorge Luis Borges, 1952
notes: Borges did not say this — he quoted it. 'The Flower of Coleridge' opens by citing Paul Valery: around 1938 Valery wrote that the history of literature should not be the history of the authors and the accidents of their careers or of their works, but rather the history of the Spirit as producer or consumer of literature. The internal quotation marks in the corpus text are the tell that something is being relayed. Credit belongs to Valery, with Borges as the conduit. | Suggested reattribution: Paul Valery (quoted by Jorge Luis Borges in "The Flower of Coleridge", Other Inquisitions, 1952)

author: Jorge Luis Borges
text: The history of the universe is an infinite sacred book that all men write and read and try to understand, and in which they are also written.
keywords: book; read; write; understand; history; people; universe
notes: Reads as Borges's own prose from Other Inquisitions (1952), most likely 'On the Cult of Books', where he traces the idea of the world-as-book through Mallarme and Leon Bloy and summarizes Bloy's conception in almost exactly these terms. Caution: as with q_0839, Borges's essays are dense with relayed voices, and this sentence may be his restatement of Bloy rather than a standalone claim of his own. I am confident it is Borges's sentence; less confident which essay, so no print source named.

author: Jorge Luis Borges & Giordano Bruno
text: The world is ‘the infinite effect of an infinite cause’ and divinity is near ‘because it is in us even more than we ourselves are in us.’
keywords: world; infinite; divinity; within; self; cause
notes: A composite, and the dual credit line is actually the right call. The two quoted fragments are Giordano Bruno's — from De la causa, principio e uno (1584) and the companion work on the infinite universe — while the connective framing is Borges's, in the essay 'Pascal's Sphere' (Other Inquisitions, 1952), where he narrates Bruno's exhilaration at the infinite before turning to Pascal's dread. So the words are Bruno via Borges's translation and paraphrase. Confident about the shape of this; not confident enough about which Bruno treatise supplies which fragment to print a citation.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: The goal of life is to make your heartbeat match the beat of the universe, to match your nature with Nature.
notes: Campbell's idiom and one of his recurring themes — aligning individual nature with Nature, the heartbeat/cosmic-rhythm figure he used in both lectures and interviews. Most often cited to A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (ed. Diane K. Osbon, 1991), which is itself a compilation of remarks from workshops rather than a primary text. Plausibly authentic, but I cannot confirm the source, so no citation.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's.
notes: This is a compressed, aphorized version of the longer remark recorded at q_0849 ('If you see your path laid out in front of you...'). Campbell said something in this vein, but I know of no text where he said it this tersely — the one-liner looks like an internet-era tightening of the Osbon-compiled passage. Sentiment authentic, wording probably not his. Recommend preferring the longer form and dropping this as a derivative duplicate.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us.
notes: One of the most heavily misattributed lines in the Campbell corpus. The Joseph Campbell Foundation has publicly addressed it and points to E. M. Forster as the source; Campbell appears to have quoted or adapted it rather than coined it. A variant closer to Campbell's own phrasing ('We must let go of the life we have planned, so as to accept the one that is waiting for us') circulates from A Joseph Campbell Companion. I cannot name the Forster work from memory, so the reattribution below is offered as the documented candidate, not as a verified citation. | Suggested reattribution: E. M. Forster (per the Joseph Campbell Foundation's own correction; specific work unconfirmed)

author: Joseph Campbell
text: “The big question is whether you are going to be able to say a hearty yes to your adventure.
notes: Authentically Campbell's voice and theme — the refusal or acceptance of the call to adventure — and I associate it with the Moyers conversations in The Power of Myth (1988), though it also circulates from the Osbon Companion. I cannot pin which, so no citation. Data note: the text begins with a stray opening curly quote and has no closing one, an ingestion artifact that should be stripped.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: If you see your path laid out in front of you -- Step one, Step two, Step three -- you only know one thing... it is not your path. Your path is created in the moment of action. If you can see it laid out in front of you, you can be sure it is someone else's path. That is why you see it so clearly.
notes: The longer, primary form of the saying compressed at q_0844, and the one I would keep. Usually cited to A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (ed. Diane K. Osbon, 1991), a compilation of Campbell's workshop remarks rather than something he wrote for print. Consistent with his idiom and I have no reason to doubt it, but a compiled-from-talks source is weaker provenance than a book he authored, so I am staying below the promotion bar and naming no citation.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: So yield to what is coming. We're in a free fall into future. We don't know where we're going. Things are changing so fast and always when you're going through a long tunnel anxiety comes along. And all you have to do to transform your hell into a paradise is to turn your fall into a voluntary act. I mean it's a very interesting shift of perspective, and that's all it is. Joyful participation in the sorrows and everything changes.
keywords: future; anxiety; hell; paradise; perspective; joy; sorrow; change; transformation; action
notes: Unmistakably Campbell speaking rather than writing — the asides ('I mean it's a very interesting shift of perspective') mark it as a lecture or interview transcript — and it closes on 'joyful participation in the sorrows', his signature rendering of the Buddhist formula and a phrase he used repeatedly. The 'free fall into future' passage circulates from his late talks and interviews. Authentic in voice and vocabulary; I cannot identify the specific recording or transcript, so no source named.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.
notes: Consistently and near-universally attributed to Campbell, who used the line in late interviews and lectures; it is commonly cited from A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (ed. Diane K. Osbon, 1991), but I cannot confirm that locus from memory, so I leave the print source null. A common variant reads 'the privilege of a lifetime is being who you are' vs. 'is to be who you are' -- the shorter form here is the one Campbell is usually quoted as saying. Note: identical text to q_0854 in this batch (duplicate record).

author: Joseph Campbell
text: You become mature when you become the authority for your own life.
notes: Attribution to Campbell is consistent across quote collections and matches his recurring theme that the mythic 'call' includes assuming authority over one's own life; the sentiment appears in his Pathways to Bliss lectures. I cannot place this exact sentence in a specific published text, so I hold it below the promotion bar rather than assign a source I cannot confirm.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.
notes: Exact duplicate of q_0851's batch-mate q_0852 -- same text, same author, differing only in the empty category field. Same verdict: widely and consistently attributed to Campbell, commonly cited from A Joseph Campbell Companion (1991), but I cannot confirm that locus from training knowledge. Recommend deduplicating against q_0852 downstream.

author: Joy Houghton
text: Spiritual growth is not made in reaction against, for all striving against imposed restrictions is imaginary. Spiritual growth is accomplished by inclination toward. We grow like the sunflower, following the light.
keywords: spiritual; growth; reaction; striving; obstacles; light; flower
notes: I have no knowledge of a writer named Joy Houghton and cannot place this passage in any published work. It circulates in inspirational-quote compilations with no traceable origin. I cannot confirm the attribution, cannot refute it, and will not guess at an alternative author. Honest answer: unknown.

author: Judith Viorst
text: Strength is the capacity to break a chocolate bar into four pieces with your bare hands - and then just eat one of the pieces.
notes: Very widely attributed to Judith Viorst, and the voice fits her humorous essays and light verse (Love and Guilt and the Meaning of Life, Etc.; her Redbook columns). Attribution is consistent across sources, which is mild evidence, but I cannot place it in a specific book, column, or year, so I cannot raise this above unverified.

author: Julia Butterfly
text: Life's circumstances sometimes seem overwhelming, but we must remember the amazing power of love. Just as the ripples in the ocean shape and form the land - from the cliffs to the tiny grains of sand - so do our actions, words, and thoughts shape and form our reality. Even more, ripples joining one another form tidal waves that change the planet. If we make sure that our every thought, word, and action are based in love then the ripples we create will bring about positive change for a positive future.
keywords: life; challenges; remember; power; love; ripples; ocean; planet; earth; interdependence; connection; unity; words; speech; action; thoughts; create; reality; change; transform; positive; future
notes: 'Julia Butterfly' is Julia Butterfly Hill, the activist who lived two years in the redwood 'Luna.' The ripple-and-love theme is consistent with her public speaking and with The Legacy of Luna (2000), but I cannot place this specific passage in that book or in a documented speech. The author name should likely be normalized to 'Julia Butterfly Hill.'

author: Kabir
text: Suppose you scrub your ethical skin until it shines, but there is no music. Then what?
notes: This reads as Robert Bly's English version of Kabir rather than a literal translation -- the diction ('scrub your ethical skin until it shines', 'but there is no music') is Bly's, from his Kabir renderings (The Kabir Book, 1977), which were themselves reworkings of Tagore's translations. So the sentiment is Kabir's tradition but the wording is Bly's. I recall the line in that Bly collection but not with enough certainty to cite it as a verified source. Consider crediting 'Kabir, versions by Robert Bly.'

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: We choose our joys and sorrows long before we experience them.
notes: The aphoristic single-sentence form is characteristic of Sand and Foam (1926), and I recall this line among Gibran's aphorisms there. Attribution to Gibran is consistent everywhere it appears. I stop short of naming the book as a verified source because I cannot confirm the locus, but I consider the authorship itself well supported.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Generosity is giving more than you can, and pride is taking less than you need.
notes: A well-known Gibran aphorism, in the paradoxical two-clause form typical of Sand and Foam (1926), where I believe it appears. Attribution to Gibran is consistent and I have no evidence pointing elsewhere; I withhold the print citation because I cannot confirm the volume.

author: Karen Sunde
text: To love is to receive a glimpse of heaven.
notes: Karen Sunde is a real American playwright, and this line circulates in quotation dictionaries under her name, but I cannot connect it to any of her plays, essays, or interviews. Short aphorisms of this kind in quote compilations frequently carry unsourced attributions. Attribution is plausible but effectively untraceable from what I know.

author: Karl Jaspers
text: An avoidance of true communication is tantamount to a relinquishment of my self-being; if I withdraw from it I am betraying not only the other but myself.
notes: Authentically Jaspersian in both content and translation register -- 'self-being' is the standard English rendering of Selbstsein in E. B. Ashton's translation of Jaspers, and the claim that refusing communication betrays both other and self is central to Jaspers's account of existential communication in Philosophie (1932), vol. 2 (Existenzerhellung). I believe that is the source but cannot confirm the volume or page, so I leave the citation field null rather than assert it.

author: Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim
text: Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible arise within us.
notes: This is the best-known line associated with the German Zen teacher and psychotherapist Karlfried Graf Durckheim (Graf Karlfried von Durckheim-Montmartin), and it matches his central theme of transformation through the 'exercise' of dying to the ego; it is usually cited from The Way of Transformation, though I cannot confirm that locus. The author field is garbled: 'Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim' should read 'Karlfried Graf Durckheim' ('Graf' is the German title Count, not a given name). Flagged as a name correction, not a change of author. | Suggested reattribution: Karlfried Graf Durckheim

author: Katharine Hepburn
text: If you obey all the rules, you miss all the fun.
notes: Consistently attributed to Katharine Hepburn and entirely in character for her public persona, but I cannot trace it to her memoir Me: Stories of My Life (1991), to a documented interview, or to any dated source. Short, quotable lines attached to famous personalities are a standard misattribution pattern, so I keep this below the promotion bar despite the consistency of the attribution.

author: Katherine Paterson
text: Peace is not won by those who fiercely guard their differences, but by those who with open minds and hearts seek out connections.
keywords: peace; differences; open; mind; heart; seek; discover; connections
notes: Katherine Paterson is a real and much-quoted author (Bridge to Terabithia; two-time Newbery winner) who wrote and spoke often on peace, difference, and empathy, so the attribution is plausible and probably comes from a speech, acceptance address, or essay collection such as Gates of Excellence or A Sense of Wonder. I cannot identify the specific occasion or text.

author: Kathleen A. Sutton
text: When you can't have what you want, it's time to start wanting what you have.
notes: I have no knowledge of Kathleen A. Sutton and cannot place her or this sentence. The sentiment is a commonplace that appears in many forms across proverb collections and self-help writing, which makes a single named originator unlikely to be verifiable. Honest answer: source unknown.

author: Ken Hakuta
text: Lack of money is no obstacle. Lack of an idea is an obstacle.
notes: Ken Hakuta is the Wacky WallWalker marketer known as 'Dr. Fad,' and the line fits his self-presentation and his 1988 book on inventing fads; it is consistently attributed to him in business-quote collections. I cannot confirm a book, article, or interview as the origin, so the attribution stays unverified.

author: Ken Kesey
text: The answer is never the answer. What’s really interesting is the mystery. If you seek the mystery instead of the answer, you’ll always be seeking. I’ve never seen anybody really find the answer – they think they have, so they stop thinking. The need for mystery is greater than the need for the answer.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Ken Kesey, and the phrasing and stance match his interview voice; it appears to come from a spoken interview rather than his published fiction. I cannot identify the interview, outlet, or year, and spoken-source quotes of this kind often drift in wording, so I hold this at unverified despite the consistency of the attribution.

author: Ken Keyes Jr.
text: A loving person lives in a loving world. A hostile person lives in a hostile world. Everyone you meet is your mirror.
keywords: love; person; hostile; perception; reflection; mirror
notes: A signature Ken Keyes Jr. formulation; 'everyone you meet is your mirror' is one of the phrases most closely associated with him and with Handbook to Higher Consciousness (1972), where I believe the passage appears. Attribution to Keyes is consistent and I know of no competing claimant, but I cannot confirm the book or edition, so I leave the print source null.

author: Ken Wilber
text: The only thing that wants to get rid of the ego is the ego.
notes: Consistent with Ken Wilber's recurring argument that ego-fighting is itself an ego project, a point he makes in No Boundary and in the One Taste journals, and the paradoxical compression is his style. I cannot place this exact sentence in a specific book, and similar formulations circulate in Advaita and Zen teaching contexts, so the wording may be a paraphrase of Wilber rather than a direct quotation.

author: Keshavan Nair
text: With courage you will dare to take risks, have the strength to be compassionate, and the wisdom to be humble. Courage is the foundation of integrity.
notes: Attributed consistently to Keshavan Nair, and the content -- courage as the ground of integrity, joined to compassion and humility -- matches the argument of his A Higher Standard of Leadership: Lessons from the Life of Gandhi (1994), which is the likely source. I cannot confirm the passage in that book, so I do not assert the citation.

author: Khalil Gibran
text: Keep me away from the wisdom which does not cry, the philosophy which does not laugh, and the greatness which does not bow before children.
keywords: children; wisdom; cry; philosophy; laughter; bow
notes: A widely circulated Gibran line whose triadic structure and tone are genuinely his; it is often traced to his Arabic-period writings in English translation (collections such as A Tear and a Smile / The Broken Wings tradition) rather than to The Prophet. Because the translation source is unsettled and translated aphorisms are prone to drift, I keep this at attributed without a citation. Author spelling should be normalized to 'Kahlil Gibran' for consistency with q_0860 through q_0863 in this batch.

author: Krishnamurti
text: It is no measure of health to be well adjusted to a profoundly sick society.
notes: Enormously widespread attribution to J. Krishnamurti, and consistent with his recurring theme that conformity to a diseased society is not sanity. However, I cannot place this exact sentence in any of his published books or transcribed talks. The wording has the compressed, aphoristic feel of a later condensation of a longer passage rather than a verbatim line. Some circulating versions cite 'Commentaries on Living' but the passages there differ. Honest verdict: attribution is plausible and near-universal, verbatim sourcing is absent from my knowledge.

author: Krishnamurti
text: When you judge, you lose love.
notes: I cannot place this five-word line anywhere in Krishnamurti's corpus. It gestures at a real Krishnamurti theme (judgment/evaluation as an obstacle to seeing, cf. his 'observing without evaluating' formulations), but the phrasing is not one I recognize from his talks or books. Reads like a social-media compression of his ideas. No traceable source.

author: Lakota proverb
text: When a man moves away from nature his heart becomes hard.
keywords: human; nature; heart; hard; separation; native american
earliest_print_source: Land of the Spotted Eagle, Luther Standing Bear, 1933
