notes: Not an anonymous proverb. This is a lightly reworded line from Luther Standing Bear (Oglala Lakota), whose 'Land of the Spotted Eagle' (1933) contains the passage rendered as 'Man's heart, away from nature, becomes hard.' The 'Lakota proverb' label is the usual folk-anonymization of a named Native author, which strips him of credit. Confidence figure reflects the weak 'Lakota proverb' attribution; my confidence in the Standing Bear reattribution is considerably higher (~0.7), though the corpus wording is a paraphrase rather than his exact sentence. | Suggested reattribution: Luther Standing Bear

author: Lama Surya Das
text: Love is found in loving.
notes: Lama Surya Das is a real American Dzogchen teacher and author ('Awakening the Buddha Within,' 1997), and the sentiment fits his register, but I cannot locate this four-word aphorism in any of his books or talks that I know. It is also generic enough to have many independent authors. No traceable source.

author: Lance Secretan
text: Leadership is not so much about technique and methods as it is about opening the heart. Leadership is about inspiration — of oneself and of others. Great leadership is about human experiences, not processes. Leadership is not a formula or a program, it is a human activity that comes from the heart and considers the hearts of others. It is an attitude, not a routine.
keywords: leadership; open; heart; inspiration; self; people; great; human; experience; process; action; attitude; routine
notes: Lance Secretan is a real leadership author ('Reclaiming Higher Ground,' 1997; 'Inspirational Leadership,' 1999) and this passage matches his documented thesis that leadership is an inspirational and heart-centered human activity rather than a technique or process. The length and paragraph structure suggest it was excerpted from one of his books, which raises my confidence in the attribution above the floor. But I cannot identify which book or confirm the wording, so no citation is recorded.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Those who flow as life flows know they need no other force.
notes: Does not correspond to any chapter of the Tao Te Ching in the standard translations I know (Legge, Waley, Feng/English, Mitchell, Lau, Addiss/Lombardo). The English is modern and idiomatic ('flow as life flows'), characteristic of the large body of free-floating pseudo-Lao Tzu circulating online. It may be a loose New Age rendering distantly inspired by the water imagery of ch. 8 or ch. 78, but I cannot connect it to a source text or a named translator.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Time is a created thing. To say 'I don't have time,' is like saying, 'I don't want to.'
notes: Not in the Tao Te Ching. No chapter treats time as a 'created thing,' and the register — a self-help reframe about scheduling and willingness, complete with quoted colloquial speech ('I don't have time') — is unmistakably modern American. This circulates heavily in productivity writing as Lao Tzu, which is a textbook case of a modern maxim borrowing an ancient name for authority. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I offer no reattribution.

author: Lao Tzu
text: The bad leader is he who the people despise. The good leader is he who the people praise. The great leader is he who the people say, we did it ourselves.
keywords: good; bad; great; taoism; leader; empowerment; community
earliest_print_source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 17 (traditionally attributed to Laozi, c. 4th century BCE)
notes: A modern managerial paraphrase built on genuine material. Tao Te Ching ch. 17 ranks rulers — the best barely known, then loved and praised, then feared, then despised — and closes 功成事遂，百姓皆謂我自然, commonly rendered 'when the work is done, the people say we did it ourselves.' The corpus wording compresses and reorders that into a three-tier leadership maxim; this formulation is popular in leadership literature (John Heider's 'The Tao of Leadership,' 1985, is one well-known vehicle for such renderings) and is not a translation. Holding at 0.70 rather than higher because the source thought is authentic but the sentence is not Lao Tzu's.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Give a man a fish and you feed him for the day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.
earliest_print_source: Mrs. Dymond, Anne Isabella Ritchie, 1885
notes: Not Lao Tzu, and not a Chinese proverb. Nothing resembling it appears in the Tao Te Ching. The earliest known form traced by quotation researchers is in Anne Isabella Ritchie's novel 'Mrs. Dymond' (1885): 'if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour; if you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn.' The saying has since been variously credited to Lao Tzu, Maimonides, and Confucius, all without support. Confidence value reflects the Lao Tzu attribution, which I regard as clearly wrong; my confidence in the Ritchie origin is high (~0.8). | Suggested reattribution: Anne Isabella Ritchie (Mrs. Thackeray Ritchie), Mrs. Dymond, 1885

author: Lao Tzu
text: Kindness in words creates confidence. Kindness in thinking creates profoundness. Kindness in giving creates love.
keywords: taoism; kindness; confidence; thinking; profound; giving; love
notes: I cannot match this triad to any chapter of the Tao Te Ching. Its parallel structure faintly echoes ch. 8, which lists virtues by domain ('in dwelling, be close to the land; in dealing with others, be gentle and kind; in speech, be true...'), but that passage does not repeat 'kindness' and does not produce 'confidence,' 'profoundness,' or 'love' as outcomes. 'Profoundness' in particular is not a word that appears in any translation I know. Most likely a modern reworking that drifted far enough from ch. 8 to count as a separate composition. Attribution to Lao Tzu is weak.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Seek not happiness too greedily, and be not fearful of unhappiness.
notes: I cannot place this in the Tao Te Ching or in the Zhuangzi. The sentiment is broadly Daoist in flavor (equanimity toward fortune and misfortune, cf. the reversals of ch. 58), but the archaic-sounding English construction 'Seek not... and be not' suggests a paraphraser imitating scriptural diction rather than a translation of a specific line. No traceable source.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Loving someone deeply gives you strength, while being deeply loved gives you courage.
notes: Not in the Tao Te Ching. This is one of the most heavily circulated pseudo-Lao Tzu lines on the internet, and the usual form is 'Being deeply loved by someone gives you strength, while loving someone deeply gives you courage' — note that the corpus version has the two clauses swapped, so it is a garbled variant of an already baseless attribution. Even the standard form has no identified author. Recommend removal or reattribution to 'Anonymous' if kept.

author: Lao Tzu
text: To see things in the seed, that is genius.
notes: I cannot find this sentence in Tao Te Ching translations. There is a real thematic neighbor in ch. 52, 見小曰明 ('seeing the small is called clarity/insight'), and ch. 64's counsel to deal with things while they are still latent, so a very free paraphrase is conceivable. But 'genius' is a European category alien to the text's vocabulary, which argues for a Western aphorist's composition later hung on Lao Tzu's name. Weak attribution.

author: Larry Eisenberg
text: For peace of mind, we need to resign as general manager of the universe.
notes: Consistently attributed to Larry Eisenberg across quotation collections, and the attribution has been stable long enough that it is unlikely to be pure invention. Complicating factor: at least two public figures share the name (the science-fiction writer and short-story author, and a clergyman), and I cannot determine which is meant or identify an originating publication. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

author: Lena Horne
text: It's not the load that breaks you down; it's the way you carry it.
notes: Very widely attributed to Lena Horne, often loosely to an interview in her later career, and the attribution is stable and specific enough to take seriously. However, I cannot confirm a primary source, and proverbial formulations of the same idea (it is not the burden but the manner of carrying it) circulated before her. Plausible that she said it and gave it currency rather than originated it. Below the promotion bar until a primary source is found.

author: Leo Burnett
text: Curiosity about life in all its aspects, I think, is still the secret of great creative people.
notes: Consistently and specifically credited to Leo Burnett throughout advertising literature, where his speeches and internal memos are unusually well preserved and were collected posthumously (notably in '100 LEO's: Wit and Wisdom from Leo Burnett,' 1995). The hedged, conversational phrasing — 'I think,' 'is still' — reads like transcribed speech rather than a manufactured aphorism, which supports authenticity. I cannot confirm the specific speech or page, so no citation is recorded and this sits just below the promotion bar.

author: Leo Buscaglia
text: We are no longer puppets being manipulated by outside powerful forces; we become the powerful force ourselves.
notes: Matches Leo Buscaglia's documented themes and first-person-plural style, and my sense is that it comes from his writing on self-determination, plausibly 'Personhood' (1978). Attribution is widespread and I have no reason to doubt it, but I cannot identify the book or confirm the wording, and Buscaglia's popularity means his name attracts unsourced uplift. Recording as unverified.

author: Leo Buscaglia
text: Only when we give joyfully, without hesitation or thought of gain, can we truly know what love means.
notes: Consistent with Buscaglia's central subject and voice; likely from 'Love' (1972) or 'Living, Loving and Learning' (1982), but I cannot confirm which or verify the wording. Attribution is widespread and plausible rather than evidenced. Same caveat as q_0897: his name is a magnet for unsourced sentiment about love.

author: Leo Tolstoi
text: Music is the shorthand of emotion
notes: Attributed to Tolstoy almost universally and for a long time, which gives it more weight than a recent internet attribution, but I cannot locate it in his works. It is not a line I can place in 'What Is Art?' (1897), his major statement on the subject, and it may originate in a letter, a diary entry, a recorded conversation, or a secondary account — or in a translator's compression of a longer passage. Also note the author name is spelled 'Leo Tolstoi'; the corpus should probably normalize to the standard 'Leo Tolstoy.' Attribution plausible, sourcing unconfirmed.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: A human can be healthy without killing animals for food. If you eat meat, you participate in taking animal life merely for the sake of your appetite.
keywords: vegetarian; morality; health; animals; death; food
notes: Tolstoy was a committed vegetarian from 1885 and argued exactly this in his 1892 essay 'The First Step' (Pervaya stupen), written as a preface to the Russian edition of Howard Williams's 'The Ethics of Diet'. The usual circulating wording is 'A man can live and be healthy without killing animals for food; therefore, if he eats meat, he participates in taking animal life merely for the sake of his appetite' — the corpus text is a gender-neutralized paraphrase of that. I cannot place the sentence at a specific page or confirm it is a direct translation rather than a summary of his argument, so I am not asserting a primary source. Attribution to Tolstoy is consistent across sources and entirely in character; the exact provenance is not.

author: Leonard Nimoy
text: The miracle is this — the more we share, the more we have.
notes: Consistently attributed to Leonard Nimoy across quote collections and often cited alongside his poetry (he published several volumes, e.g. 'You & I', 1973, and 'Warmed by Love'). The sentiment and the aphoristic style fit his published verse. I cannot place it in a specific book, poem, interview, or speech from my training knowledge, and it may be a line lifted from a longer poem. No competing attribution that I know of, so the author is plausible but unverified.

author: Leonardo Da Vinci
text: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
notes: This is a well-known false attribution. The line does not appear anywhere in Leonardo's notebooks or the Trattato della Pittura, and the Italian version circulating online ('La semplicita e l'ultima sofisticazione') is a back-translation from English, which is itself strong evidence of modern origin. Wikiquote lists it under Leonardo's disputed/misattributed section. Its popularity comes largely from twentieth-century advertising use, notably the 1977 Apple II brochure, where it appeared as a tagline. I do not reliably know the true earliest coiner, so I am not naming one rather than guessing.

author: Leonardo Da Vinci
text: From an early age, I have abjured the use of meat, and the time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they look upon the murder of men.
keywords: vegetarian; morality; animals; murder; men; food
earliest_print_source: The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci, Dmitry Merezhkovsky, 1900 (Russian; English translation 1902)
notes: A documented case of fiction laundered into a quotation. The 'time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they now look upon the murder of men' line comes from Dmitry Merezhkovsky's historical novel 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci' (1900), where it is dialogue invented for the character of Leonardo. It appears in no surviving Leonardo manuscript. Leonardo's actual vegetarianism is separately evidenced — chiefly Andrea Corsali's 1515 letter to Giuliano de' Medici describing him as eating no meat — but that is not this sentence. Wikiquote files it as misattributed. | Suggested reattribution: Dmitry Merezhkovsky (fictional dialogue in 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci', 1900)

author: Les Brown
text: Wanting something is not enough. You must hunger for it. Your motivation must be absolutely compelling in order to overcome the obstacles that will invariably come your way.
notes: Standard Les Brown motivational material, attributed to him consistently and without competing claimants. Most plausibly from his book 'Live Your Dreams' (1992) or his speaking material, but I cannot confirm a page or a specific talk, so I am leaving the print source null. Living-speaker quotes of this kind are rarely sourced in the aggregators that carry them; the attribution is likely right, the citation is unestablished.

author: Leslie Fieger
text: Any fool can run towards the light. It takes a master with courage to turn and face the darkness and shine his own light there.
notes: Leslie Fieger is a New Thought / self-development author known for the DELFIN Knowledge System trilogy. Quotes attributed to him circulate almost exclusively through quotation aggregators and mailing-list signatures rather than through cited books. I have no independent knowledge of this line in any of his published texts and cannot confirm or refute it. Low-profile author means low misattribution risk but also no verification path from training knowledge.

author: Leslie Fieger
text: Utilizing your conscious mind to direct the subconscious mind to enter into communication and harmony with the universal mind is the secret of personal power.
keywords: consciousness; unconscious; mind; communication; harmony; universal; universe; power; self
notes: Same situation as the other Fieger line. The vocabulary — conscious mind directing subconscious mind into harmony with universal mind — is squarely the New Thought idiom of Fieger's DELFIN material, so the attribution is stylistically plausible. I cannot place it in a specific book or lesson and will not invent one. No competing attribution known.

author: Lily Tomlin
text: For fast acting relief, try slowing down.
notes: A signature Tomlin one-liner, attributed to her with great consistency. Important caveat: the great majority of Lily Tomlin's stage and television material was written by Jane Wagner, her longtime collaborator and later spouse, so 'Lily Tomlin said it' often means 'Jane Wagner wrote it and Lily Tomlin performed it'. I cannot determine which show or special this line came from, so I cannot say whether Wagner authored this specific joke. Attribution to Tomlin as speaker is safe; attribution as author is not.

author: Lily Tomlin
text: I can handle reality in small doses, but as a lifestyle, it's much too confining.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Lily Tomlin, and I believe it belongs to the Trudy the bag lady material from 'The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe' (Broadway, 1985) — the same show that produced 'Reality is nothing but a collective hunch'. If that placement is right, the written author is Jane Wagner, who wrote the entire show; Tomlin performed it. I am not confident enough in the placement to state the show as a source or to file a formal reattribution, but the Wagner authorship question should be flagged before this is promoted.

author: Loren Fincher
text: The difference between holding on to a hurt or releasing it with forgiveness is like the difference between laying your head down at night on a pillow filled with thorns or a pillow filled with rose petals.
notes: I have no knowledge of Loren Fincher as an author, speaker, or public figure, and no knowledge of this line from any published source. It has the cadence of inspirational-newsletter or greeting-card writing and circulates, as far as I can tell, only through quote aggregators. Cannot confirm the person exists as attributed, cannot identify a real author, and will not guess. This is an honest 'I don't know'.

author: Louis Khan
text: Architecture is the thoughtful making of space.
notes: Genuine Kahn in substance, but two corrections are needed. First, the author's name is misspelled in the corpus: it is Louis I. Kahn (1901-1974), not 'Louis Khan'. Second, Kahn's formulation is plural — 'Architecture is the thoughtful making of spaces' — and it opens his contribution to Perspecta 4 (Yale architectural journal, 1957), continuing 'It is the creating of spaces that evoke a feeling of appropriate use.' I am confident of the sentence and of Kahn as its author; I am less certain of the exact issue and year, so I have left the print source null rather than risk a wrong citation. Fix the surname regardless of promotion outcome. | Suggested reattribution: Louis I. Kahn (spelling correction, not a change of author)

author: Louis L’Amour
text: A writer, or for that matter any artist, is continually putting demands on the subconscious and producing results.
notes: Attributed to Louis L'Amour consistently and with no competing claimant. The most likely home is his memoir 'Education of a Wandering Man' (1989), which contains extended reflection on reading, writing, and how the mind works on problems below awareness — but I cannot confirm the sentence is in that book, so I am not citing it as a source. The observation is characteristic of his prose about the writing craft. Plausible author, unestablished citation.

author: Lucille Ball
text: Love yourself first and everything else falls into line. You really have to love yourself to get anything done in this world.
notes: Attributed to Lucille Ball consistently, apparently originating in a magazine interview in which she described her 'everyday religion'. Note for the corpus editor: this is a truncated duplicate of q_0924, which carries the fuller and more likely original form beginning 'I have an everyday religion that works for me.' One of the two should be dropped, and the fuller version is the better record. Attribution plausible; no primary citation available to me.

author: Lucille Ball
text: I'm not funny. What I am is brave.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the context of interviewers asking how she developed her physical comedy. The sentiment matches her documented account of learning comedy as craft rather than possessing it as a gift. I cannot place it in a specific interview, and it may derive from her posthumously published autobiography 'Love, Lucy' (1996), but I will not cite that without confirmation. No competing attribution known.

author: Lucille Ball
text: Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.
earliest_print_source: 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', James Baldwin, New York Times Book Review, 14 January 1962
notes: This is James Baldwin, not Lucille Ball, and the misattribution is not close. The line comes from Baldwin's 1962 New York Times Book Review essay 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', on the responsibilities of American writers; it is one of his most frequently quoted sentences and is well documented in Baldwin scholarship and collections. It has nothing to do with Ball, and the corpus has additionally filed it under 'humor', which compounds the error. Strong recommendation: reattribute to Baldwin or drop. | Suggested reattribution: James Baldwin

author: Lucille Ball
text: A man who correctly guesses a woman's age may be smart, but he's not very bright.
notes: A vaudeville-era stock gag about guessing a woman's age, of the kind that circulates freely and attaches itself to whichever comedian is being quoted. It is attributed to Lucille Ball in aggregators but I have no evidence she originated it, and jokes of this shape predate her career. Weak attribution; I cannot name a true originator, which is typical for anonymous stage material.

author: Lucille Ball
text: I was shy for several years in my early days in Hollywood until I figured out that no one really gave a damn if I was shy or not, and I got over my shyness.
notes: Reads as genuine first-person interview material rather than a manufactured aphorism, and the content matches the documented arc of Ball's early years as a contract player in Hollywood before her success. That specificity is mild evidence of authenticity — invented quotes rarely include this kind of ordinary biographical detail. Still, I cannot identify the interview or publication, so the citation is unestablished.

author: Lucille Ball
text: You see much more of your children once they leave home.
notes: A free-floating domestic quip attributed to Lucille Ball in quote collections. I have no source for it and no strong reason to think it originated with her; observations of this form are common in mid-century newspaper humor columns and get reassigned to famous names. Weak attribution, no identifiable origin.

author: Lucille Ball
text: Luck? I don't know anything about luck. I've never banked on it, and I'm afraid of people who do. Luck to me is something else: Hard work -- and realizing what is opportunity and what isn't.
notes: Consistently attributed to Lucille Ball and structured like genuine transcribed interview speech — the self-interrupting 'Luck? I don't know anything about luck' opening, the correction mid-thought, the dash. Manufactured quotations tend to be smoother than this. The sentiment also matches her well-documented insistence that her career came from work rather than fortune. I cannot identify the interview, so no citation.

author: Lucille Ball
text: I have an everyday religion that works for me. Love yourself first, and everything else falls into line. You really have to love yourself to get anything done in this world.
notes: The fuller and probably original form of the line duplicated at q_0917; the 'I have an everyday religion that works for me' opening is the part that usually gets trimmed off in circulation, and its presence here suggests this version is closer to the source. Attributed to Ball consistently, apparently from a magazine interview. I cannot identify the publication. Recommend keeping this version and dropping q_0917. Also note it is filed under 'humor' but is not a joke — the category looks wrong.

author: Lucille Ball
text: One of the things I learned the hard way was that it doesn't pay to get discouraged. Keeping busy and making optimism a way of life can restore your faith in yourself.
notes: Attributed to Lucille Ball consistently across collections, with the reflective interview cadence of her later-career remarks about resilience in show business. No competing attribution known to me and nothing suspicious about it, but also no traceable source — I cannot name an interview, article, or book. Plausible but uncited. Like several others in this run it is filed under 'humor' despite being straightforwardly earnest.

author: Lucille Ball
text: I would rather regret the things that I have done than the things that I have not.
notes: Very widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the form 'I'd rather regret the things I've done than regret the things I haven't done.' I cannot place a primary interview, memoir passage, or dated print appearance from training knowledge. The sentiment also belongs to a large family of older 'regret what you didn't do' maxims (compare the apocryphal Twain 'Twenty years from now' line), which raises the baseline risk that this was retrofitted onto a famous name. Plausible but unverified.

author: Lucretius
text: The drops of rain make a hole in the stone not by violence, but by oft falling.
keywords: water; rain; hole; stone; perseverance; violence
notes: The IDEA is genuinely Lucretian: De Rerum Natura I.313 has 'stilicidi casus lapidem cavat' — the fall of dripping water hollows the stone. But this specific English wording, with the 'not by violence, but by oft falling' antithesis, is not a standard translation of that line; I recall it as English homiletic phrasing associated with Hugh Latimer's mid-16th-century preaching ('the drop of rain maketh a hole in the stone, not by violence, but by oft falling'). Related but distinct is Ovid's 'gutta cavat lapidem' (Ex Ponto IV.10.5). So the attribution is half-right: Lucretius for the thought, an English preacher's rhetoric for the sentence. Flagging rather than reattributing because my recall of the Latimer wording is good but not certain.

author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
text: When one is frightened of the truth... then it is never the whole truth than one has an inkling of.
notes: I recall a remark of this shape in Wittgenstein's Culture and Value (Vermischte Bemerkungen), the posthumous collection of personal notebook remarks from the 1930s-40s, running roughly 'When you are frightened of the truth (as I am now) then it is never the whole truth that you have an inkling of.' The 'than' in the corpus text is a transcription corruption of 'that', and the ellipsis marks an elided parenthetical. I am reasonably confident the remark is authentic Wittgenstein but cannot name page or dated entry, so I am not citing a print source and am holding confidence below the promotion bar. Worth a human check against Culture and Value.

author: M. C. Richards
text: Self-creation is an act of fire.
notes: M. C. (Mary Caroline) Richards, potter and poet, wrote Centering in Pottery, Poetry, and the Person (1962), The Crossing Point, and Toward Wholeness; this aphorism is stylistically consistent with her work and with Centering's themes of self-formation through craft. I cannot place the line in a specific book or page from training knowledge, and short epigrammatic fragments like this circulate easily without provenance. Attribution is plausible and I have no evidence against it, but nothing supports it either.

author: M. Kathleen Casey
text: Pain is inevitable. Suffering is optional.
notes: This is a modern English distillation of a Buddhist teaching (the second arrow, Sallatha Sutta), not a translation of any canonical text. The 'M. Kathleen Casey' credit propagates through 20th-century recovery and daily-meditation literature and through quote aggregators, but I cannot identify a book, page, or date for it, and Casey herself is a thinly documented figure easily confused with Karen Casey (Each Day a New Beginning, Hazelden). The line was popularized in the wider culture by Haruki Murakami's What I Talk About When I Talk About Running (2007), where he presents it as an anonymous runners' mantra rather than crediting Casey. Attribution is a convention, not evidence.

author: M.C. Escher
text: Only those who attempt the absurd will achieve the impossible.
notes: Circulates under Escher's name in design and business collections, but I know a closely matching line from Miguel de Unamuno — 'Solo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible' / 'Only he who attempts the absurd is capable of achieving the impossible' — which reads as the likelier origin. I cannot place the sentence in Escher's own writings (his essays and letters are fairly well documented and this is not a phrasing I associate with them). My Unamuno recall is solid on the Spanish wording but I cannot name the specific work, so the reattribution is offered as probable, not established, and the Escher attribution should not be promoted. | Suggested reattribution: Miguel de Unamuno (probable, not established)

author: Macrina Wiederkehr
text: Everything in life can be nourishing. Everything can bless us, but we've got to be there for the blessing to occur. Being present with quality is a decision we are invited to make each day.
notes: Macrina Wiederkehr (1939-2020), Benedictine sister and author of A Tree Full of Angels (1988), Seasons of Your Heart, and Behold Your Life. The passage is idiomatically hers — the vocabulary of blessing, presence, and daily decision matches her devotional prose — and I have no reason to doubt the attribution. But I cannot identify which of her books it comes from, and prose excerpts from devotional writers are frequently re-cut and re-punctuated by anthologists. Attribution plausible, source unplaced.

author: Macrina Wiederkehr
text: We live in a world of theophanies. Holiness comes wrapped in the ordinary. There are burning bushes all around you. Every tree is full of angels. Hidden beauty is waiting in every crumb. Life wants to lead you from crumbs to angels, but this can happen only if you are willing to unwrap the ordinary by staying with it long enough to harvest its treasure.
keywords: world; holy; ordinary; burning; fire; tree; angel; hidden; beauty; crumb; discovery; treasure; perception; divine
earliest_print_source: A Tree Full of Angels: Seeing the Holy in the Ordinary, Macrina Wiederkehr, 1988
notes: Strong internal evidence: the passage contains both halves of the book's own title — 'Every tree is full of angels' and the seeing-the-holy-in-the-ordinary theme — and theophany-in-the-ordinary is the organizing argument of A Tree Full of Angels (Harper & Row, 1988). This is the single most-anthologized Wiederkehr passage and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I am confident in the book but cannot give a page, and I am citing from recall rather than from a copy in front of me, so I am stopping short of 'verified'.

author: Maharishi
text: Love looks upon the world peacefully and accepts. The ego searches for shortcomings and weaknesses. Love watches for any sign of strength. It sees how far each one has come and not how far he has to go. How simple it is to love, and exhausting it is always to find fault, for every time we see a fault we think something needs to be done about it. Love knows that nothing is ever needed but more love.
keywords: love; world; acceptance; ego; search; weakness; strength; simple; exhausting; fault; nothing; appreciation; criticism
notes: 'Maharishi' is a title, not an author — presumably Maharishi Mahesh Yogi is intended, but the corpus entry does not say so, and the passage does not read like his teaching or like translated Indian devotional prose. The idiom is modern American therapeutic-spiritual English ('the ego searches for shortcomings', 'nothing is ever needed but more love') and sits much closer to the A Course in Miracles milieu — Jampolsky, Prather, Williamson and their imitators — than to Vedic commentary. I cannot identify the actual author, and I will not guess one. The attribution as it stands is unusable and the text should not be promoted under this name.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: The best way to find youself is to lose yourself in the service of others.
notes: One of the more defensible Gandhi attributions: the sentiment is squarely his (seva as self-realization) and the line is generally treated as sourced in his writings rather than as folk attribution. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the Young India issue, so I am not citing a source. Held at 0.6 rather than higher because Gandhi is a misattribution magnet and 'widely cited with consistent wording' is weaker evidence for him than for almost any other author. Note the corpus text has a typo: 'youself' should be 'yourself'.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: The future depends on what you do today.
notes: The form usually treated as closer to Gandhi is 'The future depends on what we do in the present.' The 'what you do today' version in the corpus is a later, punchier simplification of that, of the kind motivational-poster culture produces. I cannot place either form in a primary Gandhi text. Given how heavily Gandhi's name attracts unsourced aphorisms, and given that this specific wording appears to be a rewrite rather than the earliest form, it should not be promoted.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: If I believe I cannot do something, it makes me incapable of doing it. But when I believe I can, then I acquire the ability to do it, even if I did not have the ability in the beginning.
notes: This is a modern condensation of q_0938 in the same batch ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be...'), which is the longer and better-documented form of the same passage. The underlying thought is authentically Gandhi's, but this compressed first-person rewrite is not his sentence. Recommend the corpus keep q_0938 and treat this as a duplicate paraphrase rather than a separate quote.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Man often becomes what he believes himself to be. If I keep on saying to myself that I cannot do a certain thing, it is possible that I may end by really becoming incapable of doing it. On the contrary, if I have the belief that I can do it, I shall surely acquire the capacity to do it even if I may not have it at the beginning.
notes: This longer form is the one that appears in serious Gandhi collections and is generally treated as sourced to his own writings, with stable wording across citations — a good sign, since spurious Gandhi lines tend to drift. The prose rhythm ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be', 'On the contrary...') is consistent with his English. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the periodical and date, so no print source is cited and I am holding just below the promotion bar. A human check against the Collected Works would likely confirm it.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Keep my word positive. Words become my behaviors. Keep my behaviors positive. Behaviors become my habits. Keep my habits positive. Habits become my values. Keep my values positive. Values become my destiny.
notes: This is the 'thoughts become words, words become actions, habits become values, values become destiny' chain, one of the most durable false Gandhi attributions. No Gandhi source exists for it. Its ancestor is the 19th-century English maxim 'Sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny', variously credited to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles and itself of contested origin; the modern positive-thinking chain is a 20th-century self-help reworking that later acquired Gandhi's name. I can identify the family the saying descends from but not a single true author, so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing. Should not appear in the corpus under Gandhi.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: There is more to life than increasing its speed.
notes: Ubiquitous under Gandhi's name, especially in slow-living and productivity writing, but I cannot place it in any primary text and I associate it with the unsourced tier of the Gandhi quote literature rather than the documented tier. The epigram's shape — a single modern aphorism about 'speed' — fits mid-to-late 20th-century Western anxieties about pace more naturally than Gandhi's own idiom. Plausible in sentiment, unsupported in provenance.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: There is no path to peace. Peace is the path.
notes: The documented origin of this formula is the American pacifist A. J. Muste, who said 'There is no way to peace; peace is the way' — a line strongly associated with him in the 1960s and quoted in coverage around his death in 1967. The corpus's 'no path to peace / peace is the path' is a variant of Muste's sentence, and the Gandhi credit appears to be later drift onto a bigger name, a pattern well documented for pacifist aphorisms. I am confident enough in the Muste attribution to name it, though I cannot cite the specific speech or article. | Suggested reattribution: A. J. Muste

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: I have learned through bitter experience the one supreme lesson: to conserve my anger; and as heat conserved is transmitted into energy, even so, our anger controlled, can be transmitted into a power that can move the world.
notes: I believe this is authentic Gandhi, from his journalism of the 1920s (the Young India period), and it is one of the Gandhi passages that circulates with a real source trail rather than as a bare aphorism. Two textual notes for the corpus: the authentic wording is 'transmuted', not 'transmitted' — the corpus text has the corruption twice, which flattens the heat/energy metaphor — and 'a power which can move the world' is the more usual ending. Recommend correcting to 'transmuted' before any promotion. Not citing a dated source because I cannot pin the issue.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: My life is my message.
notes: Well attested by the standards of Gandhi quotation. The line comes with a consistent anecdote — Gandhi, pressed by a journalist for a message and having no time to talk, wrote 'My life is my message' on a scrap of paper — and it is established enough to have been used as the title of Narayan Desai's multi-volume Gandhi biography. I cannot fix the date or the journalist with confidence, so no print source is cited, but the attribution itself is solid.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: It is unwise to be too sure of one's own wisdom. It is healthy to be reminded that the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err.
notes: Consistently attributed to Gandhi with stable wording, and I associate it with his own writing rather than with the aggregator tier — the balanced construction ('the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err') and the theme of humility before one's own certainty are characteristic. It appears in the standard Gandhi anthologies of the All Men Are Brothers type. I cannot name the original article or speech, so it stays below the promotion bar pending a check against the Collected Works.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Be the change you want to see in the world.
notes: The single most famous thing Gandhi never said in these words. No source exists in his writings or speeches. The genuine passage it compresses is 'If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him' — a different and more careful claim. The imperative-slogan wording appears to originate in 1970s American self-help; Arleen Lorrance's The Love Project material (c. 1974) carried 'Be the change you want to see happen', and the Gandhi credit attached later. Brian Morton's widely read 2011 New York Times piece 'Falser Words Were Never Spoken' laid this out. I name Lorrance as probable origin of the phrasing, but the sentiment is a fair paraphrase of Gandhi, so the corpus may prefer to carry the authentic longer passage instead. Do not promote under Gandhi as written. | Suggested reattribution: Arleen Lorrance (probable origin of the wording); the underlying sentiment paraphrases Gandhi

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: The greatness of a nation and its moral progress can be judged by the way its animals are treated.
notes: Extremely widely quoted — it is a fixture of animal-welfare campaigning — but I know it as one of the Gandhi lines for which no source in the Collected Works has been located, and it is commonly listed in the unsourced or disputed tier of Gandhi quotation. Related sentiments do appear in his writing on cow protection and ahimsa, which is likely how the attribution took hold. Ubiquity here is a function of the cause it serves, not of evidence.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Consciously or unconsciously, every one of us does render some service or other. If we cultivate the habit of doing this service deliberately, our desire for service will steadily grow stronger, and will make, not only our own happiness, but that of the world at large.
keywords: consciousness; service; habit; cultivate; intention; desire; grow; strengthen; happiness; world; community
notes: Reads as authentic: it is long, syntactically unpolished, argumentative rather than epigrammatic, and it develops a thought about seva step by step — all features that spurious Gandhi quotes lack, since fabrications tend to be short and quotable. The wording is stable across the citations I recall. I cannot place the source text, so this is a judgment from style and internal evidence rather than from provenance, and I am keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the Collected Works.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: An eye for an eye makes the whole world blind.
notes: The pre-flag is correct. No Gandhi source exists. The earliest credited appearances run through mid-20th-century secondary literature — Louis Fischer's The Life of Mahatma Gandhi (1950) carries a version of the thought as biographer's paraphrase rather than as a transcribed Gandhi sentence — and the line reached mass currency through Attenborough's Gandhi (1982), which drew on Fischer. The underlying reversal of lex talionis is older than Gandhi and circulated independently in English. Fischer is the likeliest proximate source of the wording, but as a paraphraser rather than an author, so I am recording that in notes rather than naming him as the quote's author.
suspect_reason: No Gandhi source; appears first in Louis Fischer's 1950 biography as paraphrase.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.
notes: Generally treated as authentic Gandhi and traced to his periodical writing of the early 1930s; the wording is stable across citations and the aphorism-plus-gloss structure matches his editorial style. I cannot name the issue or date, so no print source is given. Held at 0.62 for the standing Gandhi caution — the line is short and quotable, the profile of quotes that drift — but I have no positive evidence against it.

author: Majjhima Nikaya
text: My teaching does not require anyone to become homeless or resign the world unless he wants to, but it does require everyone to free himself from the illusion that he is a permanent self and to act with integrity while giving up his craving for pleasure.
keywords: teaching; world; freedom; self; illusion; permanence; integrity; desire; pleasure
notes: Not a canonical translation. The Majjhima Nikaya credit points at a 152-sutta collection without naming a sutta, and this English does not match any translation tradition I know — not Horner, not Nanamoli/Bodhi. Telltales: 'illusion that he is a permanent self' is a doctrinal gloss on anatta in modern comparative-religion register, not sutta idiom, and the sutta form (address to named interlocutors, formulaic repetition, similes) is entirely absent. This reads as a Western summary of Buddhist teaching later given a scriptural label — a common pattern in inspirational anthologies. Treat the citation as decorative; I cannot identify the actual writer.

author: Malcolm Forbes
text: Too many people overvalue what they are not and undervalue what they are.
notes: Consistently attributed to Malcolm Forbes across quotation collections, and it matches the aphoristic register of his 'Fact and Comment' column in Forbes magazine and the 'Thoughts on the Business of Life' compilations. I cannot place a specific issue, page, or book from training knowledge, so the attribution rests on secondary consistency rather than a primary source. No competing claimant that I know of.

author: Marc Allen
text: Fools never learn from their mistakes. Smart people learn from their mistakes. Wise people learn from other people's mistakes.
notes: Marc Allen (New World Library founder, author of 'Visionary Business' and 'The Millionaire Course') is a plausible modern popularizer, but the three-tier fool/smart/wise structure is a long-standing proverbial form with many older analogues, notably the aphorism commonly given to Bismarck ('Fools say they learn by experience; I prefer to profit by others' experience') and the 'learn from the mistakes of others, you can't live long enough to make them all yourself' family attributed variously to Eleanor Roosevelt, Groucho Marx, and Hyman Rickover. I cannot confirm that Allen originated this wording, and I will not guess a true source.

author: Margaret Gatty
text: The days are too short even for love; how can there be enough time for quarreling?
notes: Margaret Gatty (1809-1873), author of 'Parables from Nature' and 'The Book of Sun-Dials' (1872), is the name attached to this line in quotation collections, and the epigrammatic form is consistent with the sundial mottoes she gathered. But I cannot confirm whether she wrote it, translated it, or merely recorded it from an older inscription, and I have no page or edition to cite. Deliberately leaving the print source null rather than guessing at The Book of Sun-Dials.

author: Margaret Mead
text: We are continually faced with great opportunities which are brilliantly disguised as unsolvable problems.
notes: The well-documented form of this line belongs to John W. Gardner (Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare; founder of Common Cause): 'We are continually faced by great opportunities brilliantly disguised as insoluble problems,' associated with his mid-1960s writing and speeches. The saying has also drifted to Lee Iacocca and Charles Swindoll, and the Margaret Mead version appears in collections without any source in her published anthropological work. I know of no Mead text containing it. Confidence figure reflects the strength of the Mead attribution, which is weak. | Suggested reattribution: John W. Gardner

author: Margaret Stortz
text: When we are grateful for the good we already have, we attract more good into our life. On the other hand, when we are ungrateful, we tend to shut ourselves off from the good we might otherwise experience.
notes: Margaret Stortz is a Religious Science / New Thought minister and author, and the sentiment fits that tradition's gratitude-and-attraction idiom, but I have no specific book, article, or sermon in training knowledge that carries this passage. I cannot rule out that it circulates from an anthology or daily-reader compilation. No competing attribution known; the honest answer here is that I cannot place it.

author: Marian Wright Edelman
text: Being considerate of others will take you further in life than a college degree.
notes: Consistently attributed to Marian Wright Edelman and consistent in voice and content with the numbered life lessons in 'The Measure of Our Success: A Letter to My Children and Yours' (1992), which is where I believe it originates. I am not certain enough of the lesson number or wording in that book to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null. No competing claimant.

author: Marianne Williamson
text: Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.
earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 - Text, Ch. 1, 'Principles of Miracles', principle 3
notes: This is not original to Marianne Williamson. It is, essentially verbatim, the third of the Fifty Miracle Principles that open the Text of A Course in Miracles: 'Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.' Williamson's 'A Return to Love' (1992) is a commentary on ACIM and quotes the Course extensively, which is how the line came to be tagged with her name. The attribution to her is a quoter-for-author error. | Suggested reattribution: A Course in Miracles (Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976)

author: Marianne Williamson
text: Most of the time, we fall in love but can’t remain there. The world then calls the state we were in a delusion or infatuation ... But we merely lacked, or someone else lacked, the emotional skills to hold on to the magic when the morning came. ... In truth, we can go to the moon and retain its magic for a lifetime.
keywords: love; delusion; emotional; skill; magic; morning; moon; lifetime; truth
notes: The voice, vocabulary, and subject matter are strongly consistent with Williamson's writing on romantic love, most plausibly 'Enchanted Love: The Mystical Power of Intimate Relationships' (1999) rather than 'A Return to Love.' The ellipses indicate the text was stitched from a longer passage, which is typical of a real book excerpt but also makes it hard to match. I cannot confirm the book or page from training knowledge, so no citation is recorded.

author: Marianne Williamson
text: The practice of forgiveness is our most important contribution to the healing of the world.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Marianne Williamson, and forgiveness-as-world-healing is a central and repeated theme of her work. I cannot locate a specific book or page. One caution given q_0961 in this same batch: Williamson's writing is saturated with A Course in Miracles material, so there is a residual risk that a line like this restates Course teaching; I do not recognize it as verbatim ACIM, but I flag the possibility rather than certify the attribution above the promotion bar.

author: Marie-Louise von Franz
text: If a man devotes himself to the instructions of his own unconscious, it can bestow this gift [of renewal], so that suddenly life, which has been stale and dull, turns into a rich unending inner adventure, full of creative possibilities.
keywords: devotion; unconscious; gift; life; adventure; possibility; person
notes: I believe this comes from Marie-Louise von Franz's chapter 'The Process of Individuation' in 'Man and His Symbols' (C. G. Jung, ed., 1964), which is her best-known writing in English and matches this passage's theme of renewal through attending to the unconscious. The editorial bracket '[of renewal]' suggests the corpus entry was taken from a careful print quotation rather than a meme. I am not confident enough of the chapter or page to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null and the attribution rests on style and subject match plus consistent secondary citation.

author: Marilyn Ferguson
text: Fear is a question: What are you afraid of, and why? Just as the seed of health is in illness, because illness contains information, our fears are a treasure house of self-knowledge if we explore them.
notes: Consistently attributed to Marilyn Ferguson, author of 'The Aquarian Conspiracy' (1980) and editor of the Brain/Mind Bulletin, and the framing of fear as information matches her idiom. The passage's length and structure suggest an excerpt from her writing rather than an aphorism assembled by anthologists. I cannot confirm the book or issue, so no citation is recorded.

author: Marilyn Ferguson
text: Ultimately we know deeply that the other side of every fear is a freedom.
notes: One of the most-reproduced lines credited to Marilyn Ferguson, with consistent attribution but, as far as I know, no cited source anywhere in that circulation. Short aphorisms of this kind are the ones most likely to be detached from an author or absorbed from workshop culture, so consistent repetition is weak evidence on its own. Plausibly hers - it reads like a condensation of the same material as q_0966 - but unverified.

author: Mario Andretti
text: If everything feels under control, you’re just not driving fast enough.
notes: Solidly and consistently attributed to Mario Andretti in interviews and racing literature, though I cannot name the original interview or date. Important wording caveat: the canonical form is 'If everything seems under control, you're not going fast enough.' The recorded text ('feels under control ... just not driving fast enough') is a drifted variant. Recommend normalizing to the standard wording before promotion.

author: Mark Twain
text: History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme.
notes: The pre-flag is correct. No such line appears in Twain's published work, letters, or notebooks, and the attributions to him begin decades after his death in 1910 - the earliest instance I know of is a 1970 John Robert Colombo 'found poem' that presents 'History never repeats itself but it rhymes' as a Twain saying, which is a repetition of the claim rather than evidence for it. I cannot identify a true originator, so no reattribution is offered; classifying as apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed for exactly that reason. See also q_0975, a near-duplicate of this entry.
suspect_reason: No Twain source; earliest attributions to Twain post-date his death by decades.

author: Mark Twain
text: Do the thing you fear most and the death of fear is certain.
notes: The pre-flag is correct: no source in Twain's published work or correspondence. The same sentence circulates just as often under Ralph Waldo Emerson's name, and that attribution is equally unsourced - Emerson's actual related line, from 'Heroism,' is 'Always do what you are afraid to do,' which he credits to his aunt Mary Moody Emerson. Because both major claimants fail and I cannot identify a real origin, apocryphal with no reattribution.
suspect_reason: No Twain source found in his published work or letters.

author: Mark Twain
text: Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things you didn't do than by the things you did. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Explore. Dream.
earliest_print_source: P.S. I Love You, H. Jackson Brown Jr., 1990
notes: The pre-flag matches what I know. Nothing in Twain's corpus contains this, and 'throw off the bowlines / sail away from the safe harbor' is not his register. The earliest documented appearance is in H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s 'P.S. I Love You' (1990), a collection of sayings from his mother, Sarah Frances Brown; the Twain tag attached afterwards and spread through 1990s self-help and graduation-speech material. Recording the true origin here because it is documented, not inferred - but note that Brown's book presents it as his mother's saying, so 'H. Jackson Brown Jr.' is the compiler rather than strictly the author. | Suggested reattribution: Sarah Frances Brown, as recorded by her son H. Jackson Brown Jr. in P.S. I Love You (1990)
suspect_reason: No Twain source. First appears in 1990s self-help material attributed to H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s mother.

author: Mark Twain
text: Worrying about something is like paying interest on a debt you don't even know if you owe.
notes: Not pre-flagged, but it should have been. No Twain source exists for this. It is a wordy variant of the unsourced 'Worrying is like paying a debt you don't owe,' which circulates under Twain, Will Rogers, and others without a citation for any of them. The one genuinely documented aphorism in this family belongs to William Ralph Inge, Dean of St Paul's: 'Worry is interest paid on trouble before it falls due.' The recorded wording differs enough that I will not reattribute it to Inge, but his line is the likely ancestor of the metaphor. Recommend flagging this entry as suspect.

author: Mark Twain
text: History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes.
notes: Same verdict as q_0970, of which this is a near-duplicate differing only by the word 'does' - the corpus is carrying both variants and should deduplicate. No Twain source; attributions post-date his 1910 death by decades, with the earliest I know of being John Robert Colombo's 1970 found poem. No identifiable true author, hence apocryphal with no reattribution.

author: Mark Twain
text: The human race has one really effective weapon, and that is laughter.
earliest_print_source: The Mysterious Stranger, Mark Twain, 1916 (posthumous)
notes: The idea is genuinely Twain's, from the Satan monologue in the Mysterious Stranger manuscripts: the human race 'has unquestionably one really effective weapon - laughter.' The exact sentence as quoted here is a smoothed condensation rather than Twain's printed wording, and the 1916 text itself was editorially assembled by Paine and Duneka from Twain's drafts. Correct author, imprecise wording.

author: Mark Twain
text: Age is an issue of mind over matter. If you don't mind, it doesn't matter.
notes: Not found in Twain's works or letters; Twain attributions for this line are late and unsupported. The 'if you don't mind, it doesn't matter' pun on mind/matter circulated as a stock joke well before it was pinned to any famous name. It is most commonly credited to Satchel Paige ('Age is a question of mind over matter...'), but Paige popularized rather than originated it, so I am not asserting a replacement author.

author: Mark Twain
text: Don't go around saying the world owes you a living. The world owes you nothing. It was here first.
notes: I cannot place this in any Twain text - not in the novels, essays, letters, or notebooks I know. It reads like a newspaper-filler aphorism that later collected a Twain byline, the standard pattern for spurious Twain. I do not have a confident true origin, so I am recording honest uncertainty rather than a reattribution.

author: Mark Twain
text: When I was a boy of 14, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be 21, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years.
keywords: ignorance; father; parent; man; learn; boy
notes: A classic spurious Twain. It appears in no Twain work; documented appearances postdate his 1910 death, and it is biographically impossible as autobiography - John Marshall Clemens died when Samuel Clemens was eleven, so there was no father to rediscover at twenty-one. Origin unknown; the joke circulated anonymously in periodicals before acquiring Twain's name.

author: Mark Twain
text: The secret to success is making your vocation your vacation.
notes: No Twain source known to me. The vocation/vacation pun circulates in several forms ('Make your vocation your vacation') attached to various names, and I cannot trace any of them to a document. Twain's name here looks like the usual gravitational pull of a famous humorist on an unowned wordplay.

author: Mark Twain
text: You can't depend on your eyes when your imagination is out of focus.
notes: Consistently attributed to Twain across quote collections and stylistically plausible for him; I have a weak recollection of it sitting in one of the late novels but cannot place the work or chapter with enough confidence to name it, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Author plausible, citation unconfirmed.

author: Mark Twain
text: Kindness is a language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see.
notes: Widely printed over Twain's name but absent from his writings so far as I know; the Twain attribution surfaces decades after his death, and quote-tracing work on this line has failed to find any contemporaneous support. Related sentiments about kindness as a universal language predate the Twain version. True origin unknown to me.

author: Mark Twain
text: The best way to cheer yourself up is to try to cheer somebody else up.
notes: Very consistently attributed to Twain and usually pointed at his notebooks, but I cannot confirm which entry or letter, and I have not seen it quoted with a page citation. Plausible but unconfirmed - keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the notebooks.

author: Marquis de Vauvengras
text: There is nothing that fear does not make men believe.
earliest_print_source: Reflexions et maximes, Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues, 1746
notes: The maxim is Vauvenargues': 'Il n'est rien que la peur ne fasse croire,' from his Reflexions et maximes (published 1746 with the Introduction a la connaissance de l'esprit humain). The author field is misspelled and mistitled - it should read 'Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues', not 'Marquis de Vauvengras'. I am confident of the author, less so of the exact maxim number, so I have not cited one. | Suggested reattribution: Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues (author name is misspelled in the record)

author: Marsha Norman
text: Dreams are illustrations from the book your soul is writing about you.
notes: Consistently credited to the playwright Marsha Norman with no competing claimants, and it circulated widely after appearing in magazine quote features in the 1990s. I cannot name the interview, play, or essay it came from, so the citation stays null. Author likely right, source unlocated.

author: Marsha Sinetar
text: Instead of frittering away your vibrancy with worry or distraction, realize your mind and body are inextricably united. What calms and tones up one, soothes and improves the other.
notes: Attributed to Marsha Sinetar, whose subject matter (right livelihood, mind-body integration, contemplative practice) fits the content well - most likely from one of her books such as Do What You Love, the Money Will Follow (1987) or Ordinary People as Monks and Mystics (1986), but I cannot confirm which and will not guess a title.

author: Marsha Sinetar
text: When flowing water meets with obstacles on its path, a blockage in its journey, it pauses. It increases in volume and strength, filling up in front of the obstacle and eventually spilling past it... Emulate the example of the water: pause and build up your strength until the obstacle no longer represents a blockage.
keywords: water; obstacle; overcome; breakthrough; strength; path; journey; pause
notes: Attributed to Marsha Sinetar in quote collections; the water-and-obstacle imagery reads like her commentary on an I Ching hexagram, which is consistent with her writing, but I cannot place the book or page. The ellipsis in the text indicates it is already an excerpt from a longer passage, which makes verification harder rather than easier.

author: Marshall McLuhan
text: There are no passengers on spaceship earth. We are all crew.
notes: Widely and consistently credited to McLuhan, but I know of no primary citation - no book, lecture, or interview I can point to. Complicating it: 'Spaceship Earth' is Buckminster Fuller's frame (Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, 1969), and the line is sometimes handed to Fuller instead. McLuhan is the more common attribution and is plausible, but the evidence I have is secondary repetition, not a source.

author: Martha Graham
text: We look at the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life, to energize the spectator into keener awareness of the vigor, the mystery, the humor, the variety, and the wonder of life.
keywords: dance; life; affirmation; energy; awareness; mystery; humor; wonder
notes: Genuine-sounding Graham and consistently attributed to her, from her writing on modern dance in the 1930s-50s. Note a probable transcription corruption: the standard wording is 'We look FOR the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life,' not 'look at the dance.' I cannot name the essay or collection with confidence, so no citation.

author: Martha Graham
text: There is only one of you in the world, just one. And if that is not fulfilled, then something has been lost.
notes: A variant rendering of the same de Mille conversation behind q_0999 ('because there is only one of you in all time'). It circulates as a standalone Graham line, but I cannot match it word for word to de Mille's text, so it may be a paraphrase in transmission rather than a distinct utterance. Author right, exact wording unverified.

author: Martia Nelson
text: True self simply refers to the aspect of our being that is completely aware of its expanded nature no matter what we may be experiencing in our lives.
keywords: true; self; being; aware; experience; life; vast
notes: Martia Nelson is a real author whose best-known book is 'Coming Home: The Return to True Self' (New World Library, 1993), and this line's vocabulary ('true self', 'expanded nature') is consistent with that book's subject. I cannot confirm from training knowledge that this exact sentence appears there, and I have no independent citation for it. Attribution is plausible but unverified.

author: Martin LeBlanc, Iconfinder
text: A user interface is like a joke. If you have to explain it, it’s not that good.
notes: Consistently attributed across design literature and talks to Martin LeBlanc, founder of Iconfinder; it circulated widely from around 2013 as a LeBlanc line and I am not aware of any competing attribution. The underlying joke formula ('if you have to explain it, it isn't good') is much older, so LeBlanc's contribution is the UI application rather than the structure. No primary source (original tweet, post, or talk) that I can cite from memory, so this stays below the verified bar.

author: Marvin Minsky
text: Science and religion are not so different except that in science, the ultimate sin is believing too strongly.
notes: The sentiment is very characteristic of Minsky, who repeatedly argued that scientific commitment must stay revisable and criticized belief held past the evidence. I have a weak recollection of this specific phrasing circulating as a Minsky line from an interview or a talk, but I cannot place a book, article, or date, and I will not guess at one. Plausible but unsourced.

author: Mary Kay Ash
text: For every failure, there is an alternate course of action. You just have to find it.
notes: Consistently attributed to Mary Kay Ash in business and motivational quote collections, and consistent in tone with her writing in 'Mary Kay on People Management' (1984) and her autobiography. I cannot locate the sentence in a specific book, speech, or company publication from training knowledge, and much of the Mary Kay Ash quote canon circulates through corporate motivational material without sourcing.

author: Mary Lou Cook
text: Creativity is inventing, experimenting, growing, taking risks, breaking rules, making mistakes, and having fun.
keywords: invent; experiment; growth; rules; break; mistake; fun
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Mary Lou Cook, the Santa Fe calligrapher, peace activist, and volunteer-movement figure. The attribution is stable — I know of no competing claimant — but I can point to no book, article, or interview containing it; it appears to have entered circulation through quote anthologies and greeting-card style collections. Stable attribution, absent source.

author: Mary Manin Morrissey
text: Even though you may want to move forward in your life, you may have one foot on the brakes. In order to be free, we must learn how to let go. Release the hurt. Release the fear. Refuse to entertain your old pain. The energy it takes to hang onto the past is holding you back from a new life.
notes: Attributed with reasonable consistency to Mary Manin Morrissey, the New Thought minister and author of 'Building Your Field of Dreams' (1996) and 'No Less Than Greatness' (2001). The 'one foot on the brakes' image and the letting-go framing match her teaching. I cannot confirm which book, sermon, or newsletter it comes from, and much of her circulating quote material originates in unarchived talks and columns.

author: Mary Manin Morrissey
text: It's easy to feel grateful when we receive a raise, meet the love of our life, or watch our children succeed, but spiritual gratitude is not circumstantial. It arises from a true knowing that God is our Source. We can feel thankful for every day, even in the middle of life's challenges.
keywords: gratitude; feeling; love; children; spiritual; knowing; god; source; challenges; life; day
notes: Reads as authentic Morrissey — New Thought vocabulary, 'God is our Source' capitalized in the movement's convention — and is attributed to her wherever it appears. But this looks like material from a devotional column, newsletter, or Thanksgiving-season message rather than a book, and I cannot identify the original venue. No source, honest uncertainty.

author: Mary Pickford
text: If you have made mistakes, even serious ones, there is always another chance for you. What we call failure is not the falling down but the staying down.
notes: Long attributed to Mary Pickford and consistent with the inspirational writing she published in the 1930s, notably 'Why Not Try God?' (1934) and 'My Rendezvous with Life' (1935), which are full of exactly this kind of counsel about failure and second chances. The second sentence ('failure is not the falling down but the staying down') also circulates as an anonymous proverb, which raises the possibility that Pickford was repeating a current saying rather than coining it. I cannot confirm the book or page.

author: Matt Hardy
text: Beauty can be seen in all things, seeing and composing the beauty is what separates the snapshot from the photograph.
notes: This line saturates photography quote lists attributed to a bare 'Matt Hardy' with no identifying detail, no publication, and no date. I cannot establish who this Matt Hardy is — the name is shared by a well-known professional wrestler, who is almost certainly not the source, and by several photographers. No traceable origin; the attribution is a name floating free of a person. Treat as effectively anonymous.

author: Max Lucado
text: Conflict is inevitable, but combat is optional.
notes: Commonly attributed to Max Lucado, the Christian author, and the aphoristic construction fits his style. The same line also circulates in conflict-resolution and mediation training material with no attribution at all, and occasionally credited to others, which suggests it may be a stock saying that attached to Lucado's name rather than a line he coined. I cannot place it in any of his books.

author: Maxwell Maltz
text: Accept yourself as you are. Otherwise you will never see opportunity. You will not feel free to move toward it; you will feel you are not deserving.
notes: Attributed to Maxwell Maltz, the plastic surgeon who wrote 'Psycho-Cybernetics' (1960); the self-image thesis and the link between self-acceptance and perceived opportunity are core Maltz themes, so the attribution is coherent. I cannot confirm the sentence appears in Psycho-Cybernetics or his later books, and the large body of 'Maltz quotes' online includes material from later ghostwritten and revised editions.

author: Maxwell Maltz
text: The most delightful surprise in life is to suddenly recognize your own worth.
notes: Widely circulated as Maxwell Maltz and thematically consistent with Psycho-Cybernetics' argument about self-image and self-worth. No specific book, chapter, or date that I can confirm; this is one of the short aphorisms that spread through motivational compilations detached from any source text.

author: Maya Angelou
text: I long, as does every human being, to be at home wherever I find myself.
notes: Genuinely Angelou's in voice and theme, and consistently cited to 'All God's Children Need Traveling Shoes' (1986), the memoir of her years in Ghana, whose central subject is exactly this longing for home. The better-known companion line from that book — 'The ache for home lives in all of us' — is firmly sourced there. I believe this sentence is from the same work but cannot confirm the passage, so I am leaving the print source field empty rather than asserting a citation I have not confirmed.

author: Maya Angelou
text: I think we all have empathy. We may not have enough courage to display it.
notes: Attributed to Maya Angelou consistently and without competing claimants; it comes from her spoken remarks — interviews and public conversations in her later years, where she returned often to the theme that empathy is common and the courage to act on it is not. Spoken origin means no clean print citation; I cannot name the specific interview or date.

author: Maya Angelou
text: If you are always trying to be normal, you will never know how amazing you can be.
notes: This is a social-media staple attributed to Angelou and it should be treated with suspicion. I cannot place it in any of her memoirs, poetry, essay collections, or documented interviews, and its register — short, motivational-poster cadence — is unlike her usual construction. Angelou is a strong misattribution magnet: lines by Mary Anne Radmacher, Rumi translators, and anonymous inspirational writers are routinely assigned to her, and 'Still I Rise' fame pulls unattributed uplift toward her name. I have no evidence of a true author, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but the attribution should not be treated as sound.

author: Maya Angelou
text: I believe talent is like electricity. We don't understand electricity. We use it.
notes: Angelou used this electricity analogy for talent in interviews, typically extending it — talent, like electricity, is not understood but used, and it makes no judgment about who uses it. The attribution is consistent and the extended form's survival in the record argues for authenticity rather than a manufactured aphorism. I recall it from an interview context but cannot identify the publication or year, so no citation.

author: Maya Angelou
text: I have found that among its other benefits, giving liberates the soul of the giver.
notes: Consistently attributed to Angelou and usually cited to 'Wouldn't Take Nothing for My Journey Now' (1993), her collection of short essays, which contains a piece on giving and the giver. The sentence structure ('I have found that among its other benefits') matches that book's essayistic voice more than her memoir prose. I cannot confirm the passage, so the print source field is left empty rather than asserted.

author: Meg Blackburn Losey
text: I had to accept the assignment of my own existence. The responsibility of this seemed immense but in actuality my acceptance became the freedom to fly.
notes: Meg Blackburn Losey is a real author ('The Children of Now', 2007; 'Conversations with the Children of Now', 2008), and the line's vocabulary fits her genre. I have no knowledge of this specific sentence in her published work and cannot find any independent trace of it in what I know. Low confidence; the attribution may be correct but rests on nothing I can check.

author: Meister Eckhart
text: God is not found in the soul by adding anything, but by a process of subtraction.
notes: The thought is authentically Eckhartian — the via negativa, Abgeschiedenheit (detachment), and his insistence that the soul approaches God by emptying rather than acquiring are central to the German sermons. But this exact English sentence is a modern paraphrase, not a translation of an identifiable sermon passage, and it spread largely through twentieth-century popularizers (Blakney's 1941 translation, and later Matthew Fox's Creation Spirituality writings, which loosely render Eckhart for contemporary readers). Eckhart is a heavy paraphrase magnet: much of what circulates under his name is compression of his ideas rather than his words. Faithful to his theology, unverifiable as his wording.

author: Meister Eckhart
text: As long as I am this or that, I am not all things.
notes: Consistently attributed to Eckhart and consonant with his German sermons on detachment and poverty of spirit; the fuller form usually runs 'As long as I am this or that, or have this or that, I am not all things and I have not all things.' It circulates through 20th-century English translations (Blakney 1941 and later Matthew Fox anthologies), but I cannot name the specific sermon with confidence from training knowledge, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing a sermon number.

author: Meister Eckhart
text: Christ’s birth is always happening. And yet if it doesn’t happen now, how can it help me? Everything depends on that.
notes: The thought is unmistakably Eckhart's central Christmas-sermon theme — the eternal birth of the Word in the soul, and his repeated challenge 'what good is it to me that this birth is always happening, if it does not happen in me?' The wording here reads as a modern loose rendering (of the sort found in devotional anthologies such as Matthew Fox's Meditations with Meister Eckhart) rather than a scholarly translation. Authentic in substance, uncertain as an exact quotation, so I am holding it below the promotion bar.

author: Melody Beattie
text: Gratitude unlocks the fullness of life. It turns what we have into enough, and more. It turns denial into acceptance, chaos to order, confusion to clarity. It can turn a meal into a feast, a house into a home, a stranger into a friend. Gratitude makes sense of our past, brings peace for today, and creates a vision for tomorrow.
earliest_print_source: The Language of Letting Go, Melody Beattie, 1990
notes: Genuinely Beattie's, from her codependency-recovery daily-meditation writing; the attribution is consistent everywhere it appears and the voice matches her published work. The book citation is the one given in most reputable secondary sources, but I cannot confirm the page or rule out an earlier appearance in Beyond Codependency (1989), so treat the title as probable rather than confirmed. Note that q_1030 is a verbatim duplicate of this entry and should be deduplicated upstream.
