author: Meredith L. Young-Sower
text: When we allow today to be as meaningful as possible and fill it with a positive, hopeful, and loving perspective, then we are much more likely to have a tomorrow, and it is more likely to also be good and healing.
notes: The author's name is almost certainly Meredith L. Young-Sowers (Agartha, Angelic Messenger Cards, Spiritual Crisis), not 'Young-Sower' — worth correcting in the corpus. I have no independent knowledge of this passage in her published work; it circulates on gratitude and healing quote sites without a source. Honest answer is that I cannot place it.

author: Michael Altshuler
text: The bad news is time flies. The good news is you're the pilot.
keywords: time; flight; pilot; bad; good; news
notes: Uniformly attributed to Michael Altshuler, an American motivational speaker, and I know of no competing claimant — but the attribution rests entirely on quote aggregators and graduation-speech roundups, not on a book, talk transcript, or dated first appearance I can point to. Plausible but unsourced.

author: Michael Gerber
text: If you don't know where you are going, any path will get you there.
notes: Confidence reflects the strength of the Gerber attribution, which is weak. This is a floating proverb that long predates Michael Gerber; it is the popular paraphrase of the Cheshire Cat exchange in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) — 'if you don't much care where you want to get to, then it doesn't matter which way you go' — and also circulates in Yogi Berra's form ('you'll end up someplace else'). Gerber may well have used it in E-Myth-era writing, but quoting is not coining. No original-author claim should be recorded for him. | Suggested reattribution: Popular paraphrase of Lewis Carroll's Cheshire Cat passage, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865); not original to Michael Gerber

author: Michael J. Fox
text: I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection. Excellence, I can reach for; perfection is God's business.
earliest_print_source: Lucky Man: A Memoir, Michael J. Fox, 2002
notes: This is one of Fox's signature lines and matches the register of his Parkinson's-era memoir; my recollection places it in Lucky Man (2002), which is also the citation given in most secondary sources. I cannot confirm the page, and Fox has repeated the line in interviews, so the memoir may be a repetition rather than the first appearance. Strong on authorship, softer on the exact source.

author: Michael LeBeuf
text: The world is your mirror and your mind is a magnet. What you perceive in this world is largely a reflection of your own attitudes and beliefs. Life will give you what you attract with your thoughts think, act and talk negatively and your world will be negative. Think and act and talk with enthusiasm and you will attract positive results.
keywords: world; mind; life; attraction; speech; reflection; mirror
notes: The name is misspelled — the author credited is Michael LeBoeuf (Working Smart; The Greatest Management Principle in the World; How to Win Customers and Keep Them for Life). The passage is consistently attributed to him on quote sites but I cannot place it in any of his books, and the text as given is garbled ('what you attract with your thoughts think, act and talk negatively'), which is a common signature of aggregator-copied material. Unsourced.

author: Michael Levy
text: Allow the heavens and stars to praise your ability to become no-thing in a comfortable state of forgiving mindlessness. From this location God exists as your partner and you dance together as one spirit inside the rhythm of the cosmos.
keywords: heaven; stars; nothing; comfort; forgiveness; self; god; partner; dance; rhythm; universe; oneness; unity
notes: Michael Levy is a contemporary inspirational poet and author (Point of Life), and the style here matches that body of work, so the attribution is plausible. But I have no knowledge of the specific book or poem it comes from, and a living aggregator-circulated author of this kind is exactly the case where I should not manufacture a citation.

author: Milarepa
text: The affairs of the world will go on forever. Do not delay the practice of meditation.
notes: Consistently and traditionally ascribed to Milarepa (11th-century Tibetan yogi), and entirely in keeping with the counsel in the Mila Grubum (The Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa). But I cannot identify which song or which translation this English wording comes from, and Tibetan devotional sayings are heavily paraphrased in circulation. Plausible attribution, unlocated text.

author: Milton
text: I love everything that flows.
earliest_print_source: Tropic of Cancer, Henry Miller, 1934
notes: Confidence refers to the recorded attribution to 'Milton,' which appears to be a parsing error rather than a real claim about John Milton. The line is Henry Miller's, from the celebrated passage in Tropic of Cancer (1934): 'I love everything that flows...' — and Miller's own sentence contains the phrase 'said the great blind Milton of our times,' his epithet for James Joyce. Almost certainly the corpus captured the word 'Milton' out of that clause. Note this sits adjacent to q_1040, also a Miller entry with a truncated author field, which supports the parsing-error reading. | Suggested reattribution: Henry Miller

author: Milton Glaser
text: Design and art are independent coordinates that provide their greatest satisfactions when experienced simultaneously.
notes: Thematically very Glaser — the art/design relationship was a lifelong preoccupation of his, running through Art Is Work (2000) and his lectures and essays — but I cannot match this exact sentence to any of his published writing or talks. The formulation 'independent coordinates' is distinctive enough that I would expect to recall it if it were a well-known Glaser line. Plausible, unverified.

author: Mohammed
text: Whoever knows himself knows God.
notes: This is the famous Sufi maxim 'man arafa nafsahu faqad arafa rabbahu' — 'he who knows himself knows his Lord' — widely quoted in Sufi literature (Ibn Arabi among many others) and often presented as a hadith. Classical hadith scholars rejected it: it appears in none of the canonical collections, and al-Nawawi, Ibn Taymiyya and al-Zarkashi among others judged it not established as a saying of the Prophet. It is sometimes ascribed instead to the early Sufi Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi. Attributing it flatly to Muhammad is not defensible. | Suggested reattribution: Sufi maxim of uncertain origin, sometimes ascribed to Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi; not a canonical hadith

author: Mohammed Ali
text: Service to others is the rent you pay for your room here on earth.
notes: The name should be Muhammad Ali. Ali did use this line and it appears on materials associated with him, but he did not originate it — 'service is the rent you pay for your room on this earth' is an older circulating aphorism with earlier claimants including Shirley Chisholm and Marian Wright Edelman ('service is the rent we pay for living'), and earlier still it has been credited to the missionary physician Wilfred Grenfell. I do not know the true earliest instance well enough to name one, so I am leaving the reattribution null and flagging Ali as popularizer rather than author.

author: Mohandas Gandhi
text: Never use violence of any kind. Never threaten violence in any way. Never even think violent thoughts. Never argue because it attacks another’s opinion. Never criticize because it attacks another’s ego. And your success is guaranteed.
keywords: violence; thoughts; opinion; criticize; attack; ego; success
notes: Almost certainly not Gandhi. The register is late-20th-century American self-help — the escalating 'never / never / never' construction and especially the closing promise 'and your success is guaranteed' are wholly foreign to Gandhi, who framed ahimsa as a discipline and a truth-practice, not as a technique with a guaranteed payoff. I know of no passage resembling this in the Collected Works or in his letters and speeches. Gandhi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in the corpus, and this has the hallmarks of a seminar handout attributed to him for authority. No true origin identifiable, so no reattribution offered.

author: Morris L. West
text: One has to abandon altogether the search for security, and reach out to the risk of living with both arms. One has to court doubt and darkness as the cost of knowing.
earliest_print_source: The Shoes of the Fisherman, Morris L. West, 1963
notes: I recognize this as West's, and my recollection places it in The Shoes of the Fisherman (1963), where it belongs to a longer reflective passage that continues into a statement about accepting every consequence of living and dying. The attribution to West is consistent wherever the line appears. Holding at 0.7 because I am working from recall of the novel rather than a checked page, and West reused similar material across his fiction and essays.

author: Mother Teresa
text: The miracle is not that we do this work, but that we are happy to do it.
notes: Consistently attributed to Mother Teresa and fully in keeping with how she spoke about the Missionaries of Charity's work — joy as the surprising thing, not the labor. But I cannot locate it in a specific address, interview, or book; it circulates through devotional collections and secondhand quotation. Plausible and in-voice, but unsourced, so it stays below the promotion bar.

author: Mother Teresa
text: People are often unreasonable, illogical, and self centered; Forgive them anyway. If you are kind, people may accuse you of selfish, ulterior motives; Be kind anyway. If you are successful, you will win some false friends and some true enemies; Succeed anyway. If you are honest and frank, people may cheat you; Be honest and frank anyway. What you spend years building, someone could destroy overnight; Build anyway. If you find serenity and happiness, they may be jealous; Be happy anyway. The good you do today, people will often forget tomorrow; Do good anyway. Give the world the best you have, and it may never be enough; Give the world the best you've got anyway. You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and God; It was never between you and them anyway.
keywords: good; action; forgiveness; kindness; selfish; success; enemies; honesty; truth; build; destroy; serenity; happiness; jealousy; forget; give; god; self
earliest_print_source: The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council, Kent M. Keith, 1968
notes: This is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The text is an adapted version of 'The Paradoxical Commandments,' written by Kent M. Keith in 1968 while he was a Harvard undergraduate, published in his booklet The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council. A shortened version titled 'Anyway' was posted on the wall of Mother Teresa's children's home in Calcutta, which is how her name became attached; it was later reprinted in books about her, cementing the error. The closing 'it is between you and God' line is part of that Calcutta adaptation. Keith's authorship is well established and he has written about it publicly. | Suggested reattribution: Kent M. Keith

author: Mother Teresa
text: The dying, the cripple, the mental, the unwanted, the unloved-- they are Jesus in disguise.
notes: The idiom is authentically hers — 'Jesus in his distressing disguise' was a formula Mother Teresa used repeatedly about the poor and the dying, and the sentence structure matches her spoken English. I cannot, however, tie this exact sentence to a dated address, interview, or book, and the wording varies across versions. Note also that the corpus text carries dated and dehumanizing phrasing ('the cripple, the mental') that may be a transcription of her idiom or an aggregator's corruption; worth a human editorial decision independent of the provenance question.

author: Mother Teresa
text: I'm not here to be successful. I'm here to be faithful.

notes: Circulates most often as 'God has not called me to be successful; He has called me to be faithful,' consistently ascribed to Mother Teresa in devotional literature and quote collections. I cannot place it in any of her published writings, letters, or recorded addresses, and the wording varies noticeably between sources, which is a common signature of an oral/secondhand attribution. Plausible but unverified.

author: Mother Teresa
text: If you judge people, you have no time to love them.
notes: Agrees with the input flag. Extremely widely attributed to Mother Teresa and consistent with her recorded themes, but I know of no primary source — no speech, interview, or book of hers that I can place it in. It spread heavily through greeting-card and internet quote compilations. Honest answer: attribution is plausible and uncontested, evidence is absent.
suspect_reason: Commonly attributed to her but no primary source.

author: Mother Teresa
text: We realize that what we are accomplishing is a drop in the ocean. But if this drop were not in the ocean, it would be missed.
notes: A genuine and consistently attributed Mother Teresa saying, though this is one of several circulating wordings. Better-known variants: 'I know that the work is only a drop in the ocean, but if the drop were not there, the ocean would be missing something,' and 'We ourselves feel that what we are doing is just a drop in the ocean. But the ocean would be less because of that missing drop.' Attribution is strong and uniform across sources; the specific phrasing here I cannot tie to a primary text, so I am holding below the 0.80 promotion bar.

author: Mother Theresa
text: We can not do great things, just small things with great Love.
notes: One of the most durable and consistently attributed Mother Teresa lines; standard wording is 'We can do no great things, only small things with great love.' Attribution is uniform across decades of sources and she is recorded using the formulation in talks. The corpus entry has two hygiene problems: the author is misspelled 'Mother Theresa,' and the text is a garbled variant ('We can not do great things, just small things...') with inconsistent capitalization of 'Love.' I could not place the exact primary utterance, so this stays at strong-secondary rather than verified. | Suggested reattribution: Mother Teresa (author-name spelling correction only)

author: Mu Mon-kwan
text: It is so clear it is very hard to see. You must know that the fire which you are seeking is the fire in your own lantern, and that your rice has been cooked from the very beginning.
keywords: perception; see; fire; lantern; food; self; mystical
notes: 'Mu Mon-kwan' is not a person — it is a garbling of Mumonkan (無門關), the Japanese title of The Gateless Gate, the 1228 koan collection compiled by the Chinese Chan master Wumen Huikai (Japanese: Mumon Ekai). The underlying saying is Wumen's verse commentary, familiar in English from Paul Reps' Zen Flesh, Zen Bones as roughly: 'It is too clear and so it is hard to see. A dunce once searched for fire with a lighted lantern. Had he known what fire was, he could have cooked his rice much sooner.' The text here is a loose modern paraphrase, not any translation I recognize, so I am not citing the Mumonkan as the print source for this wording. The idea is authentically Wumen's; the sentence is not. | Suggested reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate / Mumonkan, c. 1228 — as a paraphrase, not a quotation

author: Muhammad Ali
text: The man who has no imagination has no wings.
notes: Consistently attributed to Muhammad Ali and stylistically plausible for him, but I cannot place it in a specific interview, press conference, or in The Greatest: My Own Story (1975). Ali is a moderate misattribution magnet — motivational copy written for and about him is routinely recirculated as his own words (see q_1057). Attribution here is uncontested but unsourced.

author: Muhammad Ali
text: Impossible is just a word thrown around by small men who find it easier to live in the world they've been given than to explore the power they have to change it. Impossible is not a fact. It's an opinion. Impossible is potential. Impossible is temporary. Impossible is nothing.
notes: This is advertising copy, not Ali. The passage is the manifesto text of the adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign launched in 2004, developed by the agency 180/TBWA, whose flagship spots featured Muhammad Ali (and archival footage of him alongside his daughter Laila). The final line 'Impossible is nothing' is the campaign tagline, which is the strongest tell. Ali's name and image were licensed to the campaign; the words were written for it. Widely recirculated as an Ali quotation ever since, including in books and on quote sites. I am confident the campaign is the origin and correspondingly low-confidence in the Ali attribution. | Suggested reattribution: adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign copy (agency 180/TBWA), 2004

author: Myla & Jon Kabat-Zinn
text: Mindfulness means moment-to-moment, non-judgmental awareness. It is cultivated by refining our capacity to pay attention, intentionally, in the present moment, and then sustaining that attention over time as best we can. In the process, we become more in touch with our life as it is unfolding.

notes: The joint byline points to Everyday Blessings (Hyperion, 1997), which is Myla and Jon Kabat-Zinn's only co-authored book, so the source attribution is near-certain even though I cannot confirm the sentences verbatim against the text. The definition also closely tracks Jon Kabat-Zinn's standard formulation ('paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgmentally,' Full Catastrophe Living, 1990 / Wherever You Go, There You Are, 1994), which is consistent with a co-authored restatement rather than a fabrication. Holding below 0.80 because the wording is unverified.

author: Myla Kabat-Zinn
text: Each difficult moment has the potential to open my eyes and open my heart.
notes: Attributed to Myla Kabat-Zinn, most likely drawn from Everyday Blessings (1997), the book she co-wrote with Jon Kabat-Zinn, where she writes in her own voice in places. I cannot confirm the line appears there or anywhere else I can name. Myla Kabat-Zinn has a thin independent publication record, which makes the quote hard to source and easy to misassign between the two authors. Honest verdict: unverified.

author: Nagarjuna
text: Contentment is true wealth.
notes: The canonical form of this saying is Buddhist scripture, not Nagarjuna: Dhammapada 204, 'santuṭṭhī paramaṃ dhanaṃ' — 'contentment is the greatest wealth.' Nagarjuna does echo it in the Suhṛllekha (Letter to a Friend), where he cites the Buddha to the effect that contentment is the supreme form of wealth, so the ascription is not baseless — but it makes Nagarjuna a transmitter rather than the author, and this four-word English form matches the Dhammapada rendering, not a specific Suhṛllekha translation I can name. Attribution as it stands is weak. | Suggested reattribution: Dhammapada 204 (attributed to the Buddha); Nagarjuna restates it in the Suhṛllekha, quoting the Buddha

author: Naoto Fukasawa
text: Great design is a multi-layered relationship between human life and its environment.
notes: Naoto Fukasawa is a real and well-documented Japanese industrial designer (MUJI, ±0, Naoto Fukasawa Design), and the sentiment matches his stated 'without thought' philosophy of design as embedded in everyday behavior and environment. The line circulates in design-quote collections, most plausibly extracted from an interview or from his Phaidon monograph (2007). I cannot place it in a specific text or interview, and designer quotes of this kind are frequently paraphrased in circulation.

author: Napoleon Hill & W. Clement Stone
text: It is in quiet that our best ideas occur to us. Don't make the mistake of believing that by a frantic kind of dashing around you are being your most effective and efficient self. Don't assume that you are wasting time when you take time out for thought.

notes: The joint byline points to Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960), the only book Napoleon Hill and W. Clement Stone wrote together, and the passage's content — quiet reflection, warning against confusing motion with effectiveness — fits that book's register. I cannot confirm the wording appears there, and I have no independent recollection of this passage, so I am not asserting the citation. Attribution to the pair is plausible on structural grounds only.

author: Natalie Goldberg
text: If you're having difficulty coming up with new ideas, then slow down. For me, slowing down has been a tremendous source of creativity. It has allowed me to open up -- to know that there's life under the earth and that I have to let it come through me in a new way. Creativity exists in the present moment. You can't find it anywhere else.

notes: Natalie Goldberg is the author of Writing Down the Bones (1986) and Wild Mind (1990), and this is entirely consistent with her teaching on slowness, composting, and present-moment creativity. The conversational register ('For me, slowing down has been...') reads like an interview or magazine Q&A rather than her published prose. I cannot place the specific interview or book, so the attribution stands as plausible-but-unsourced.

author: Nathaniel Alexander Owings
text: We will find our way because of a desire to create, and joie de vivre will move us rather than threats of death or extinction. What we do must be done for love, not fear.
notes: Nathaniel Alexander Owings (1903-1984) was a real architect, co-founder of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, and author of The American Aesthetic (1969) and the memoir The Spaces in Between: An Architect's Journey (1973); the environmental-humanist tone fits The American Aesthetic in particular. But I have no recollection of this passage in either book or in any secondary citation, and a quote this obscure with no accompanying source is hard to distinguish from a misattribution. Low confidence, no citation offered.

author: Nathaniel Branden
text: How do we nurture the soul? By revering our own life. By treating it as supremely important. By reaching for the best within ourselves. By learning to love it all, not only the joys and the victories, but also the pain and the struggles.
notes: Consistent with Nathaniel Branden's body of work on self-esteem and self-honoring — most likely from Honoring the Self (1983) or The Six Pillars of Self-Esteem (1994) — but 'nurture the soul' is a slightly atypical register for Branden, who generally wrote in secular psychological language. I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and cannot rule out that it comes from a self-help anthology quoting him loosely.

author: Nathaniel Branden
text: Self-acceptance is my refusal to be in an adversarial relationship to myself.
notes: This is a recognizable Branden formulation and is attributed to him with unusual consistency; 'the practice of self-acceptance' is one of the six pillars in The Six Pillars of Self-Esteem (1994), and the refusal-to-be-adversarial framing is how he defines it there. I believe the book is the source but cannot confirm the sentence verbatim, so I am naming it in these notes rather than asserting it as a citation, and holding below the 0.80 promotion bar.

author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
text: Nathaniel Hawthorne once famously said, “Happiness is a butterfly, which, when pursued, is always just beyond your grasp, but which, if you will sit down quietly, may alight upon you.”
notes: Two problems. First, data hygiene: the stored text includes its own framing ('Nathaniel Hawthorne once famously said, ...') plus curly quotes — the quotation itself should be extracted and the frame dropped. Second, provenance: the documented Hawthorne passage on this theme is from his American Note-Books and runs, in substance, 'Happiness in this world, when it comes, comes incidentally. Make it the object of pursuit, and it leads us a wild-goose chase... Follow some other object, and very possibly we may find that we have caught happiness without dreaming of it.' The butterfly simile is the popular, much-later circulating form, and I cannot confirm Hawthorne wrote the butterfly wording himself. It may be a paraphrase that hardened into a quotation. Attribution to Hawthorne for the idea is sound; for these words, unverified.

author: Navajo saying
text: Bless those who challenge us to grow, to stretch, to move beyond the knowable, to come back home to our elemental and essential nature. Bless those who challenge us for they remind us of doors we have closed and doors we have yet to open. They are big medicine teachers for us.
keywords: challenge; bless; essence; self; medicine; learning; teacher; native american
notes: No credible traditional source. 'Navajo saying' is a generic ascription of exactly the kind that inspirational literature invents, and the language here is modern therapeutic English — 'challenge us to grow,' 'move beyond the knowable,' 'elemental and essential nature' — not translated Diné oral tradition. 'Big medicine teachers' reads as a settler-inflected pastiche of Native idiom. Pseudo-Native-American attributions are a well-documented category of fabrication (cf. the Chief Seattle speech). I know of no Navajo prayer, ceremonial text, or ethnographic record containing this. Recommend rejecting or relabeling as anonymous modern.

author: Neale Donald Walsch
text: Life begins at the end of your comfort zone.
notes: Attributed to Neale Donald Walsch with strong consistency across sources, and he has used and endorsed it himself, which distinguishes it from the usual orphan aphorism. The sentiment appears in the Conversations with God material ('Life begins at the end of your comfort zone' is often traced to that body of work), but I cannot pin it to a specific book or page. Note this is one of the most heavily recirculated single-sentence quotes on the internet, which tends to detach lines from their sources.

author: Neale Donald Walsch
text: Yea, let all those who have ears to hear, listen. For I tell you this: at the critical juncture in all human relationships, there is only one question: What would love do now?
keywords: love; action; ears; listen; human; relationships; question
earliest_print_source: Conversations with God: An Uncommon Dialogue, Book 1, Neale Donald Walsch, 1995
notes: 'What would love do now?' is a signature question of the Conversations with God material and is closely identified with Book 1 (1995); the surrounding cadence here — 'Yea, let all those who have ears to hear' — matches the book's deliberately scriptural voice. I am confident about the work; I cannot confirm this exact passage or its page, so the citation is at book level and the score stays below the promotion bar.

author: Nelson Henderson
text: The true meaning of life is to plant trees, under whose shade you do not expect to sit.
earliest_print_source: Under Whose Shade: A Story of a Pioneer in the Swan River Valley of Manitoba, Wes Henderson, 1986
notes: This one has a real and unusually well-traced provenance for a folk-sounding aphorism: it is reported as the advice of Nelson Henderson, a Manitoba farmer, recorded by his son Wes Henderson in the family memoir Under Whose Shade (1986) — the book's title comes from the saying. The frequently seen preface is 'The true meaning of life is to plant trees under whose shade you do not expect to sit.' I am confident in the Henderson origin and reasonably confident in the book; note the broader tree-planting sentiment is ancient (cf. the Greek proverb about old men planting trees) and Nelson Henderson is the reporter of this phrasing, not the inventor of the idea.

author: Nelson Mandela
text: It always seems impossible until it's done.
notes: Ubiquitously attributed to Nelson Mandela and quoted as his during his lifetime without evident objection, which is meaningful evidence — but I cannot place it in any speech, letter, or book of his, and the attribution appears to become common only around the 2000s. It also circulated widely through advertising and campaign copy, a route that manufactures false attributions. Mandela is a moderate misattribution magnet. Plausible, unsourced; treat as attributed-unverified until a primary text is found. NOTE: this quote is duplicated in this batch as q_1075 — deduplicate.

author: Nelson Mandela
text: You see, when there is danger, a good leader takes the front line. But when there is celebration, a good leader stays in the back room. If you want the cooperation of human beings around you, make them feel that they are important. And you do that by being humble.
keywords: danger; leader; celebrate; people; human; humility
notes: This is Mandela's well-documented 'lead from the front / lead from the back' teaching, which reached wide circulation through Richard Stengel — his TIME cover story 'Mandela: His 8 Lessons of Leadership' (July 2008) and his book Mandela's Way (2010), both drawing on years of recorded conversations while ghostwriting Long Walk to Freedom. Stengel is a credible firsthand channel, so this sits well above the usual orphan-quote baseline. I cannot confirm the exact wording against either text, so I am naming the likely channel here rather than asserting a citation.

author: Nelson Mandela
text: It always seems impossible until it's done.
notes: Exact duplicate of q_1073 within this batch — same text, same author. Verdict is identical: ubiquitously attributed to Nelson Mandela and quoted as his during his lifetime, but I cannot place it in any speech, letter, or book, and it spread heavily through advertising and campaign copy. Plausible, unsourced. Recommend merging with q_1073 at the dedupe stage.

author: Nicholas Evans
text: Sometimes what seems like surrender isn't surrender at all. It's about what's going on in our hearts. About seeing clearly the way life is and accepting it and being true to it, whatever the pain, because the pain of not being true to it is far, far greater.
notes: Consistently attributed to Nicholas Evans and, in most citations, to his 1995 novel The Horse Whisperer, where it reads as Tom Booker's voice. I recall the passage as belonging to that novel but cannot confirm chapter or exact wording from memory, and a similar sentiment appears in the 1998 film adaptation, so I am leaving the print source blank rather than asserting a page. Author attribution is plausible and uncontested; the work-level citation is not confirmed.

author: Niels Bohr
text: Great innovations when they appear, seem muddled and strange. They are only half understood by their discoverer and remain a mystery to everyone else. But if an idea does not appear bizarre there is no hope for it.
notes: Widely circulated as Bohr but I cannot place it in any Bohr paper, lecture, or documented conversation. Bohr's genuinely sourced remark in this family is the 'crazy enough' exchange reported second-hand by Freeman Dyson (recounting a 1958 Columbia seminar on Heisenberg and Pauli's unified field theory): 'we are all agreed that your theory is crazy... whether it is crazy enough to have a chance of being correct.' The wording here reads like a later prose expansion of that idea, possibly from a management or innovation anthology rather than Bohr himself. No primary source; attribution unconfirmed.

author: Nietzsche
text: The higher we soar the smaller we appear to those who cannot fly.
notes: Universally attributed to Nietzsche and stylistically consistent with the flight imagery of Zarathustra, but I cannot locate it in a specific work from memory. My recollection is that this line sits in the unsourced or disputed section of Nietzsche quotation compilations rather than being traced to a published aphorism. Plausible but unconfirmed; I am not inventing a locus.

author: Nietzsche
text: The belief in truth begins with the doubt of all truths in which one has previously believed.
notes: Corresponds to a German aphorism I associate with Nietzsche's middle period - roughly 'Der Glaube an die Wahrheit beginnt mit dem Zweifel an allen bisher geglaubten Wahrheiten' - most often cited to Human, All Too Human, Volume II (Assorted Opinions and Maxims). I am confident enough in the authorship to call it plausible but not confident enough in the volume or aphorism number to print a citation. Author likely correct; source unverified.

author: Nietzsche
text: The growth of wisdom may be gauged exactly by the diminution of ill-temper.
notes: Attributed to Nietzsche in quotation collections. The epigrammatic form is consistent with Human, All Too Human or the Nachlass, but I cannot place it in any specific text and I have no recollection of a German original for it, which weakens my confidence that it is Nietzsche at all rather than a translator's or anthologist's line. Unverified.

author: Nietzsche
text: I have a song to sing and I will sing it, although I am alone in an empty house and must sing to my own ears.
keywords: song; sing; alone; empty; house; ears; solitude
notes: I cannot place this in Nietzsche's published works or correspondence. The image (singing alone in an empty house) is not one I can match to any passage I know, and the sentence rhythm reads more like a modern inspirational paraphrase than like Nietzsche's aphoristic style in translation. Possibly a loose rendering of a letter, possibly not his at all. No source; honest answer is that I do not know.

author: Isaac Newton
text: If I have made any valuable discoveries, it has been owing more to patient attention, than to any other talent.
notes: Newton's remark on patient thought is genuinely documented, but the best-attested wording is the one recorded in David Brewster's Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton (1855): 'If I have done the public any service, it is due to patient thought.' The variant here ('any valuable discoveries... patient attention... than to any other talent') circulates widely in 19th and 20th century collections and may derive from a separate reported conversation, but I cannot confirm which. Attribution to Newton is sound in substance; the exact wording is a variant I will not cite to a page.

author: Nikos Kazantzakis
text: By believing passionately in something that still does not exist, we create it. The non-existent is whatever we have not sufficiently desired.
notes: Consistently attributed to Kazantzakis and thoroughly consistent with his metaphysics of will in The Saviors of God and Report to Greco. Most citations point to Report to Greco (1961, English 1965). I recall the sentiment strongly as his but cannot confirm which book or translation the English wording comes from, so no print source is asserted.

author: Nikos Kazantzakis
text: A man needs a little madness, or else he never dares cut the rope and be free.
notes: Zorba's line from Zorba the Greek. Note that this exact English phrasing is the one spoken in Michael Cacoyannis's 1964 film adaptation ('A man needs a little madness, or else he never dares cut the rope and be free'), which is where its popularity comes from; the corresponding passage in Kazantzakis's 1946 novel (English translation by Carl Wildman, 1952) carries the same sense in different words. So the sentiment is Kazantzakis's, but the wording may be the screenwriter's. Attributing to the author is defensible; I am not printing a page citation because I cannot distinguish novel wording from screenplay wording.

author: Norman Cousins
text: All things are possible once enough human beings realize that everything is at stake.
notes: Attributed to Norman Cousins across many collections and entirely consistent with his nuclear-age advocacy writing (Modern Man Is Obsolete, 1945; Human Options, 1981). I cannot place it in a specific book, essay, or Saturday Review editorial from memory. Author plausible; source unverified.

author: Norman Vincent Peale
text: It is an absolute, demonstrable fact that the person who really practices love - real love - rises so high above fear that it can no longer touch him. Where love is, fear cannot live. Love withers fear.
keywords: love; fear; fact; practice; high; touch; live
notes: Reads authentically as Peale - the flat assertion of a 'demonstrable fact' followed by the love/fear inversion is his characteristic register, and the theme runs through The Power of Positive Thinking (1952) and his later devotional writing. But I cannot pin it to a specific book or Guideposts piece, and Peale's corpus is large and heavily anthologized. Attribution plausible, source not established.

author: O. Wayne Rollins
text: There’s no such thing as a self-made person. I’ve had much help and have found that if you are willing to work, many people are willing to help you.
keywords: self; success; help; support; work; people
notes: O. Wayne Rollins (1912-1991), founder of Rollins Inc., is a low-profile figure whose quoted remarks come almost entirely from business-quotation compilations and company/foundation retrospectives rather than from published writing. I have no independent knowledge of where or when he said this. The sentiment is a commonplace of American business memoir, so the attribution could easily have drifted. Unverified.

author: Og Mandino
text: Count your blessings. Once you realize how valuable you are and how much you have going for you, the smiles will return, the sun will break out, the music will play, and you will finally be able to move forward the life that God intended for you with grace, strength, courage, and confidence.
notes: Consistent with Og Mandino's late motivational writing, and 'Count your blessings' is one of the numbered rules in A Better Way to Live (1990), his book of seventeen 'Rules to Live By.' I believe this expanded passage is that rule's text, but I cannot confirm the wording or the rule number from memory, so no citation is printed. Author attribution reliable; exact source unconfirmed.

author: Og Mandino
text: I will love the light for it shows me the way, yet I will endure the darkness for it shows me the stars.
notes: One of the best known lines credited to Og Mandino and stylistically his (the 'I will...' vow construction is the scroll form used throughout The Greatest Salesman in the World, 1968). I cannot confirm whether it comes from that book, from A Better Way to Live, or from one of his lectures, so the source is left blank. Author attribution well established in secondary sources.

author: Og Mandino
text: Your only limitations are those you set up in your mind, or permit others to set up for you.
notes: Generic self-help maxim of a kind that circulated in New Thought and success literature well before Mandino (close variants appear in Napoleon Hill and Charles Popplestone-era writing). Attributed to Mandino in modern collections but with no traceable source, and the idea is too common for the attribution to be safe. Unverified and possibly drifted.

author: Og Mandino
text: Laugh at yourself and at life. Not in the spirit of derision or whining self-pity, but as a remedy, a miracle drug, that will ease your pain, cure your depression, and help you to put in perspective that seemingly terrible defeat and worry with laughter at your predicaments, thus freeing your mind to think clearly toward the solution that is certain to come. Never take yourself too seriously.
keywords: laughter; miracle; drug; pain; depression; help; perspective; defeat; worry; freedom; mind; think; clarity; solution; serious
notes: Same provenance situation as the 'Count your blessings' passage - this is almost certainly one of the seventeen rules in A Better Way to Live (1990), whose entries share exactly this structure (imperative opening, long qualifying clause, short closing command: 'Never take yourself too seriously'). I cannot confirm the rule number or verify the wording, so no citation. Author attribution reliable.

author: Olga Broumas
text: She who loves roses must be patient and not cry out when she is pierced by thorns.
notes: Attributed to the Greek-American poet Olga Broumas in quotation collections, but I cannot locate it in Beginning with O (1977) or her later books, and it does not read like her line-broken, Sappho-inflected verse. The sentiment matches a family of older proverbs about roses and thorns (commonly given as Persian or Turkish, e.g. 'he who wants a rose must respect the thorn'), which is the more likely origin. I do not know the true source, so no reattribution is asserted - only doubt about this one.

author: Oliver Goldsmith
text: Success consists of getting up just one more time than you fall.
notes: Goldsmith did write on this theme: in The Citizen of the World (1760-62) he gives 'Our greatest glory consists not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall' - and he presents it there as a Confucian saying, not his own. The wording in this record ('getting up just one more time than you fall') is a modern counting-style rewording that I cannot trace to Goldsmith or to any 18th-century text; it appears in 20th-century motivational literature and is variously credited to Goldsmith and to others. So the attribution is at best inherited from a paraphrase of a paraphrase. Not calling it likely_misattributed only because the idea does descend from Goldsmith's page; the words almost certainly are not his.

author: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr.
text: One's mind, once stretched by a new idea, never regains its original dimensions.
earliest_print_source: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., 1858
notes: Two errors compounded. The original is by Oliver Wendell Holmes SENIOR, the physician-essayist, not his son the Supreme Court justice: 'Every now and then a man's mind is stretched by a new idea or sensation, and never shrinks back to its former dimensions.' The familiar 'One's mind, once stretched by a new idea, never regains its original dimensions' is a 20th-century compression of that sentence, not Holmes's wording. Father/son confusion is the standard failure mode with this quote. Recommend reattributing to Holmes Sr. and, if the corpus wants exactness, restoring the 1858 wording. | Suggested reattribution: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: The public is wonderfully tolerant. It forgives everything except genius.
notes: Authentic Wilde in substance and voice; my recollection places it in the critical prose of Intentions (1891), most likely The Critic as Artist, where he returns repeatedly to the public's hostility toward genius and its indulgence of mediocrity. Because I cannot confirm the essay with certainty - it could equally be from The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), which treats the same theme - I am not printing a source. Authorship strongly supported; locus unconfirmed.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Imagination is a quality given a man to compensate him for what he is not, and a sense of humor was provided to console him for what he is.
notes: Circulates in 20th-century quote compilations under Wilde's name, but I cannot place it in any Wilde play, essay, novel, or letter I know. The epigrammatic balance is Wilde-like, which is exactly what makes aphorisms stick to him. No source; treating as unverified rather than assuming the collections are right.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Always forgive you enemies; nothing annoys them so much.
notes: Very widely attributed to Wilde and one of the most-reprinted 'Wilde' lines, but to my knowledge it sits in the unsourced/attributed section of the Wilde record rather than in any of his published works. Consistent attribution, zero primary evidence. (Input text has a typo: 'you enemies' should read 'your enemies'.)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Be yourself; everone else is already taken.
notes: A well-known false Wilde. It appears nowhere in his works and the Wilde attribution is a late-20th-century development; earlier circulation of the sentiment is anonymous aphorism/greeting-card material. Classic misattribution-magnet behaviour. No credible author is identifiable, so apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed. (Input also misspells 'everone'.)

author: Osho
text: Sharing is the very foundation, the source. Share your truth, share your meditation, share your love. Share whatsoever inner beauty arises in you, whatsoever inner glow arises in you. Share your inner flame and never be a miser, and you will become richer and richer, and there is no end to that richness.
keywords: sharing; giving; generosity; truth; meditation; love; beauty; inner; self; glow; flame; fire; wealth
notes: Diction, cadence, and subject are strongly consistent with Osho's transcribed discourses, and the line circulates under his name. But his corpus is thousands of transcribed talks compiled into hundreds of volumes, and I cannot name the specific discourse or book. Plausible author, unlocatable source.

author: Osho
text: Everybody has to be alert, aware, and drop all false hopes. Nobody can save you, and nobody has ever saved anybody. Masters have only shown the way. Because they have traveled on the path, they can save you unnecessary wandering, they can show you the straight way. But nobody can walk for you.
keywords: false; hope; save; self; masters; teachers; search; path; walk; straight
notes: The 'masters only show the way, nobody can walk for you' theme is a recurring Osho motif and the phrasing reads as a genuine discourse transcript. I cannot identify which talk or published volume it comes from. Attribution plausible but unsourced.

author: Osho
text: You are simply unique, incomparable. Accept this, love this, celebrate this -and in that very celebration you will start seeing the uniqueness of the others, the incomparable beauty of the others. Love is possible only when there is a deep acceptance of oneself, the other, the world. Acceptance creates the milieu in which love grows, the soil in which love blooms.
keywords: unique; love; celebrate; people; beauty; acceptance; self; world; growth; soil; bloom; flower
notes: Widely circulated as Osho and consistent with his teaching on uniqueness, acceptance, and love. I have a vague sense it appears in one of the compiled volumes on love or courage, but I cannot confirm which, and I will not guess a title. Unsourced.

author: P. T. Barnum
text: The noblest art is that of making others happy.
notes: Long associated with P. T. Barnum and often described as his motto; it recurs in circus histories and Barnum memorial contexts. I cannot place it in his autobiography or his published writings, and I do not know the earliest printing. Consistent attribution to a non-magnet figure is mild positive evidence, but not enough for 'attributed'.

author: P. T. Barnum
text: No one ever made a difference by being like everyone else.
notes: This is dialogue written for the fictionalised Barnum in the 2017 film The Greatest Showman, not a saying of the historical showman. The phrasing is modern-motivational and unlike 19th-century Barnum's prose. A large wave of pseudo-Barnum quotes entered circulation after that film. Reattribution is to the film's screenwriters; I am confident about the film origin but will not name individual credits from memory. | Suggested reattribution: The Greatest Showman (2017 film) — dialogue written for the P. T. Barnum character

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Art washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life.
notes: One of the most-reprinted 'Picasso' lines, consistently attributed to him across mid-20th-century onward compilations, but I know of no primary source — no interview, letter, or recorded conversation I can point to. Picasso is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphorisms about art. Attribution plausible, evidence weak.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: I am always doing that which I cannot do, in order that I may learn how to do it.
notes: Widely quoted as Picasso in compilations and business/creativity literature; I cannot locate it in Brassaï's or Gilot's recorded conversations or any interview I know. No primary source, and the sentiment is generic enough to have drifted onto him.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Everything is a miracle. It is a miracle that one does not dissolve in one's bath like a lump of sugar.
notes: The lump-of-sugar image is distinctive and specific rather than generic-inspirational, which argues for a real recorded remark, and my sense is that it comes from one of the memoir-conversation books about Picasso (Gilot or Brassaï). I cannot confirm which, so I am not citing one. Attribution likely correct, source unconfirmed.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: The important thing is to create. Nothing else matters; creation is all.
notes: Circulates under Picasso's name in creativity anthologies. Possibly a condensation of remarks recorded in the conversation memoirs, but I cannot place it and the flat phrasing reads like a compilation paraphrase rather than a transcribed utterance. Unsourced.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Good artists copy. Great artists steal.
notes: No evidence Picasso ever said this. The attribution was massively amplified by Steve Jobs quoting it in the 1990s/2000s. The documented antecedents belong to the literary-criticism tradition: W. H. Davenport Adams (1892) on poets who 'imitate and improve' versus those who 'steal and spoil', and T. S. Eliot in The Sacred Wood (1920), 'Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal.' Those are ancestors, not the same sentence, so I am not naming a single true author.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: I took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child.
notes: There is a real documented root: Herbert Read reported Picasso's remark on seeing an exhibition of children's drawings, roughly 'When I was as old as these children I could draw like Raphael; it took me many years to learn how to draw like these children' (reported in the British press in the mid-1950s). The version here — 'four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child' — is a later mutation with no documented basis. Kernel genuine, this wording not. (Input also has a typo: 'I took me'.)

author: Pamela Harper
text: Without intentional, purposeful thought we might start to think that life events are somehow random. We might also venture onto the path of the "victim". My mantra states there are no victims - only volunteers. Every step of my journey is paved with a knowing that I am surrounded by divine opportunities to fulfill my purpose in prosperity.
keywords: purpose; thought; path; journey; opportunity; prosperity
notes: I have no knowledge of Pamela Harper as a quoted author and cannot place this passage. The register — mantra, divine opportunities, prosperity — suggests a contributor piece in a prosperity or affirmation anthology. Nothing traceable in my training knowledge; honest answer is that I do not know.

author: Papaji
text: The thief of peace is the desire for the transient.
notes: Consistent with Papaji's (H. W. L. Poonja's) satsang idiom, and his recorded corpus is largely transcribed dialogues compiled by students, which makes any single aphorism hard to source. I cannot place this line in any specific compilation. Low confidence, no source.

author: Paramahansa Yogananda
text: To me there is no difference between one person and another; I behold all as soul-reflections of the one God. I can't think of anyone as a stranger, for I know that we are all part of the One Spirit.
keywords: difference; person; god; reflection; soul; thought; stranger; oneness; unity
notes: Thoroughly characteristic of Yogananda's voice and doctrine ('soul-reflections of the one God', 'One Spirit'), and likely drawn from the Self-Realization Fellowship collections of his talks (Man's Eternal Quest, The Divine Romance, or similar). I cannot confirm which volume, so I am not citing one. Attribution plausible, source unlocated.

author: Patanjali
text: When you are inspired by some great purpose, some extraordinary project, all your thoughts break their bonds. Your mind transcends limitations. Your consciousness expands in every direction. And you find yourself in a new, great and wonderful world. Dormant forces, faculties and talents become alive and you discover yourself to be a greater person by far than you ever dreamed yourself to be.
keywords: world; mind; purpose; consciousness; dream; creativity
notes: This passage does not appear in the Yoga Sutras in any translation I know. The Sutras are terse aphorisms in Sanskrit; this is expansive 20th-century motivational English ('dormant forces, faculties and talents'). It spread widely through Western business-creativity and New Thought literature in the 1980s-90s while carrying a 'Patanjali' label. Not Patanjali; I cannot identify the actual modern author, so no reattribution is offered.

author: Patricia Nourot
text: If I get to pick what I want to do, then it's play... if someone else tells me that I have to do it, then it's work.
notes: Patricia Monighan Nourot was a scholar of children's play and a co-author in that literature, so the work/play distinction here is topically apt for her. But I cannot place the sentence in any of her publications, and lines like this in play scholarship are often quoted from a child rather than authored by the researcher. Weak evidence.

author: Paul Boese
text: Forgiveness does not change the past, but it does enlarge the future.
notes: Consistently attributed to Paul Boese across decades of quote collections, with circulation traceable to 1960s-era newspaper quote columns/fillers. The attribution's stability to an otherwise obscure name is itself decent evidence — misattributions drift toward famous people, not away from them. I do not know the exact original printing, so I am leaving the citation null rather than guessing.

author: Paul Ferrini
text: Every lesson is a widening and deepening of consciousness. It is a stretching of the mind beyond its conceptual limits and a stretching of the heart beyond its emotional boundaries. It is a bringing of unconscious material into consciousness, a healing of past wounds, and a discovery of new faith and trust.
keywords: learning; consciousness; emotions; heart; healing; discovery
notes: Paul Ferrini is a real author in the Course-in-Miracles-adjacent tradition (Love Without Conditions and related titles), and this passage matches his register closely. I cannot identify the specific book or article. Plausible author, no locatable source.

author: Paul Hawken
text: Only an organization that does not presume to know will be able to detect and use fresh new information from its environment. Planning must be firmly based on inquiry. Questions keep a business alive.
keywords: planning; knowledge; fresh; information; environment; inquiry; questions
notes: Strongly consistent with Paul Hawken's thinking on inquiry-driven enterprise, and my impression is that it comes from Growing a Business (1987), whose argument leans on questions over expertise. I am not confident enough to enter that as a citation, so the source field stays null. Attribution likely correct, source unconfirmed.

author: Paul Jewkes
text: I would rather see a crooked furrow than a field unplowed.
notes: I cannot identify 'Paul Jewkes' as a documented author, executive, or public figure in my training knowledge, and I cannot place this line in any published source. The underlying image is an old agricultural proverb ('a crooked furrow is better than an unplowed field') that circulates in farming, LDS, and management-advice contexts with no fixed attribution; the named attribution here may be to a private individual or a local speaker. No evidence either way, so no reattribution is offered.

author: Paul Tillich
text: The first duty of love is to listen.
notes: Very widely and consistently attributed to Paul Tillich, and the sentiment fits his theology of love, justice, and power. However, I cannot place it in a specific sermon, essay, or volume, and the line circulates almost entirely through quote collections rather than through citation to a Tillich text. Plausible but unconfirmed; kept below the promotion bar for that reason.

author: Paulo Coelho
text: You can become blind by seeing each day as a similar one. Each day is a different one, each day brings a miracle of its own. It's just a matter of paying attention to this miracle.
notes: Attributed consistently to Paulo Coelho and stylistically consistent with his aphoristic writing (possibly from 'Like the Flowing River' or from his blog/social posts, which are a genuine and heavily quoted source for him). I cannot identify the specific book or post, and a large volume of Coelho-attributed material online is unsourced, so I am holding confidence at the moderate level.

author: Pema Chodron
text: Gloriousness and wretchedness need each other. One inspires us, the other softens us.
earliest_print_source: Start Where You Are: A Guide to Compassionate Living, Pema Chödrön, 1994 (commonly cited; not confirmed)
notes: The gloriousness/wretchedness pairing is a signature Pema Chödrön teaching from her lojong material, and I associate this formulation with 'Start Where You Are' (1994). I am confident about the author and the teaching; I am less certain which of her books this exact sentence appears in — 'The Wisdom of No Escape' covers similar ground — so the source is flagged as unconfirmed.

author: Pema Chodron
text: A further sign of health is that we don't become undone by fear and trembling, but we take it as a message that it's time to stop struggling and look directly at what's threatening us.
keywords: fear; health; message; look; perception; threat; struggle
notes: Consistently attributed to Pema Chödrön and characteristic of her writing on fear; I associate it with 'When Things Fall Apart' (1997), where she treats fear and trembling as a signal rather than an enemy, but I cannot confirm the book or chapter well enough to record it as a citation. Author attribution is solid; the source is not.

author: Pema Chodron
text: If we learn to open our hearts, anyone, including the people who drive us crazy, can be our teacher.
notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Pema Chödrön, and squarely within her recurring teaching that difficult people are the practice. I cannot pin it to a specific book ('The Wisdom of No Escape' and 'Start Where You Are' are both plausible), so no print source is recorded.

author: Pema Chodron
text: When you begin to touch your heart or let your heart be touched, you begin to discover that it's bottomless, that it doesn't have any resolution, that this heart is huge, vast, and limitless. You begin to discover how much warmth and gentleness is there, as well as how much space.
keywords: heart; touch; discover; vast; infinite; warmth; gentleness; space
notes: Attribution to Pema Chödrön is consistent across sources and the passage reads as transcribed teaching in her voice (the bottomless-heart image recurs in her bodhichitta talks). I cannot identify which book or talk it comes from, so the source is left null.

author: Pema Chodron
text: The truth you believe and cling to makes you unavailable to hear anything new.
notes: Attributed to Pema Chödrön across quote collections and consistent with her teaching on fixed views and 'the truth we cling to'. I cannot locate a specific source text, and this shorter aphoristic form is the kind most vulnerable to being condensed from a longer passage, so I am holding confidence moderate.

author: Pema Chödrön
text: You are the sky. Everything else – it’s just the weather.
notes: Extremely widely circulated as Pema Chödrön, and she does use the sky-and-weather metaphor for mind and passing states. The caution is that the sky/clouds image is common across Tibetan Buddhist teaching generally (it long predates her), so this compressed slogan form may be a popularized condensation of her wording rather than a verbatim sentence. Author attribution is likely correct; wording and source are unconfirmed.

author: Pema Chödrön
text: Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible in us be found.
notes: This is Pema Chödrön quoting someone else. The line originates with Karlfried Graf Dürckheim, the German psychotherapist and Zen teacher — his formulation runs roughly 'Only to the extent that a man exposes himself over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in him.' Chödrön quotes it (with attribution to Dürckheim) in her own work, most likely 'When Things Fall Apart', which is how it got detached and re-credited to her. I am confident about Dürckheim as the source author; I cannot name the specific Dürckheim title from memory. | Suggested reattribution: Karlfried Graf Dürckheim

author: Philip Toshido
text: We are, all of us, the divine spirit gazing upon itself in a gigantic mirror.
notes: I can find no author named 'Philip Toshido' in my training knowledge — not as a writer, teacher, or public figure — and the name itself looks irregular (Toshido is not a standard surname; this may be a corrupted or invented name). The sentiment is a generic Advaita/perennialist formulation that appears in many unattributed forms. Absence from my knowledge is not proof the person does not exist, but there is no credible attribution to record here and no basis for a reattribution.

author: Plato
text: Do not keep children to their studies by compulsion but by play.
earliest_print_source: Republic, Plato, Book VII, ~536d–537a (paraphrase)
notes: This is a genuine Platonic position, loosely rendered. In Republic Book VII Socrates argues that early education should not be enforced by compulsion but conducted as play, because nothing learned under compulsion stays in the mind. The English here is a paraphrase rather than any standard translation (compare Jowett's 'do not use compulsion, but let early education be a sort of amusement'), so I am recording it as attributed to Plato in substance, not verified as a quotation.

author: Plato
text: Music gives a soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and life to everthing.
notes: A well-documented pseudo-Plato. This sentence does not appear anywhere in the Platonic corpus and has no Greek original; it is routinely listed among misattributed Plato quotations. Plato does discuss music's effect on the soul (Republic III, Timaeus), which is presumably how the line got attached to him, but the wording is modern and its actual author is unknown to me, so I am not offering a reattribution. Note this is a near-duplicate of q_1149, and this copy additionally contains a typo ('everthing').

author: Plato
text: Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.
earliest_print_source: Ian Maclaren (Rev. John Watson), c. 1897–1898 — 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.'
notes: Not Plato. This is one of the best-known false Plato attributions; it appears in the misattributed section of Plato's Wikiquote page and has been traced by Quote Investigator to Ian Maclaren, the pen name of the Scottish author and clergyman John Watson, in the late 1890s, in the form 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.' The modernized 'Be kind... everyone you meet' wording is a later drift. The quote has also been falsely credited to Philo of Alexandria and to J.M. Barrie. Recording the reattribution to Maclaren with high confidence. | Suggested reattribution: Ian Maclaren (pen name of Rev. John Watson)

author: Plato
text: One cannot make a slave of a free person, for a free person is free even in a prison.
notes: I cannot locate this sentence in any Platonic dialogue I know, and its phrasing is much closer to Stoicism — the claim that the free person remains free in chains is characteristically Epictetus (Discourses, Enchiridion), not Plato. Plato does argue that the tyrant is the true slave (Republic IX), but that is a different claim. I am not confident enough in a Stoic origin to assert a reattribution; I am confident enough to say the Plato attribution is unsupported.

author: Plato
text: Music gives a soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination and life to everything.
notes: Same pseudo-Plato as q_1144, in its cleaner and more commonly circulated form. No such passage exists in Plato's works and there is no Greek original; it is a standard entry in lists of misattributed Plato quotations. Origin of the English sentence is unknown to me, so no reattribution is offered. Flagging as a duplicate of q_1144 for deduplication.

author: Pythagoras
text: Rest satisfied with doing well, and leave others to talk of you as they please.
notes: Pythagoras left no writings, so every quotation credited to him is by definition secondhand, arriving through much later compilers (the Golden Verses, Stobaeus, Diogenes Laertius, Iamblichus) or through early-modern anthologies. This particular English sentence has the cadence of an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century maxim collection rather than a translation from a classical source, and I cannot place it in any ancient text. Attribution exists by convention only.

author: Buckminster Fuller
text: How often I found where I should be going only by setting out for somewhere else.
notes: Consistently attributed to R. Buckminster Fuller across quotation collections and Fuller-related writing, and the phrasing matches his idiom (serendipity as method, 'precession'). I cannot place it in a specific book from memory — some collections point to his poetic works of the late 1960s/early 1970s, but I will not assert a title I cannot confirm. Attribution is stable and plausible; the primary source is unlocated.

author: Reginald Horace Blyth
text: Zen is the unsymbolization of the world.
notes: The formulation is characteristic of R. H. Blyth, whose 'Zen in English Literature and Oriental Classics' (1942) and multi-volume 'Zen and Zen Classics' argue exactly this — that Zen strips the world of symbolic overlay. I recall the line circulating as Blyth's and believe the attribution is genuine, but I cannot pin the volume or page from memory and will not guess between the two works.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: I slept and dreamt that life was joy. I awoke and saw that life was service. I acted and behold, service was joy.
notes: This is a known misattribution. The joy/service triplet is a 20th-century reworking of Ellen Sturgis Hooper's short poem published in The Dial (1840): 'I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty; / I woke, and found that life was Duty.' The 'service was joy' variant has been floated under Tagore, Gandhi, and Kahlil Gibran in different collections — a spread that is itself diagnostic — and I know of no passage in Tagore's works containing it. Quote Investigator has treated this family of variants and traced it back to Hooper. | Suggested reattribution: Derived from Ellen Sturgis Hooper's 1840 poem ('I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty'); the joy/service wording has no known author

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: I have become my own version of an optimist. If I can't make it through one door, I'll go through another door - or I'll make a door. Something terrific will come no matter how dark the present.
notes: Almost certainly not Tagore. The diction is modern colloquial American English ('my own version of an optimist', 'something terrific'), incompatible with Tagore's register in either Bengali or his own English renderings. I recognize this as a Joan Rivers line, widely quoted from her later interviews and her writing on resilience; the Tagore label appears to be a quote-site scrambling. I am confident it is not Tagore and reasonably confident it is Rivers, though I cannot name the specific book or interview. | Suggested reattribution: Joan Rivers

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: Love is the only reality and it is not a mere sentiment. It is the ultimate truth that lies at the heart of creation.
notes: Consistent with Tagore's metaphysics as expressed in 'Sadhana: The Realisation of Life' (1913) and 'The Religion of Man' (1931), and the attribution to him is stable across collections. I cannot locate the sentence in a specific text from memory, so I will not name a source. Plausible and uncontested but unverified.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: The highest education is that which does not merely give us information but makes our life in harmony with all existence.
notes: A genuine and much-cited Tagore line on education, used institutionally in connection with Santiniketan and Visva-Bharati. It comes from his essays on education (collections such as 'Personality' (1917) and the 'A Poet's School' material are the usual pointers), but I cannot fix the exact essay from memory and will not guess. Strong, consistent attribution; specific citation unlocated.

author: Rainer Maria Rilke
text: This is the miracle that happens every time to those who really love; the more they give, the more they possess of that precious nourishing love from which flowers and children have their strength and which could help all human beings if they would take it without doubting.
notes: Reads as authentic Rilke prose from his correspondence — the paradox of love increasing by being given, tied to flowers and children, is his register and imagery. It circulates widely through John J. L. Mood's anthology 'Rilke on Love and Other Difficulties' (1975), which gathers passages from the letters. I cannot identify which letter it comes from, so I will not cite one. Genuine-seeming but unsourced.

author: Rainer Maria Rilke
text: You must give birth to your images. They are the future waiting to be born. Fear not the strangeness you feel. The future must enter you long before it happens. Just wait for the birth, for the hour of new clarity.
keywords: birth; future; images; fear; time; wait; clarity; patience
notes: A popular verse-shaped collage rather than a translation. One sentence has a real source: 'The future enters into us, in order to transform itself in us, long before it happens' is from Letters to a Young Poet (the letter of 12 August 1904 in the standard sequence). The surrounding lines — 'You must give birth to your images', 'the hour of new clarity' — do not correspond to any standard translation I can recall, and the arrangement into short lines is a modern editorial creation. Rilkean in origin but not a quotable Rilke text as it stands.

author: Rainer Maria Rilke
text: Whoever makes himself freer and more human in his own existence is doing his part towards peace.
keywords: freedom; human; existence; peace; world; service
notes: Plausibly from Rilke's wartime or post-war correspondence, where he links inner freedom to peace, and the sentence structure suggests translated German. I cannot place it in any letter or published work, and it does not appear in the well-trodden Letters to a Young Poet material. Attribution is uncontested but I have no evidence for it.

author: Ralph Gerard
text: Reason can answer questions, but imagination has to ask them.
notes: Attributed consistently to Ralph W. Gerard, the American neurophysiologist, and the thought matches his published interest in the biology of imagination and creative thinking (he wrote on 'the biological basis of imagination' in the mid-1940s). The attribution is stable and the author obscure enough that misattribution pressure is low — nobody invents a quote to hang on Ralph Gerard. Specific source unlocated.

author: Ralph Marston
text: There is a thought in your mind right now. The longer you hold on to it, the more you dwell upon it, the more life you give to that thought. Give it enough life, and it will become real. So make sure the thought is indeed a great one.
notes: Ralph Marston writes The Daily Motivator, a long-running series of short daily messages, and this is characteristic of that output in both voice and structure. Attribution to Marston is consistent wherever it appears. Individual Daily Motivator entries are dated but I cannot supply the date from memory, so no citation is given.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To laugh often and much; to win the respect of intelligent people and the affection of children; to earn the appreciation of honest critics and endure the betrayal of false friends; to appreciate beauty; to find the best in others; to leave the world a bit better, whether by a healthy child, a garden patch, or a redeemed social condition; to know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.
notes: The 'What is Success?' passage — one of the most thoroughly documented Emerson misattributions. It originates with Bessie Anderson Stanley, whose prize-winning 1904 contest entry read 'He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'. The version here is a mid-20th-century expansion (the 'healthy child, a garden patch, a redeemed social condition' clauses are later accretions) that acquired Emerson's name in anthologies and greeting cards. It appears in no edition of Emerson's works. Emerson scholars and Quote Investigator both reject the attribution. | Suggested reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), in an evolved and expanded form by later hands

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.
notes: Not found in Emerson's published works, journals, or letters as far as I know; the Emerson attribution is a 20th-century label with no textual support. The thought and structure track e. e. cummings closely: 'To be nobody-but-yourself in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight' (A Poet's Advice to Students, 1955). The circulating 'Emerson' sentence looks like a compressed rewording of cummings. Emerson is a misattribution magnet for self-reliance aphorisms precisely because 'Self-Reliance' makes the sentiment sound like his. | Suggested reattribution: Probably a compressed rewording of e. e. cummings, 'A Poet's Advice to Students' (1955)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A good intention clothes itself with power.
notes: I believe this is genuine Emerson, but the canonical wording carries an extra word: 'A good intention clothes itself with sudden power.' The dropped 'sudden' suggests transmission through a quote collection rather than the text. My recollection places it in the Essays: First Series (1841) period, most likely 'Spiritual Laws', but I am not certain enough of the essay to cite it, and naming the wrong essay would be worse than naming none.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: We are all inventors, each sailing out on a voyage of discovery, guided each by a private chart, of which there is no duplicate. The world is all gates, all opportunities.
notes: Genuine Emerson prose in my judgment — the passage continues '...all opportunities, strings of tension waiting to be struck', a cadence and image that belong to him and that no anthologist would invent. My recollection associates it with the later essays, 'Works and Days' in Society and Solitude (1870) being the most likely home, but I cannot confirm the essay and so leave the citation blank. Note the quote as given truncates the passage mid-thought.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Adopt the pace of Nature. Her secret is patience.
notes: Universally attributed to Emerson and entirely consistent with his thought, but I cannot place it in any essay, and its compact epigram form is the shape misattributions usually take. It may come from his journals, which are less well indexed in quote culture and therefore both a plausible home and a convenient one. Holding below the promotion bar until a text can be pointed to.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Most of the shadows of this life are caused by standing in one's own sunshine.
notes: Circulates almost exclusively as Emerson, and occasionally as an anonymous proverb. I cannot locate it in his essays or journals, and the neat paradox reads more like a 19th- or 20th-century aphorism collection than like Emerson's sentence rhythm, which rarely lands this tidily. No evidence against him either — the honest verdict is that I do not know.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: When it is dark enough, you can see the stars.
notes: Doubtful as Emerson. I know of no passage in his published works containing it. In 20th-century usage the line is most strongly associated with the historian Charles A. Beard, who offered it as one of his 'lessons of history', and it was later used by Martin Luther King Jr.; both are transmitters rather than demonstrable origins. Related dark/stars proverbs predate all of them, so the true source may be proverbial. Treating this as unverified rather than reattributed because I cannot identify who said it first.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Society is a masked ball, where everyone hides his own character, and reveals it by hiding.
earliest_print_source: The Conduct of Life, Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1860
notes: Genuine Emerson, from The Conduct of Life (1860); my recollection places it in the essay 'Worship'. One wording note: the canonical text reads 'where every one hides his real character, and reveals it by hiding' — the quote here has 'his own character', a small corruption worth correcting against the printed text before promotion.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To laugh often and much; to win the respect of intelligent people and affection of children; to earn the appreciation of honest critics and endure the betrayal of false friends; to appreciate beauty, to find the best in others; to leave the world a bit better, whether by a healthy child, a garden patch or a redeemed social condition; to know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.
keywords: success; people; children; respect; appreciation; criticism; beauty; world; improvement; health; garden; life
notes: This is the well-documented 'Success' poem misattribution. Emerson never wrote it; it appears in the Misattributed section of his Wikiquote page and has been traced by Quote Investigator to a 1904 prize-winning contest entry by Bessie Anderson Stanley ('He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'). The 'To laugh often and much / to win the respect of intelligent people' wording is a much later 20th-century rewrite of Stanley's text, circulated anonymously before being pinned on Emerson. I am confident it is not Emerson; I am less confident about who produced this specific rewrite. | Suggested reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), heavily reworded by an unknown later hand

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Don't waste your life in doubts and fears: spend yourself on the work before you, well assured that the right performance of this hour's duties will be the best preparation for the hours or ages that follow it.
keywords: life; waste; doubt; fear; work; right; time
notes: Consistently attributed to Emerson across anthologies and stylistically authentic to him (the cadence and the 'this hour's duties' construction are characteristic). I cannot place the specific essay, address, or journal entry from memory, so I am not asserting a print source. Attribution is plausible and stable but unverified at the primary-source level.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Common sense is genius dressed in its working clothes.
notes: Extremely common in quote collections under Emerson's name, but I cannot recall it in any of his essays, addresses, or journals.
