Emerson is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphoristic one-liners of this shape. The epigram feels more like late-19th/early-20th-century American maxim writing than Emerson's own prose. No source found in training knowledge; treat the attribution as unsupported rather than disproven.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Great men are they who see that spiritual is stronger than any material force, that thoughts rule the world.
keywords: great; people; spiritual; force; material; perception; see; thoughts
earliest_print_source: Letters and Social Aims, Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1876 (essay 'Progress of Culture')
notes: I recall this line being cited to Emerson's 'Progress of Culture,' the Phi Beta Kappa address delivered at Harvard in July 1867 and collected in Letters and Social Aims (1876). The sentiment ('thoughts rule the world') is squarely Emerson's and I have reasonable confidence in the placement, but I am reporting a recollection, not a checked citation — the essay attribution should be confirmed against the text before the source line is trusted.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The world is his, who can see through its pretension… See it to be a lie, and you have already dealt it its mortal blow.
notes: I am confident this is genuine Emerson prose — the fuller passage runs '...what deafness, what stone-blind custom, what overgrown error you behold is there only by sufferance — your sufferance. See it to be a lie, and you have already dealt it its mortal blow.' My recollection points to 'Compensation' (Essays: First Series, 1841), but I am not confident enough in the essay placement to record it as a citation. The ellipsis in the corpus text also elides an intervening clause.

author: Ralph Waldo Trine
text: A miracle is nothing more or less than this. Anyone who has come into a knowledge of his true identity, of his oneness with the all-pervading wisdom and power, this makes it possible for laws higher than the ordinary mind knows of to be revealed to him.
keywords: miracle; laws; knowledge; wisdom; power; mind; revelation
notes: Ralph Waldo Trine is a real New Thought author (1866-1958) and the vocabulary here — 'the all-pervading wisdom and power,' oneness, higher laws — is his signature phrasing, strongly suggesting In Tune with the Infinite (1897). I cannot place the passage precisely enough to assert the book and page, so no print source is recorded. Note the author is distinct from Ralph Waldo Emerson; the corpus has them adjacent and they are frequently confused.

author: Ram Das
text: The quieter you become, the more you can hear.
notes: Ubiquitously attributed to Ram Dass (born Richard Alpert) and consistent with his teaching, but I know of no primary source — no book passage, lecture transcript, or dated talk. It circulated widely as poster and software-splash-screen text before most quote sites indexed it, which is a typical pattern for floating attributions. Also note the corpus spells the author 'Ram Das'; the standard spelling is 'Ram Dass'.

author: Ram Das
text: All spiritual disciplines are done with a view to still the mind. The perfectly still mind is universal spirit.
keywords: stillness; quiet; mine; perfect; mind; spirit; spiritual
notes: This does not read as Ram Dass; it reads as Advaita source material. I recall this wording — 'All spiritual practices are done with a view to still the mind. The perfectly still mind is universal spirit' — from Nisargadatta Maharaj's I Am That, the Maurice Frydman translation. My confidence in the reattribution is moderate (roughly 0.6), not high, and it could alternatively trace to Ramana Maharshi's recorded talks, which share this idiom. Either way the Ram Dass attribution looks incorrect. | Suggested reattribution: Nisargadatta Maharaj (probable; I Am That)

author: Ram Das
text: The next message you need is right where you are.
notes: A genuinely Ram Dass-sounding line, usually quoted as 'The next message you need is always right where you are.' It is associated with his talks and with the Be Here Now era, and the attribution is stable across sources, but I cannot point to a book, transcript, or date. Attribution plausible, evidence thin. Author name should be 'Ram Dass'.

author: Ram Das
text: In India when we meet and part we often say, "Namaste," which means I honor the place in you where the entire universe resides, I honor the place in you of love, of light, of truth, of peace. I honor the place within you where if you are in that place in you and I am in that place in me, there is only one of us. Namaste.
keywords: spirit; universe; unity; oneness; truth; peace; love; light; india
notes: This 'I honor the place in you...' gloss on Namaste is most often credited to Ram Dass and does match his idiom and his role in popularizing the greeting for Western audiences. However the same passage circulates attributed to Mahatma Gandhi and to anonymous yoga-studio tradition, which is a warning sign. No primary text or talk identified in my training knowledge. Author name should be 'Ram Dass'.

author: Rama Choomarasawmy
text: No distinction can be drawn between art and contemplation. The artists is first of all required to remove himself from human to celestial levels of appreciation; at this level and in a state of unification, no longer having in view anything external to himself, he sees and realizes, that is to say becomes, what he is afterwards to represent…
keywords: art; artist; contemplation; human; celestial; realm; appreciation; unity; external; perception; realization; self
notes: 'Rama Choomarasawmy' is not a real person — it is a phonetic corruption of Ananda K. Coomaraswamy (1877-1947), the Ceylonese-British metaphysician and art historian. The passage is characteristic Coomaraswamy, from his writing on traditional art and the artist's identification with the form contemplated; my recollection points toward The Transformation of Nature in Art (1934) or Christian and Oriental Philosophy of Art (1943), but I cannot fix the book, so no print source is recorded. Confidence in the author correction is high (~0.85); confidence in the recorded name as given is near zero. Note also 'The artists is' in the corpus text is a typo for 'The artist is'. | Suggested reattribution: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy

author: Ramakrishna
text: The fabled musk deer searches the world over for the source of the scent which comes from itself.
keywords: animal; perception; deer; search; world; self; mystical; hindu
notes: The musk-deer parable — the deer roaming in search of a fragrance emanating from its own navel — is a genuine and very old motif in Indian devotional literature, used by Kabir, by Ramakrishna, and in later Vedanta teaching. Ramakrishna did employ it, so the attribution is not baseless, but this compressed English sentence is an anthologist's paraphrase rather than a line from The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna as far as I can tell. The image is effectively traditional and predates any single speaker.

author: Ramana Maharshi
text: From silence came the ego, from the ego came thought, and from thought came speech. If speech is effective, how much more effective must be its source!
keywords: silence; thought; speech; ego; effective; source; spirit
notes: Consistent with Ramana Maharshi's recorded teaching on silence as the highest and most potent form of instruction, and I associate this passage with Talks with Sri Ramana Maharshi (Munagala Venkataramiah's transcripts) or Maharshi's Gospel. The usual ordering in his teaching runs silence to ego to thought to speech, matching this text. I cannot cite a specific talk number, so no print source is recorded.

author: Raymond Inmon
text: If you are seeking creative ideas, go out walking. Angels whisper to a man when he goes for a walk.
keywords: walk; creative; ideas; angels; whisper; inspiration; listen
notes: 'Raymond Inmon' appears in my knowledge only as a name attached to this one sentence in motivational quote collections — no biography, no book, no other work, no dates. That pattern usually indicates either a private individual quoted once in a newsletter or a name that accreted to an orphan line. The quote itself is real and widely circulated; the attribution is untraceable. Honest answer here is that I do not know who said it.

author: Reggie Leach
text: Success is not the result of spontaneous combustion. You must set yourself on fire.
keywords: success; fire; self; effort; result; spontaneous; artist
notes: Reggie Leach is a real person — NHL winger, 'the Riverton Rifle,' Philadelphia Flyers — and this line is attributed to him with near-total consistency across motivational anthologies, which is mild evidence. But I know of no interview, book, or speech where it originates, and no date. Sports one-liners of this kind are commonly attached to whichever athlete an anthologist had to hand. Plausible but unverified.

author: Rev. Mary Manin Morrissey
text: Spirit has placed a dream in your heart for a better world, starting with your family, extending to your work, community, country and stretching beyond your nation. Speak your truth and inspire others, for you are meant to make a significant and sizable difference.
keywords: spirit; heart; world; improvement; family; work; action; community; nation; country; inspire; change
notes: Mary Manin Morrissey is a real New Thought/Unity minister and author (Building Your Field of Dreams, 1996) and the language here — 'Spirit has placed a dream in your heart' — matches her register exactly, so the attribution is plausible. But it reads like newsletter or spoken-message material rather than a passage from a specific book, and I cannot locate it. No source recorded.

author: Reverend Cecil Williams
text: "You've got to pray like it's all up to God, and work like it's all up to you."
notes: Cecil Williams of Glide Memorial in San Francisco may well have said this from the pulpit, but he did not originate it. The aphorism is centuries older and circulates in two mirrored forms: 'Pray as though everything depended on God, work as though everything depended on you,' commonly credited to Ignatius of Loyola and also to Augustine of Hippo. Scholarship on the Ignatian version (Joseph de Guibert and others) notes the two halves get swapped between retellings, which is itself evidence of a long oral history. Treat this as a traditional Christian saying quoted by Williams, not authored by him. | Suggested reattribution: Traditional Christian aphorism, commonly attributed to Ignatius of Loyola

author: Richard Avedon
text: Start with a style and you are in chains, start with an idea and you are free.
notes: Widely quoted under Richard Avedon's name in design and photography collections, and the sentiment fits a working photographer's outlook. I cannot place it in an Avedon interview, essay, or monograph, and I have some recollection of near-identical 'style is chains, ideas are freedom' formulations circulating under other designers' names, which weakens confidence. Attribution plausible but unsupported.

author: Richard Bach
text: Sooner or later, those who win are those who think they can.
notes: Consistently attributed to Richard Bach and consonant with the Messiah's Handbook aphorisms in Illusions (1977), which is my best guess for the source. I am noticeably less confident than for the caterpillar line — I cannot confirm the book, and the sentiment is generic enough that it could belong to the broader 'those who think they can' tradition running back to Virgil's 'possunt quia posse videntur.' No print source recorded.

author: Richard Carlson
text: Reflection is one of the most underused yet powerful tools for success.
notes: Richard Carlson is a real author (Don't Sweat the Small Stuff, 1997, and its many sequels) and this sentence is consistent with his advice register, but it is generic enough that it could come from almost any business or self-help writer. I cannot place it in a specific title or chapter. Plausible attribution, no evidence.

author: Richard M DeVos
text: If I had to select one quality, one personal characteristic that I regard as being most highly correlated with success, whatever the field, I would pick the trait of persistence. Determination. The will to endure to the end, to get knocked down seventy times and get up off the floor saying, ‘Here comes number seventy-one.’
keywords: success; perseverance; determination; will; end; obstacle
notes: Attributed with good consistency to Richard M. DeVos, Amway co-founder, and the 'Here comes number seventy-one' formulation is distinctive enough that it is unlikely to have drifted from another speaker. It matches the content of his motivational speaking and his book Believe! (1975), which is my best guess for the source, but I cannot confirm the book or a speech date, so no print source is recorded. Note the corpus name should probably be punctuated 'Richard M. DeVos'.

author: Richard Nelson Bolles
text: One of the saddest lines in the world is, 'Oh come now - be realistic.' The best parts of this world were not fashioned by those who were realistic. They were fashioned by those who dared to look hard at their wishes and gave them horses to ride.
notes: Attributed to Richard Nelson Bolles, author of What Color Is Your Parachute?, and it strongly matches his voice and his argument against 'realistic' career advice; my recollection is that it appears in the book, whose editions run annually from 1970, but I cannot pin an edition or page and will not guess a year. The closing image, 'gave them horses to ride,' echoes the old proverb 'if wishes were horses, beggars would ride,' which Bolles was plausibly inverting deliberately. Attribution stable, primary source unconfirmed.

author: Richard Schechner
text: Excellence in art is, ultimately, a function of wholeness as a human being.
notes: Richard Schechner is a real and well-documented performance studies theorist (Environmental Theater, Performance Theory, Between Theater and Anthropology), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings. The register is more aphoristic than Schechner's usual analytic prose, which makes me mildly suspicious that it entered quote collections secondhand. No source located; not fabricating one.

author: Robert A. Johnson
text: When I say that ‘I love,’ it is not I who love, but in reality Love who acts through me. Love is not so much something I do as something that I am. Love is not a doing but a state of being - a relatedness, a connectedness to another mortal, an identification with her or him that simply flows within me and through me, independent of my intentions or my efforts.
keywords: self; love; action; being; connection; oneness; effort; intention; flow
notes: Consistent in voice and content with Robert A. Johnson's Jungian writing on love, most plausibly 'We: Understanding the Psychology of Romantic Love' (1983), which argues precisely this distinction between love as a doing and love as a state of being. I have a genuine but not firm recollection of the passage from that book, and cannot confirm chapter or page, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting a citation I cannot stand behind. Attribution to Johnson itself is plausible and consistently reported.

author: Robert Allen
text: There is no such thing as security. There are only varying degrees of risk.
notes: Consistently attributed to Robert G. Allen, the real-estate and 'Multiple Streams of Income' author, across business quote collections. The sentiment matches his investing rhetoric. However, every occurrence I know of is a quote-collection citation with no book or page, so this is secondary evidence only. Note the ambiguity of the bare name 'Robert Allen' — the corpus should probably disambiguate to Robert G. Allen.

author: Robert Allen
text: Every rejection is valuable to those who persist.
keywords: persistence; determination; valuable; rejection; obstacle; work
notes: I cannot place this line in Robert G. Allen's published work. It circulates in motivational-quote lists with the bare name 'Robert Allen' attached. Generic enough in phrasing that it could belong to any number of sales/persistence writers. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know.

author: Robert Allen
text: Herb True once said, “What people don’t realize is that successful people often have more failures than failures do. But they keep going.” You don’t drown by falling in the water. You drown by staying there.
keywords: success; failure; perseverance; people; water; drown; action; work
notes: This is a composite passage, not a single quote, and that matters. The inner quotation is credited in the text itself to Herb True (the Notre Dame marketing professor), and the 'more failures than failures do' line is indeed the one commonly attributed to him. The closing 'You don't drown by falling in the water. You drown by staying there' is widely attributed elsewhere to Edwin Louis Cole. The framing prose is plausibly Robert G. Allen quoting both, likely in one of his books, but I cannot confirm which. Recommend the corpus either drop this entry or split it, since attributing the whole block to Allen misrepresents two embedded attributions.

author: Robert Browning
text: Our aspirations are our possibilities.
notes: Widely attributed to Robert Browning in nineteenth- and twentieth-century quote anthologies, but I cannot locate it in any specific poem or letter of his, and Browning's actual verse rarely reduces to a clean epigram like this. The same line also circulates attributed to Samuel Johnson in some collections, which is a classic signature of an unsourced anthology quote drifting between famous names. Attribution unresolved.

author: Robert F. Kennedy
text: Progress is a nice word, but change is its motivator and change has enemies.
notes: I recall this line, usually punctuated as three sentences ('Progress is a nice word. But change is its motivator. And change has its enemies.'), from Robert F. Kennedy's Day of Affirmation Address at the University of Cape Town, 6 June 1966 — the same speech as the 'ripple of hope' passage. The attribution to RFK is consistent and I consider it sound. I am withholding the speech as a formal print source because I cannot confirm the exact verbatim placement from memory, which is the difference between 'attributed' and 'verified' here.

author: Robert Fulghum
text: “For all my good intentions, there are days when things go wrong or I fall into old habits. When things are not going well, when I'm grumpy or mad, I'll realize that I've not been paying attention to my soul and I've not been following my best routine.”
keywords: intention; habit; wrong; anger; soul; attention
notes: The plainspoken, self-deprecating voice is very much Robert Fulghum's, and the content fits his essay collections (All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten, From Beginning to End, Words I Wish I Wrote). But I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and it reads like it may come from an interview rather than a book. Plausible but unsourced.

author: Robert H. Schuller
text: Impossible situations can become possible miracles.
notes: Squarely in the idiom of Robert H. Schuller's 'possibility thinking' and consistently attributed to him in inspirational collections; the sentence is essentially a compressed statement of his central theme (cf. 'Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do!'). No specific book, sermon, or Hour of Power broadcast identified, so this rests on secondary evidence only.

author: Robert L. Peters
text: Design creates culture. Culture shapes values. Values determine the future.
notes: Robert L. Peters is a real Canadian graphic designer and past president of Icograda, and this three-clause line is his best-known statement — it is quoted consistently under his name throughout design literature and conference material, and he has spoken about it publicly as his own. I have no single originating publication or talk to cite, so it stays at 'attributed' rather than 'verified,' but the attribution itself is unusually stable for a design aphorism.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson
text: Saints are sinners who kept going.
notes: Very widely attributed to Robert Louis Stevenson (usually as 'Saints are sinners who kept on going'), but I cannot locate it in any of his essays, novels, letters, or prayers. Its circulation pattern — heavy in devotional and recovery literature, absent from Stevenson scholarship — is characteristic of an unsourced attribution attached to a famous literary name. I do not know a true origin, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but the Stevenson claim should be treated as doubtful.

author: Robert Service
text: Be master of your petty annoyances and conserve your energies for the big, worthwhile things. It isn't the mountain ahead that wears you out - it's the grain of sand in your shoe.
notes: The 'grain of sand in your shoe' image is attributed to the Yukon poet Robert W. Service in many quote collections, but I cannot find it in his verse or his memoirs, and the surrounding sentence ('Be master of your petty annoyances...') reads like self-help prose rather than Service. A near-identical formulation is widely credited to Muhammad Ali ('It isn't the mountains ahead to climb that wear you out; it's the pebble in your shoe'), which suggests a floating aphorism rather than a fixed authorship. Origin genuinely unclear; not proposing Ali either, since his version is also unsourced.

author: Roberta Sage Hamilton
text: In our deepest moments of struggle, frustration, fear, and confusion, we are being called upon to reach in and touch our hearts. Then, we will know what to do, what to say, how to be. What is right is always in our deepest heart of hearts. It is from the deepest part of our hearts that we are capable of reaching out and touching another human being. It is, after all, one heart touching another heart.
keywords: frustration; fear; confusion; struggle; touch; heart; action; being; right; deep; human
notes: I have no knowledge of Roberta Sage Hamilton as a writer and can find no work of hers in my training. The passage appears to live entirely inside inspirational quote collections and greeting-card style compilations. The name may be real but obscure, or may itself be a corruption. No verification possible; this is an honest 'I do not know.'

author: Roger Williams
text: The greatest crime in the world is not developing your potential. When you do what you do best, you are helping not only yourself, but the world.
notes: 'Roger Williams' is ambiguous and none of the candidates resolve it. The seventeenth-century founder of Rhode Island would not have written in this idiom of self-actualization; the biochemist Roger J. Williams and the pianist Roger Williams are both possible but I have no evidence for either. The vocabulary ('developing your potential') places the line in twentieth-century human-potential writing. Untraceable as given.

author: Ron Rathbun
text: Be at peace with yourself. If you are not at peace with yourself, you are at peace with nothing.
notes: Ron Rathbun is a real author — 'The Way Is Within: A Spiritual Journey' (1995) and related meditation writing — and this line is attributed to him with reasonable consistency in quote collections. I cannot confirm it against the book itself, and the sentiment is generic enough to have multiple independent origins. Plausible but unverified.

author: Ron Rathbun
text: What you find in your mind is what you put there. Put good things in there.
notes: Same author and same situation as the preceding entry: consistently attributed to Ron Rathbun in quote compilations, consistent with the plain instructional voice of 'The Way Is Within,' but with no source I can confirm. Weak evidence.

author: Rosemary Fillmore Rhea
text: The world we are experiencing today is the result of our collective consciousness, and if we want a new world, each of us must start taking responsibility for helping create it.
notes: Rosemary Fillmore Rhea is a real figure — granddaughter of Unity's founders Charles and Myrtle Fillmore, and a Unity broadcaster and author — and the New Thought vocabulary of 'collective consciousness' fits Unity writing closely. But I cannot place this sentence in any of her books or broadcasts. Attribution plausible on stylistic grounds only.

author: Rousseau
text: The golden age, which blind superstition situated behind or ahead of us is in us.
keywords: time; within; golden; superstition; self; creativity; perception; inner
notes: Attributed to Rousseau in quote collections, but I cannot locate it in the Discourses, Émile, the Social Contract, or the Reveries. Two warning signs: the English is awkward in the way that anthology-chain translations tend to be (the missing comma before 'is in us' is present in most circulating copies, indicating they all descend from one source), and the bare author name 'Rousseau' with no first name is typical of unsourced compilation entries. The sentiment is broadly Rousseauian, which is exactly what makes a misattribution easy. I do not know the true origin.

author: Rumi
text: What bread looks like depends on whether you’re hungry or not.
notes: Rumi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in circulation, and the English Rumi corpus is dominated by Coleman Barks's loose renderings, which are not translations and often have no close counterpart in the Persian. I cannot match this line to any passage of the Masnavi or the Divan-e Shams that I know. The bread-and-hunger image is genuinely Rumi-adjacent in theme, which is not evidence. Treat as unverified pending a check against a scholarly translation (Nicholson or Arberry) with a book-and-line reference.

author: Rumi
text: Let the beauty you love be what you do.
earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: From the Barks rendering beginning 'Today, like every other day, we wake up empty and frightened... Take down a musical instrument. Let the beauty we love be what we do. There are hundreds of ways to kneel and kiss the ground.' The corpus text alters 'we love' to 'you love', a common web variant. Barks worked from earlier English translations rather than the Persian, so the English wording is his; the underlying poem is genuinely Rumi's. Cannot place the Persian original (Divan-e Shams ghazal) from memory.

author: Rumi
text: I have lived on the lip of insanity, wanting to know reasons, knocking on a door. It opens. I've been knocking from the inside!
keywords: life; confusion; insanity; crazy; door; knock; inside; reason; thinking; search; sufi
earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: A Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain; I recall it in The Essential Rumi with consistent attribution across reputable Rumi collections. Wording is Barks' English, not a literal translation. No Persian source located from memory.

author: Rumi
text: To grasp God’s beauty, you must become God.
notes: I cannot place this line in any Rumi translation I know — not Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, or Helminski. The theological compression ('you must become God') is unlike the standard renderings, which speak of annihilation in the Beloved rather than becoming God. Possibly a loose paraphrase of a fana passage, possibly a modern invention. Honest answer: unknown.

author: Rumi
text: A grain of sand left its father. Its father was a boulder. Only then was it introduced to an oyster, and became a pearl.
notes: Cannot place this in any Rumi translation. The grain-of-sand-becomes-pearl motif is a stock modern inspirational image; the flat declarative diction here matches none of the standard English Rumi translators. Circulates on quote sites without any cited source. Likely a modern composition attached to Rumi's name, but I have no evidence of a true author.

author: Rumi
text: Don’t be like the rider who gallops all night and never sees the horse that is beneath him.
keywords: sufi; perception; horse; animal; mystical; self
notes: Rumi does use the rider-who-cannot-see-his-own-mount figure (the Mathnawi has teaching stories about a man searching for the animal he is riding), so the image is authentically Rumi's. But I cannot place this exact English sentence in any translation, and it reads like a paraphrase rather than a rendering. Image plausible, wording unverified.

author: Rumi
text: The minute I heard my first love story, I started looking for you, not knowing how blind that was. Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.
earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: A well-known Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain, appearing in The Essential Rumi. Attribution to Rumi is consistent across reputable collections; the English phrasing ('Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.') is Barks'. Persian original not identified from memory.

author: Rumi
text: The soul is here for its own joy.
notes: I recall this short line from Coleman Barks' Rumi versions and believe it appears in The Essential Rumi, but I am not confident enough in the specific volume to cite it as a print source. Attribution to Rumi (via Barks) is consistent in the sources I know; the underlying Persian is not identified.

author: Rumi
text: Your task is not to seek for love, but merely to seek and find all the barriers within yourself that you have built against it.
notes: One of the most heavily circulated 'Rumi' lines on the internet and one of the most doubted. I cannot place it in Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, Helminski, or any other translation, and its vocabulary ('your task', 'barriers within yourself') is modern therapeutic English rather than Sufi poetics — it reads closer to twentieth-century self-help or A Course in Miracles-adjacent writing than to a thirteenth-century ghazal. I suspect it is not Rumi, but I cannot name a true author, so I am not asserting a reattribution.

author: Rumi
text: Your body is woven from the light of heaven.
notes: I have a weak recollection of this line in a Barks-style Rumi rendering (sometimes quoted with a following sentence about the body's purity), but I cannot confirm the volume or the Persian original. The imagery is consistent with Rumi's treatment of the body as woven of light. Attribution plausible, evidence thin.

author: Rumi
text: The wound is the place where the Light enters you.
notes: Among the most quoted Rumi lines in English, and consistently attributed to him via Coleman Barks' versions. However, Rumi scholars (Omid Safi among them) have noted that Barks' most famous lines often have no close Persian counterpart, and I cannot point to the ghazal or Mathnawi passage behind this one. Attribution is consistent but the sourcing chain stops at a modern English rendering, so I am not putting it above the promotion bar.

author: Rumi
text: Every soul becomes gold when touched by the Beloved.
notes: Cannot place this line. Alchemical gold imagery is genuinely Rumi's territory (the Beloved as the philosopher's stone that transmutes copper to gold), but this specific one-sentence formulation appears only on quote aggregators with no source. Unknown.

author: Rumi
text: Dance, when you’re broken open. Dance, if you’ve torn the bandage off. Dance in the middle of the fighting. Dance in your blood. Dance when you’re perfectly free.
earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: A recognized Coleman Barks rendering ('Dance, when you're broken open...'), appearing in The Essential Rumi and widely reprinted with consistent attribution to Rumi. English wording is Barks'; Persian original not identified from memory.

author: Sabrina Ward Harrison
text: The pain is equal to the attachment.
notes: Sabrina Ward Harrison is a real author-artist (Spilling Open: The Art of Becoming Yourself, 1999; Brave on the Rocks, 2000), and this aphorism's register fits her handwritten-journal books. But I cannot place the line in a specific title, and the thought is a commonplace of Buddhist-inflected popular writing, so it could easily have drifted onto her name. Unconfirmed.

author: Saint Augustine
text: The key to immortality is first living a life worth remembering.
notes: This does not read as Augustine in any register — not the Confessions, not the City of God, not the sermons — and 'a life worth remembering' as a route to 'immortality' inverts Augustine's actual theology, where immortality is God's gift and earthly fame is explicitly disparaged. The line circulates far more commonly attributed to Bruce Lee, in the sayings collected from his notebooks and popularized posthumously; that attribution is itself unverified, so I am flagging the Augustine attribution as wrong without asserting Lee as confirmed. | Suggested reattribution: Widely circulated as Bruce Lee (that attribution is itself unverified); not Augustine

author: Salvador Dali
text: Have no fear of perfection—you’ll never reach it.
notes: Consistently attributed to Salvador Dali across quotation dictionaries and Dali literature, and the sentiment matches his public persona of grandiose self-deprecation. I cannot name the interview, book, or date of first appearance, so the sourcing chain is secondary only. Attribution steady, primary source not established.

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Every submission to our fear enlarges its domain.
notes: Johnson wrote at length on fear in The Rambler (No. 126 contains the well-known 'Fear is implanted in us as a preservative from evil; but its duty, like that of other passions, is not to overbear reason, but to assist it'), and this sentence is stylistically compatible with that essay. But the crisp epigrammatic form suggests a later condensation of Johnson's prose rather than his own sentence, and I cannot confirm the exact wording in any Rambler or Idler number. Plausible but unconfirmed; deliberately not citing a number I cannot verify.

author: Samuel Rogers
text: It doesn't much signify whom one marries, for one is sure to find out the next morning that it was someone else.
earliest_print_source: Recollections of the Table-Talk of Samuel Rogers, Alexander Dyce, 1856
notes: A stock Regency epigram consistently credited to the poet and celebrated conversationalist Samuel Rogers (1763-1855), whose remarks survive chiefly through Dyce's posthumous Table-Talk. Quotation dictionaries routinely source Rogers quips to that volume and I believe this is one of them, but I cannot confirm the page or that this specific quip appears there rather than in another memoir of Rogers, so treat the citation as probable rather than checked.

author: Samurai maxim
text: The angry man will defeat himself in battle as well as in life.
notes: Attributed only to an anonymous collective ('Samurai maxim'), which is not an attribution at all. I cannot trace it to Hagakure, the Book of Five Rings, Budoshoshinshu, or any classical bushido text, and the English is modern. Most 'samurai maxims' in circulation are twentieth-century Western compositions. Origin unknown.

author: Sanaya Roman & Duane Pack
text: View money and things not as something you create to fill a lack, but as tools to help you more fully express yourself and realize your potential.
notes: Sanaya Roman and Duane Packer are real co-authors whose Creating Money: Keys to Abundance (1988) covers exactly this material, so the pairing of quote to authors is plausible. I cannot confirm this sentence appears in that book or in another of their titles. Also note the author field misspells the second name as 'Duane Pack' (should be Duane Packer) and so does not match q_1248's spelling.

author: Sanaya Roman & Duane Packer
text: Don’t discard your fantasies as merely wishful thinking. Honor them as messages from the deepest part of your being about what you can do and directions you can choose.
keywords: fantasy; thinking; honor; message; deep; being; self; direction; choice; dream
notes: Consistent in content and voice with the Roman/Packer Earth Life Series (Creating Money, Living with Joy, Spiritual Growth), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific volume or year. Real authors, plausible attribution, no confirmable source.

author: Sandra Anne Taylor
text: "All of your self-honoring choices will tend to promote your sense of dignity, personal and authentic power, and sense of balance. Sometimes the most self-honoring choices don't come easy and don't feel good at all; They may feel risky, difficult and uncertain. Other times the most self-honoring choices will feel completely natural to you -- they'll feel exhilarating, giving you a sense of liberation and joyous self-actualization."
keywords: authentic; honor; power; balance; self; choice; dignity; good; risk; difficult; liberation; actualization
notes: Sandra Anne Taylor is a real author (Quantum Success, Secrets of Attraction, Truth, Triumph and Transformation) and the vocabulary of 'self-honoring choices' and 'authentic power' fits that genre and era. I cannot locate this passage in any specific title of hers. Unconfirmed. The corpus text also retains stray enclosing quotation marks and an anomalous capital after a semicolon.

author: Sara Paddison
text: Sincere forgiveness isn't colored with expectations that the other person apologize or change. Don't worry whether or not they finally understand you. Love them and release them. Life feeds back truth to people in its own way and time...
notes: Widely circulated with consistent attribution to Sara Paddison, and usually to her book The Hidden Power of the Heart (Planetary Publications / HeartMath, 1992), which is a real title on exactly this subject. I have not confirmed the page or verified the excerpt against the text, so I am recording the attribution as consistent secondary evidence rather than citing the book as a checked source. The trailing ellipsis indicates the passage is truncated.

author: Sara Paddison
text: When you have compassion and surrender to your own heart, you are surrendering to the hidden power in your heart, God. You are surrendering to love, because God is Love, the cohesive force of the universe that connects us all. Surrender is not just a religious concept; it's a power tool for listening to the voice of your spirit and following its directions. When you surrender your head to your heart, you allow your heart to give you a wider, higher intelligence perspective. Remember the phrase, ‘The real teacher is within you.’ Very simply, that teacher is to be found in the common sense of your own heart.
keywords: compassion; heart; surrender; hidden; god; love; force; universe; connection; people; religious; concept; power; tool; voice; direction; intelligence; perspective; teacher; within; self
notes: Same author and same idiom as q_1250 — the heart-intelligence language ('surrender your head to your heart', 'the real teacher is within you') is characteristic HeartMath-school writing and consistent with Sara Paddison's The Hidden Power of the Heart (1992). But this longer passage is less commonly quoted than q_1250 and I cannot place it in a specific chapter or confirm it is not stitched together from separate paragraphs. Plausible, unconfirmed.

author: Sarah Ban Breathnach
text: We can no longer afford to throw away even one ‘unimportant’ day by not noticing the wonder of it all. We have to be willing to discover and then appreciate the authentic moments of happiness available to all of us every day.
notes: Consistently attributed to Sarah Ban Breathnach and entirely consistent with her vocabulary in the Simple Abundance books ('authentic', noticing ordinary days). I believe it comes from Simple Abundance: A Daybook of Comfort and Joy (1995) or a companion volume, but I cannot place the specific entry or page from memory, so I am not asserting that citation. Attribution to Breathnach is plausible and uncontested; the sourcing is not established.

author: Sarah Bernhardt
text: Life begets life. Energy creates energy. It is by spending oneself that one becomes rich.
notes: Very widely and consistently attributed to Sarah Bernhardt in twentieth-century quotation anthologies, but in my recollection it circulates without a source citation — it is the kind of line that appears in quote dictionaries with only a name attached. Bernhardt did publish a memoir (Ma Double Vie / Memories of My Life, 1907), and the line would not be out of character, but I cannot confirm it appears there. Honest verdict: plausible, unsourced.

author: Sathya Sai Baba
text: Man loves because he is love. He seeks joy, for he is joy. He thirsts for God for he is composed of God and he cannot exist without God.
keywords: love; being; self; joy; god; existence
notes: Circulates widely in Sathya Sai Baba devotional literature and is stylistically characteristic of his discourses. His discourses were transcribed at length in the Sathya Sai Speaks series, so a genuine origin is plausible, but I cannot identify the specific discourse, date, or volume, and Sai Baba material is heavily paraphrased and re-edited in secondary circulation. No citation asserted.

author: Saul Bass
text: Design is thinking made visible.
notes: Ubiquitous on design quote lists under Saul Bass, but I know of no documented primary source — no interview, lecture, or published essay of his that I can point to containing this sentence. Design aphorisms attach themselves to famous designers (Bass, Rand, Eames) the way general aphorisms attach to Einstein, so the popularity of the pairing is not evidence. Cannot confirm or reattribute.

author: Saul Gorn
text: It is well known that the longer one postpones a pleasure, the greater the pleasure is when one finally gets it. Therefore, if one postpones it forever, the pleasure should be infinite.
keywords: pleasure; infinite; gratification; delay; time; humor
notes: Saul Gorn was a real computer scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, known in hacker folklore for 'Saul Gorn's Compendium of Rarely Used Clichés.' This line reaches modern circulation almost entirely through the Unix fortune-cookie database, which is a weak provenance chain — fortune files carry many attributions that were never checked. I cannot place the line in anything Gorn actually published. Plausible but essentially unsourced.

author: Saul Gorn
text: I am a firm believer in optimism because without optimism, what else is there?
notes: Same fortune-file provenance problem as q_1256, and weaker: this is a generic optimism line with nothing distinctive tying it to Saul Gorn. I have no independent knowledge of Gorn saying or writing it, and I have a vague sense the sentence also circulates under other names, though I cannot confirm which and will not guess. Attribution should be treated as unsupported.

author: Seng T'san, Third Zen Patriarch
text: Step aside from all thinking, and there is nowhere you can’t go.
notes: Almost certainly a translation of the Hsin Hsin Ming line more commonly rendered 'Stop talking and thinking, and there is nothing you will not be able to know' (Suzuki/Conze) — the sense and position in the poem match. But I cannot identify which translation produces this exact English, and 'step aside from all thinking' is loose enough that it may be a popular paraphrase rather than a published rendering. Source text is confident; this specific wording is not, so I am holding below the verified bar.

author: Sequichie Comingdeer
text: The death of fear is in doing what you fear to do.
notes: Sequichie Comingdeer was a real Cherokee teacher and author, and this line circulates consistently under his name in inspirational collections. I cannot place it in any book, lecture, or documented interview, and quotations attributed to Native American teachers are unusually prone to unsourced circulation and invented attribution. Attribution is uncontested but unsupported by anything I can point to.

author: Shakti Gawain
text: Ultimately, what we are looking to is the deepest connection within ourselves. As we get more connected to that, we begin to feel in harmony with other people and with the rest of the world.
notes: Consistent with Shakti Gawain's published voice and themes, and attributed to her without competition. Most likely from Living in the Light (1986) or an interview, but I cannot place it, and this is generic enough New Age phrasing that I would not bet on the specific book. No citation asserted.

author: Shakti Gawain
text: Most of us are in touch with our intuition whether we know it or not, but we're usually in the habit of doubting or contradicting it so automatically that we don't even know it has spoken.
notes: Distinctively Gawain in content — the doubting-and-contradicting-intuition observation is a central argument of Living in the Light (1986), and I believe the line comes from that book, but I cannot confirm the chapter or exact page from memory and so am not asserting the citation. Attribution to Gawain is strong on internal evidence; the print source is unestablished.

author: Shakti Gawain
text: Evil (ignorance) is like a shadow - it has no real substance of its own, it is simply a lack of light. You cannot cause a shadow to disappear by trying to fight it, stomp[ing] on it, by railing against it, or any other form of emotional or physical resistance. In order to cause a shadow to disappear, you must shine light on it.
notes: Attributed consistently to Shakti Gawain and consistent with her work on light, shadow, and non-resistance. The shadow-and-light image itself is ancient and appears in many traditions, so the metaphor is not evidence of authorship — only this particular formulation would be. I cannot place the formulation in a specific Gawain title. Note the text carries a bracketed editorial fix ('stomp[ing]'), suggesting it was transcribed from a secondary source rather than a book.

author: Shakti Gawain
text: The most positive and empowering way to relate to money is to let it be a teacher for you. Assume that whatever is happening in your financial reality is in some way a reflection of your internal process, something you can learn from, and something that can help you in your self-development.
keywords: money; teacher; learning; finances; reality; reflection; inner; process; self; help
notes: Subject matter points to Creating True Prosperity (1997), Gawain's book specifically about money and abundance, and the framing of money as a mirror of internal process is that book's core thesis. I cannot confirm the sentence appears there verbatim, so I am not asserting the citation. Attribution to Gawain is plausible and uncontested.

author: Shakti Gawain
text: The people we are in relationship with are always a mirror, reflecting our own beliefs, and simultaneously we are mirrors reflecting their beliefs. notes: The relationships-as-mirror teaching is a signature Gawain theme, developed at length in Living in the Light (1986), and the passage reads like continuous prose from a book rather than a manufactured aphorism — the internal ellipsis suggests it was excerpted from a longer paragraph. Attribution is credible on internal evidence; I cannot verify the source, so no citation is asserted.

author: Shalom Ormsby

I have no training knowledge of it, which is the expected result for an unpublished original and is not evidence against it. My tooling cannot validate first-party authorship, so the low confidence here reflects the limits of my method, not doubt about the claim. This one should be settled by human confirmation at review time rather than by provenance research; if the author confirms it, it can be promoted directly.

author: Sidney Madwed
text: Our subconscious minds have no sense of humor, play no jokes and cannot tell the difference between reality and an imagined thought or image. What we continually think about eventually will manifest in our lives.
notes: Sidney Madwed was a real motivational speaker and poet whose lines circulate widely on aggregator sites, and this one is consistently attributed to him, but I cannot place it in any book, article, or speech transcript I know of. The claim itself ('the subconscious cannot tell the difference between reality and imagination') is a stock New Thought / self-help proposition that predates Madwed by decades, so he may be restating rather than originating it. No citation available.

author: Sigmund Freud
text: Thought is action in rehearsal.
notes: The idea is genuinely Freud's: he described thinking as 'Probehandeln' — trial or experimental action — notably in 'Formulations on the Two Principles of Mental Functioning' (1911), where thought is characterized as experimental action carried out with small quantities of energy, and again in later work. 'Thought is action in rehearsal' is a compressed English aphorism of that concept rather than any translator's rendering I can point to in the Standard Edition. Attribution to Freud is sound at the level of idea; the exact wording is popularizer's phrasing, so I am holding this below the promotion bar.

author: Sir Isaac Newton
text: I do not know what I am to the world, but to myself, I am but a small boy, playing on the seashore, searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell, while before me lies the great ocean of truth.
keywords: sea; ocean; perfect; seashell; truth; world; boy; play
earliest_print_source: Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton, David Brewster, 1855
notes: Newton's seashore remark is well documented, but the corpus text is a loose paraphrase, not the recorded wording. The standard version: 'I do not know what I may appear to the world, but to myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the sea-shore, and diverting myself in now and then finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.' Recorded by Joseph Spence (Anecdotes, collected in Newton's lifetime, published 1820) and given wide currency by Brewster's 1855 Memoirs. 'Searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell' is a modern rewrite. High confidence Newton said something very close to this; low confidence in this specific text, hence attributed rather than verified. Strongly recommend replacing with the canonical wording.

author: Sir John Lubbock
text: When we have done our best, we should wait the result in peace.
notes: Consistently attributed to Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury) across quotation collections, and it is stylistically at home in his popular essay collections 'The Pleasures of Life' (1887) and 'The Use of Life' (1894). I believe it comes from one of those two, but I cannot state which with confidence, so I am not citing a source. Lubbock is not a misattribution magnet and the attribution is stable, which supports a moderate rating; the missing citation keeps it below the bar.

author: Sir Winston Churchill
text: Everyone stumbles over the truth from time to time, but most people pick themselves up and hurry off as though nothing ever happened.
notes: Churchill is a documented misattribution magnet and this line has no primary source I can identify in his speeches, books, or letters. It circulates in two forms: 'Men occasionally stumble over the truth...' (the older form, found in mid-20th-century Churchill anecdote compilations) and the later gender-neutral 'Everyone stumbles...' variant used here. Churchill quotation scholarship treats sayings of this kind that surface only in compiled anecdote books with suspicion. Plausible but unconfirmed; the corpus text is in any case the later rewritten variant, not the earliest attributed form.

author: Sir Winston Churchill
text: A lie gets halfway around the world before the truth has a chance to get its pants on.
earliest_print_source: The Examiner, No. 14, Jonathan Swift, 1710
notes: The Churchill attribution is spurious. This is a modern variant of a saying with a long documented pedigree: Jonathan Swift wrote 'Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it' in The Examiner (1710), and the 'boots' form — 'A lie will go round the world while truth is pulling its boots on' — circulated in the 19th century, commonly credited to the preacher C. H. Spurgeon, who himself presented it as an old saying. 'Pants on' is a 20th-century Americanized rewrite. Versions of this line are also misattributed to Mark Twain, another magnet. There is no evidence Churchill originated it. | Suggested reattribution: Jonathan Swift (1710, earliest documented form); the 'boots' variant is commonly credited to C. H. Spurgeon in the 19th century

author: Sogyal Rinpoche

notes: The two-selves passage — the garrulous, demanding, hysterical, calculating ego versus the hidden spiritual being whose still voice of wisdom is rarely heard — is characteristic of and, to my knowledge, drawn from 'The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying' (1992). I am confident about the book but not about chapter or page, and the corpus text appears spliced: the closing clause ('you have uncovered in yourself your own wise guide') does not grammatically follow the preceding sentence and looks like material lifted from further down the same passage. Recommend re-checking against the book and repairing the ellipsis before promotion.

author: Soren Kierkegaard

notes: I know of nothing in Kierkegaard's authorship resembling this, in any standard translation. The diction is modern therapeutic/mindfulness aphorism — the Gestalt 'paradoxical theory of change' register — not Kierkegaard's, whose treatment of becoming is far more elaborated and anguished. It reads like a coaching-literature line that acquired a prestigious name. I cannot identify the real originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but I would not promote this under Kierkegaard's name.

author: Sri Chinmoy
text: Each day beckons you to walk on the road of self-transcendence. When we transcend ourselves we do not compete with others, we compete only with our previous achievements. And each time we surpass our achievements, we get joy... Life is nothing but a perpetual possibility.
notes: Self-transcendence and 'competing only with yourself' were central, endlessly repeated themes of Sri Chinmoy's talks and writings, and the vocabulary here is authentically his. But he published hundreds of volumes of aphorisms and transcribed lectures, and I cannot locate this specific text in any of them; the ellipsis suggests it has been assembled from more than one sentence. Attribution is plausible and stylistically consistent, but uncited.

author: St. Francis de Sales
text: Never confuse your mistakes with your value as a human being. You're a perfectly valuable, creative, worthwhile person simply because you exist. And no amount of triumphs or tribulations can ever change that. Unconditional self acceptance is the core of a peaceful mind.
notes: Anachronistic. 'Unconditional self acceptance' is a term of art from Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, and the whole passage — separating mistakes from intrinsic worth, 'a peaceful mind' — is 20th-century cognitive-therapy and self-esteem language with no counterpart in the devotional writing of a 17th-century bishop. Francis de Sales wrote about gentleness toward one's own faults, which is probably why his name attached itself here, but his framing is theological (worth grounded in God), not psychological. I cannot identify who actually wrote this, so I am proposing no reattribution; Ellis is the likely conceptual source rather than a confirmed author.

author: St. Francis de Sales
text: When you encounter difficulties and contradictions, do not try to break them, but bend them with gentleness and time.
notes: This one is genuinely at home in Francis de Sales: gentleness in the face of difficulty, and the counsel to bend rather than break, are signatures of his spiritual direction in 'Introduction to the Devout Life' and his letters. It appears in Catholic devotional compilations of his sayings, usually paired with 'Do not lose your inner peace for anything whatsoever.' I cannot pin it to a specific letter or chapter, and translation-era English makes exact matching hard, so no citation. Moderate confidence, unlike q_1292 which I judge to be a modern fabrication under the same name.

author: St. Francis of Assisi
text: It's no use walking anywhere to preach anything unless our walking is our preaching.
notes: This belongs to the same apocryphal cluster as 'Preach the Gospel at all times; when necessary, use words' — a line Franciscan scholars have repeatedly shown is absent from Francis's writings and from the early biographies. The 'walking is our preaching' version derives from a later retelling of an anecdote about Francis walking through town with a companion, and appears in modern devotional literature rather than in any source contemporary with him. Not found in the Writings of Francis or in Celano/Bonaventure as far as I know.

author: St. Francis of Assisi
text: Start by doing what is necessary, then do what is possible, and suddenly you are doing the impossible.
notes: No evidence connects this to Francis of Assisi. It does not appear in his authenticated writings or in the early Franciscan biographies, and the earliest instances I am aware of are 20th-century, in motivational and recovery literature, where it circulated for some time before Francis's name was attached. The rhetorical shape — necessary, possible, impossible — is a modern three-beat inspirational construction. Widely repeated, which is not evidence.
